#5505. Chemours Launches Faizeon™ Two-Phase Liquid Cooling Solutions for AI Data Centers

New Faizeonâ¢ portfolio of two-phase direct-to-chip and immersion cooling fluids address rising AI heat loads with superior performance and reduced energy and water use

WILMINGTON, Del., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Chemours Company ("Chemours") (NYSE: CC), today launched Faizeonâ¢ two-phase liquid cooling solutions1, for artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing (HPC), and high-density data centers. The portfolio includes dielectric fluids engineered for both two-phase direct-to-chip and two-phase immersion cooling, giving data center operators and technology partners highly efficient options that can support evolving system architectures and remove heat from high-power processors and servers.

Faizeonâ¢ fluids use phase change, in which the fluid absorbs heat and changes from liquid to vapor, to enable efficient, reliable heat removal as AI and HPC drive higher chip power and rack densities. In independent third-party testing, a two-phase direct-to-chip system using Faizeonâ¢ 200 fluid maintained a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) at up to 19 degrees Celsius lower than a single-phase, water-based fluid, while using a lower coolant flow rate.

"AI's rapid growth is increasing the demands on data center infrastructure, and cooling is becoming a critical constraint," said Denise Dignam, President and CEO at Chemours. "With our liquid cooling solutions, we are applying more than 90 years of thermal management expertise to help data centers manage higher heat loads while improving performance and dramatically reducing energy and water demand. Our Faizeonâ¢ liquid cooling team is collaborating across the data center ecosystem, to bring together the expertise, testing, and support needed to confidently deploy two-phase liquid cooling at scale."

Faizeonâ¢ two-phase liquid cooling fluids for direct-to-chip and immersion cooling:

To support continued innovation and accelerated adoption of advanced liquid cooling technologies, Chemours has collaborated across the data center ecosystem to help advance the adoption of two-phase liquid cooling technologies. These efforts include engagements with the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), NTT DATA, 2CRSi, DataVolt, Munters, Accelsius, and ZutaCore. Learn more at Faizeon.com.

Through our three businesses â Thermal & Specialized Solutions, Titanium Technologies, and Advanced Performance Materials â we deliver application expertise and chemistry-based innovations that solve customers' biggest challenges. Our flagship products are sold under prominent brands such as Opteonâ¢, Freonâ¢, Ti-Pureâ¢, Nafionâ¢, Teflonâ¢, Vitonâ¢, and Krytoxâ¢. Headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware and listed on the NYSE under the symbol CC, Chemours has approximately 5,700 employees and 28 manufacturing sites and serves approximately 2,400 customers in approximately 110 countries. #5504. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5503. Introducing the 2026 Tech Trendsetters

HousingWire’s 2026 Tech Trendsetters award recognizes 75 technology leaders advancing the housing industry through artificial intelligence, automation, data intelligence and digital innovation. Now in its eighth year, the program honors individuals whose leadership and execution are helping organizations improve efficiency, make smarter decisions and deliver better experiences for housing professionals and consumers.  AI Summary

Today, HousingWire announced the 2026 Tech Trendsetters, recognizing 75 technology leaders whose innovation, leadership and execution are advancing the housing industry. Now in its eighth year, the Tech Trendsetters award honors the people developing, improving and implementing the technology transforming how housing professionals work and serve their customers.

“The 2026 Tech Trendsetters are turning today’s most promising technologies into practical solutions for the housing industry,” said Sarah Wheeler, Editor in Chief at HousingWire. “Their leadership is helping organizations work more efficiently, make smarter decisions and deliver better experiences for housing professionals and consumers. We’re proud to recognize the people setting a new standard for technology and innovation across housing.”

This year’s honorees represent organizations across mortgage lending, servicing, real estate, capital markets and housing technology. Their work spans artificial intelligence, automation, data intelligence, digital lending, property technology, risk management and customer experience.

These leaders are turning emerging technologies into practical solutions that deliver measurable results. Through new platforms, smarter workflows and more connected systems, they are helping housing organizations operate more efficiently, make better-informed decisions and create stronger experiences for professionals and consumers.

“This year’s Tech Trendsetters represent the very best of housing innovation,” said Clayton Collins, CEO of HousingWire. “In a period of economic headwinds and rapid technology evolution, these leaders are turning AI, data and digital innovation into real business and consumer outcomes. Their work is making the housing industry more efficient, more connected and better prepared for what’s next, and we’re proud to recognize them.”

#5502. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5500. Could Social Security turmoil influence senior homeowners and reverse mortgage demand?

A 13% surge in early Social Security retirement claims in 2024–2025, driven by political and administrative turmoil at the agency, temporarily reversed a long-term trend of Americans claiming later. Early filing locks in permanently lower benefits, cutting annual income by thousands of dollars for some retirees. Although claim volumes have since normalized, ongoing uncertainty about Social Security’s 2032 funding cliff is pushing some near-retirees to claim sooner.  AI Summary

A sharp but temporary spike in early Social Security claims in 2024 and 2025 underscores a potential trend for the housing market — a greater number of older Americans who are locking in permanently lower retirement income in response to political and administrative uncertainty.

Over the weekend, The New York Times followed up on a report shared last year by HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD). The initial report from the Times found that from October 2024 to April 2025, retirement claims jumped by 267,000, or 13%, compared with the prior year.

Historically, year-over-year fluctuations have been closer to 2% to 3%. Analysts at the Urban Institute and the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College tied the spike to highly publicized turmoil at the Social Security Administration — including staff cuts, office-closure threats and political rhetoric questioning the program’s solvency.

Social Security claims made before the full retirement age (which is now 67 for those born in 1960 or later) permanently reduces monthly benefits. This week, the Times interviewed two claimants — one who gave up about $5,000 a year by filing at 64 and another who sacrificed about $300 a month by filing more than a year early.

These kinds of benefit cuts compound over time and can directly affect housing affordability, especially for owners or renters whose largest fixed expense is their mortgage or rent payment.

As it relates to housing professionals, including reverse mortgage professionals, lower guaranteed income in retirement can translate into a higher likelihood of mortgage payment stress or default among senior homeowners. It can also propel demand for downsizing, shared housing options or migration to lower-cost markets as retirees adjust to tighter budgets.

Additionally, it can mean increased interest for traditional reverse mortgages and similar home equity release products to backfill income gaps. Borrowers in their late 50s and early 60s may be ideally positioned for these products since Social Security filing decisions are imminent, and because seniors are denied for credit at higher rates than the general population.

From October 2025 to April 2026, new claims fell by 235,000, or 10%, essentially offsetting the prior-year surge. But the reporting shows how headlines about Social Security’s finances can directly change claimants’ behavior.

A Boston College experiment cited by the Times this week found that more alarmist headlines led people to say they would claim about a year earlier than those who saw neutral language — regardless of any changes to the underlying facts.

Without congressional action, Social Security’s retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted by late 2032, triggering an automatic benefit cut of up to 22% under current law. The ongoing uncertainty has made Americans in retirement and near retirement “anxious and unhappy,” according to a source who spoke to the Times. This can impact retirement timing, where they choose to live and how much home they can afford.

Multiple policy ideas are circulating on the Social Security front — including bipartisan proposals to lift or eliminate the current $184,500 cap on wages subject to payroll tax, which could inject about $3 trillion into the system over 10 years. But for now, reverse mortgage companies and other housing stakeholders should pay close attention to how Social Security claiming decisions interact with mortgage terms, home equity levels and long-term retirement planning.

In this week’s Monday Morning Q&A, Larissa Morrell of Longbridge Financial told RMD that the demographics of the typical borrower have shifted during her 20-plus years in the industry.

“Historically, a reverse mortgage was really something for people of the older retiree demographic — late 70s, 80s, 90s. Now we do not have that same demographic. Now we’re looking at people of a younger generation. They’re still working. They might be using a reverse mortgage to pay off credit card debt or cover increasing expenses,” Morrell said.

Federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages and proprietary reverse mortgages could allow a borrower to delay Social Security claims by generating additional cash flow or eliminating monthly mortgage payments.

The Social Security Administration notes that people who begin receiving benefits at the full retirement age of 67 get 100% of the monthly benefit. But that percentage increases for every month payments are delayed and can reach up to 124% if a recipients waits until age 70 to make a claim.

But the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has also previously reported that the costs of a reverse mortgage generally exceed the additional increase in benefits that a senior would get by delaying claims.

#5499. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5498. Hippocratic AI Unveils Polaris 6 Ultra, the First Healthcare Model With Bedside Intuition, Built on Real-Life Experience, With Lower Pricing

Larger model brings new advancements to healthcare AI: Reads the patient and plans its next sentence while speaking, more realistic voice with clinical hearing. Ran 7.4-trillion-parameter safety constellation 1.3 times faster than its predecessor

MENLO PARK, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hippocratic AI today announced Polaris 6 Ultra, a new generation of its healthcare language model that delivers six upgrades to how an AI care agent listens, thinks, and speaks. Polaris 6 Ultra is the first healthcare model with what the company calls bedside intuition: the ability to read a patient's emotional state, think mid-speech and decide what to say next in the same breath, without a pause the patient can hear.

"In healthcare, you don't get credit for reminding a patient. You get credit for the action they take," said Munjal Shah, Co-Founder and CEO of Hippocratic AI. "Polaris 6.0 was built from more than 323 million patient conversations, making it the only truly experienced frontier model for healthcare able to operate safely and autonomously to drive patient outcomes. That experience shows. Polaris 6.0 handles the healthcare edge cases of real life, it now has more human-like common sense and pacing, and it delivers the kind of empathy that persuades patients."

General-purpose models aren't built to address healthcare edge cases, or handle the realities of patient care. Traditional LLMs expect clean audio, reason before they speak, know only what is written down, read every line in one tone, and get slower as they get smarter. That doesn't work for healthcare.

"Everyone building voice AI for healthcare trades off model size for latency: speech-to-speech models are fast and shallow, reasoning models are capable and slow," said Subhabrata Mukherjee, Co-Founder and Chief Science Officer. "We refused that choice. We took the largest model that could be made safe and rebuilt the entire stack for voice, from the GPU numerics to the breath in the synthesized voice. Then, with full-parameter reinforcement learning at frontier scale, we gave Polaris 6 not just safety but common sense, intuition, and the warmth and realism of an experienced clinician."

With increased EHR integration and new flexible pricing, Polaris can now meet the needs of any healthcare client. Polaris 6.0 ships as Ultra (full constellation, all 31 supervisors, for clinical patient-facing conversations), Pro (sub-clinical workloads), Flash (high volume, subclinical), and Nano [administrative use cases], so customers can match coverage and speed to their specific needs.

Polaris 6 Ultra closes all six gaps at once:

Across generations, the clinician-measured safety of the Polaris constellation has held at its ceiling since Polaris 4; with the latest constellation, the minor-harm rate in clinician output testing retains 0.00%. What has moved is the part patients feel: how natural, how perceptive, and how fast the agent is. Polaris 6 Ultra ships under the same criterion as every Polaris release: clinically tested, validated by licensed clinicians, and governed under human oversight before it reaches a patient.

Hippocratic AI builds and deploys safe conversational voice AI agents that address healthcare's biggest problems with a mission to transform patient outcomes through healthcare abundance. Built on Polaris, the company's patented, safety tested constellation model, Hippocratic AI's agents have completed more than 250 million patient voice interactions across more than 300 live clinical use cases, with zero safety issues in production. Hippocratic AI has received a total of $444 million in funding and is backed by leading investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst, Kleiner Perkins, Avenir, NVIDIA's NVentures, Premji Invest, SV Angel, Google's CapitalG, and numerous health systems. Hippocratic AI stands behind its safety promise â its contracts allow the company to take responsibility for its agents. Founded on the principle "do no harm," the company's agents do not diagnose or prescribe. Learn more at hippocraticai.com.

#5497. Open Real Estate gets a boost from independents — and an opening from MLSs

Open Real Estate said it has secured 826 letters of support from brokerage leaders nationwide, including 493 from independent firms. Several MLS executives publicly welcomed dialogue, positioning the effort as complementary to existing MLS infrastructure.  AI Summary

A week after Open Real Estate, a broker-led initiative to build a shared infrastructure for residential listing data, launched, the initiative announced that it has secured 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders across the country.

Independent firms account for the majority of that backing, with 493 letters, or 59%, coming from independent brokerages, according to an announcement on Monday. Support spans single-office independents to some of the largest independent firms, including Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

The effort is designed as a national, shared data layer that connects brokerages, agents, multiple listing services and real estate portals. Founding organizations include AGNT Inc. (parent to eXp Realty and NextHome), HomeServices of America, Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

“We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founding members of Open Real Estate said in a joint statement.

Open Real Estate’s backers say the project is meant to complement, not replace, existing MLS organizations by expanding access to listing information for brokerages, agents and consumers.

Several prominent MLS executives publicly welcomed collaboration with the initiative.

“We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Brian Donnellan, the president and CEO of Bright MLS and a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement.

Art Carter, CEO of California Regional MLS (CRMLS), added that the effort aligns with CRMLS’s long-running work to give brokers more flexibility in how they input and manage listing data.

“Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform. It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability,” Carter, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.”

North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS) CEO Chris Carrillo framed Open Real Estate as part of a broader conversation about transparency and equal access to listings.

“NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” Carrillo said.

And NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain emphasized that broker-driven projects can coexist with MLSs.

“Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” Dain, also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.”

The push for a shared listing data infrastructure comes as the industry adapts to rapid changes in how listings are distributed and displayed, ongoing antitrust scrutiny and shifting brokerage business models. Brokerages are looking for more direct control over how their listing data flows to MLSs, portals, internal systems and third-party tools.

Open Real Estate’s founders position the initiative as a way to streamline listing distribution, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace, particularly as consumer expectations for transparent, real-time listing information continue to rise.

#5496. Canton Network and DTCC Bring $30T in Securities to Blockchain

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Canton Network and DTCC are bringing Wall Street closer to blockchain, with $30 trillion in eligible securities now available for tokenization. The launch puts tokenized stocks, exchange-traded funds, and U.S. Treasuries within reach of institutional investors through blockchain infrastructure.

All Systems standby.DTCC × Canton Network.⏱️ pic.twitter.com/ZSI2f3pnWl

This marks a significant step for real-world asset tokenization. DTCC, which sits at the heart of U.S. securities markets, is connecting traditional financial assets with digital infrastructure while retaining existing custody arrangements and investor protections.

Twenty financial firms have signed up to access the service, including JPMorgan, Citi and Morgan Stanley.

The DTCC tokenization service allows eligible participants to create digital representations of securities held at The Depository Trust Company. Registered wallets can transfer these representations around the clock, opening the door to more flexible collateral management and digital asset settlement. The securities remain within DTCC’s custody framework, while their tokenized representations can move through approved blockchain infrastructure.

DTCC’s launch brings those requirements into a live service, although its initial scope remains limited to eligible securities and registered participants.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Canton Network’s progress shows a much larger opportunity: financial assets are becoming increasingly compatible with blockchain infrastructure, but the industry still needs networks capable of handling transactions quickly and affordably.

Bitcoin has the strongest brand and one of the most established security models in crypto. Its base layer, however, was never designed to provide the same high-throughput execution environment as modern smart-contract networks.

That creates an opening for Bitcoin Layer 2 projects seeking to combine Bitcoin’s monetary foundation with faster transactions and more flexible applications.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project pursuing that approach. Its architecture uses the Solana Virtual Machine to support high-throughput execution and near-instant transaction finality, while its design includes mechanisms for verifying Bitcoin activity and periodically committing Layer 2 state to Bitcoin’s base layer.

The ambition is straightforward: make Bitcoin more useful for payments, decentralized finance, and potentially tokenized assets without abandoning its underlying network.

Solana has demonstrated how fast blockchain execution can feel when transactions settle in fractions of a second. Bitcoin Hyper developers want to bring a similarly responsive experience to Bitcoin-based applications, potentially opening the door to financial products that would otherwise be impractical on the base layer.

For tokenization, that could eventually mean faster transfers, programmable collateral and markets that operate beyond traditional trading hours.

Bitcoin Hyper is drawing attention as its presale approaches the November 26 launch, having raised more than $33.2 million with tokens priced at just $0.0137 each. The project also offers staking rewards of up to 35% APY. With the presale window narrowing and the planned launch approaching, we have less time to enter at the current advertised price before the next stage.

Canton Network and DTCC are showing how established financial infrastructure can bring tokenization into real-world workflows. Bitcoin Layer 2 developers are tackling a different challenge: making Bitcoin more practical for applications that need speed, low transaction costs, and programmable execution.

For Bitcoin, the opportunity extends beyond holding value. A faster execution layer could help connect its established monetary network with a growing market for digital assets.

The challenge is preserving meaningful security guarantees while adding speed and functionality. Bitcoin’s base layer remains the foundation, but its next chapter could depend partly on what developers successfully build above it.

If tokenization becomes a defining feature of financial markets, the networks that combine usable transaction speeds with credible security and interoperability could have a much larger role to play.

#5495. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5494. With Agentic Studio, LinearB provides the critical context needed to accelerate software delivery

Application development intelligence startup LinearB Inc. said today it’s trying to ease the growing congestion in organization’s software delivery pipelines that has arisen with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence coding tools.

It’s doing so with Agentic Studio, a new offering announced today that’s focused on providing more actionable context for human engineers and autonomous coding agents alike.

The startup says the emergence of generative AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex has led to new headaches for enterprise software development teams. Though writing software code now can be basically effortless, shipping that code into production is still as painful as it has always been, and now they have much more of it to ship.

In its recent Software Engineering Benchmarks report, the company analyzed more than 2.7 million pull requests across 250 organizations and found that those who rely on AI coding tools have almost doubled their merged code changes year-over-year. But the problem is that AI-assisted pull requests are nearly 2.6 times larger, and consequently they’re waiting more than five times longer to be reviewed.

That has led to significant backlogs. And it’s compounded by the fact that AI agent’s proposed code changes are merged just 79% of the time at “elite organizations,” compared with 92% for human-authored code.

LinearB says that human software engineers struggle to clear this backlog because the traditional dashboards they’re forced to work with only provide metrics, rather than the context needed to resolve those pull requests. With Agentic Studio, it’s trying to address this by normalizing the data and insights generated by Git repositories and project tracking tools into a unified context layer. It means that instead of muddling through various charts to try and understand why release velocity has stalled, software engineers can ask questions in plain language to understand the root cause and receive recommendations on how to speed things up.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Ori Keren said context has become the new king, not only for AI tools but also for humans. “We realized we hold a knowledge graph that nobody else has of everything that is happening across the software delivery lifecycle,” he said. “That’s exactly what agents and teams need to deliver high quality software faster, so we rebuilt LinearB around it.”

What’s different about Agentic Studio is that it’s designed to help autonomous coding agents just as much as human software engineers, Keren said. By integrating through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, it feeds historical context such as rework rates, past production incidents and code ownership to AI agents, preventing them from making blind modifications to pull requests.

Early adopters have benefited from dramatically increased productivity with Agentic Studio. A case in point is the cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, which used LinearB’s MCP integration to pinpoint why its code reviews were lagging. It discovered that timezone misalignments were the main culprit rather than pull request sizes, and subsequently reorganized its workflows to cut its review times by more than half within just four months.

“For years, engineering leaders told us the same thing: metrics are useful, but they don’t tell you what to do,” said LinearB’s chief operating officer Dan Lines. “A dashboard says your cycle time is two days, but so what? Now [with Agentic Studio] a leader can ask what to improve in their engineering organization and get a clear answer. When that same context goes to coding agents, the platform is not just reporting, it’s acting.”

To help AI agents operationalize the context it provides, LinearB is developing a bunch of new agent skills. The first one, an “effort skill,” is available in early access now and analyzes the complexity of a pull request and its proposed code changes, its rework history and risk to calibrate dynamically how much computational effort a coding agent needs to expend as it works on it.

Simple, low-risk changes are done faster with minimal tokens. More sensitive, high-priority modifications will be implemented with deeper reasoning and more exhaustive testing to ensure nothing goes wrong.

LinearB said it’s planning to expand its agent skills library in the coming months with additional skills focused on automated code review, merge governance and token cost optimization.

#5492. Could dual licensing grow as agents, LOs seek revenue opportunities?

A RETR analysis identified 3,729 potential matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers, highlighting interest in dual licensing as professionals seek additional income. Shawn McNeil, a real estate broker and mortgage originator, said holding both licenses gives him greater control over clients' financing options and another source of revenue.  AI Summary

As mortgage companies and real estate brokerage look for additional revenue to combat difficult housing market conditions, dual licensing offers professionals a way to earn income through the tasks of selling a home and originating a mortgage.

A recently published analysis by RETR identified 3,729 matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers in which the agent’s top loan officer shared the agent’s name. California accounted for 40% of these matches, while the top four states (which also include Florida, Texas and Arizona) represented nearly 71% of dual-licensed professionals.

RETR used name matching to identify agents whose top-producing loan officer shared their name. But the analysis does not independently verify dual licensure, and it excludes professionals who hold both licenses but do not originate mortgages for their own clients or primarily work in one role.

For Shawn McNeil, the broker/owner of HomeFlo and a loan officer for Mpire Financial Group, the decision to pursue both licenses came from wanting more control over his clients’ financing options.

After nine years in real estate, McNeil obtained his MLO license about 18 months ago after what he described as feeling frustrated watching friends and high-value clients turn to large lenders and receive unfavorable interest rates.

“I would watch my big, high-dollar, personal friends go to these big-box retailers and just get absolutely crushed with an interest rate,” McNeil said in an interview with HousingWire. “I was like, at first, I’m going to go get licensed so that I can talk through these things and be knowledgeable in this.”

McNeil estimates that his time spent between real estate and loan originating is about 50/50, with most business coming from friends and real estate investors. He occasionally serves as both the agent and lender in a transaction, although he said that is not common.

McNeil believes more real estate agents will pursue MLO licenses as market conditions remain challenging and AI tools make it easier to research mortgage guidelines and loan requirements.

He said agents often hear that loan officers make good partners, but they may not fully understand the mortgage process or what makes a lender a good fit until they gain experience themselves.

“I think more agents are going to realize that the job on the loan officer side is getting easier from a guideline standpoint, and I think that they’re going to more and more convert to doing both over time,” McNeil said.

McNeil clarified that he does not originate every loan for clients who work with his brokerage. He refers borrowers to other lenders when his mortgage company cannot offer a particular program or when a loan falls outside his expertise.

Dual licensing also requires attention to compensation arrangements, the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA), state licensing rules and loan program restrictions.

McNeil said he worked with legal counsel to establish disclosures, which inform all brokerage clients that he is a licensed loan officer and owns the real estate brokerage, regardless of whether they use his mortgage services.

“We require 100% disclosure. … Even if you’re not using my services, we still disclose to you that I am a licensed loan officer and I own the real estate brokerage,” he said, adding that his clients receive the disclosures electronically before a transaction goes under contract.

RETR’s analysis does not establish whether dual licensing is becoming more common or how profitable the model is. But McNeil expects more agents to consider it as they look for additional income opportunities.

“I just hope that the trend continues and more and more realize that there’s a huge opportunity to do both,” he said.

#5491. Exclusive: Guardz brings Palo Alto Networks browser protection to MSPs serving small businesses

Cybersecurity startup Guardz Cyber Ltd. today added browser protection from Palo Alto Networks Inc.’s Prisma Browser for Business to its security platform for managed service providers that protect small businesses.

The integration is aimed at phishing attacks that slip between separate security tools. A typical one starts with an email that lures an employee to a counterfeit login page, and the credentials typed there can put connected accounts at risk. “For most small businesses, the browser is now the office,” said Shivam Srivastava, vice president of product at Palo Alto Networks.

Prisma Browser for Business can block the page when the link is clicked. Guardz then matches that browser event to the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity and endpoint telemetry for the same user identity. From there, the provider and Guardz’s 24/7 managed detection and response team can work the whole chain as a single incident.

The browser-side detection comes from Palo Alto Networks. Inline machine-learning models screen pages for phishing, and Advanced URL Filtering helps block malicious sites, including fake sign-in pages and attacks built to steal live session tokens. The company’s WildFire service analyzes suspect files. Uploads and downloads are scanned as they pass through the browser, which also picks out risky extensions.

Guardz Co-founder and Chief Executive Dor Eisner called the browser “the primary gateway to the modern workspace.” Traditional security tools work in silos that leave gaps in visibility and response, he said, and the agents running on Guardz’s platform are meant to let providers investigate threats autonomously anywhere in that workspace.

Setup falls to Guardz, which handles provisioning and default configuration. Kevin Kehoe of early-access provider Datawise Networks Inc. said the rollout through his firm’s remote monitoring and management software was “super smooth.” Within minutes, he said, the browser extension was “on every Chrome and Edge profile.”

For generative artificial intelligence services used in the browser, Guardz’s AI Usage and Control features let technicians set a separate policy for each client. Those policies can restrict copying, pasting and file transfers by website or by category. Guardz has also introduced a report that gives providers a per-client view of AI tool usage.

Palo Alto Networks moved into enterprise browsers with its 2023 acquisition of Israeli startup Talon Cyber Security Ltd. Prisma Browser for Business, its version for small businesses, went on sale in the U.S. in March.

Guardz is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $84 million, including a $56 million Series B round led by ClearSky in June 2025.

#5490. Real estate is moving toward more data privacy. Appraisers say UAD 3.6 is moving the other way

UAD 3.6 takes effect Monday, requiring appraisers to use dropdown selections that standardize property details sent to the GSEs. Appraisers are focused on Certification 25, which expands downstream rights to store, analyze, and distribute report data, including interior photos.  AI Summary

Monday marks the implementation date of UAD 3.6, which requires appraisers to select specific data points from dropdown menus for every feature of a property, as opposed to writing text descriptions of the home as they previously did, increasing the amount of detail included in appraisal reports delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Within UAD 3.6 is the new Certification 25, which has generated quite the buzz among appraisal professionals.

Certification 25, which was established by the government sponsored entities (GSEs), expands the data reuse beyond the parameters set in UAD 2.6, which included Certification 21, which largely governed who could receive or distribute a physical appraisal report.

Under Certification 25, entities that receive appraisal reports like lenders, GSEs, secondary market participants and data collection services to store, copy, reproduce, analyze, use and distribute all data within the report, including interior photos and property details, for internal or external purposes without needing the appraiser’s further consent.

While the certification does state that the appraiser and supervisory appraiser bear no liability for any use of the report outside of the specific mortgage finance transaction, appraisers are still concerned about this change and how it could impact their relationship with brokerages and real estate professionals.

In posts on social media and articles written on Appraisers Blog, Desiree Mehbod, a Virginia-based appraiser, has raised concerns about what would happen if interior photos of a child’s bedroom with the property address are leaked, reproduced and shared, ultimately ending up on the dark web.

But the ability for downstream actors to have access to data like this is not new. According to Frank Gregoire, a Florida-based appraiser, Certification 25 is fairly similar to the statute it is replacing, Certification 21.

“Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac maintain a proprietary database about every single dwelling that has ever had a loan on it,” Gregoire said. “So, the ability for downstream users to have access to that data has been there since these forms were introduced in the early 2000s. But, what is new is that it now specifies that the appraiser is aware that some parties may be using the data from their reports without their permission.”

While Ryan Lundquist agrees that this is the only primary change with Certification 25, he still finds it incredibly concerning.

“They can take the information and share it with whoever they want and the appraiser doesn’t have any control over that,” Lundquist, a Sacramento-based appraiser, said. “I know a lot of appraisers feel conflicted about that as it feels like it puts appraisers in a tough spot where a blank check to mine whatever data they want exists.”

Lundquist said he would love to know who this information will be shared with or sold to.

Gregoire is also concerned about appraisers including copyrighted data, such as images in the MLS in their report.

“If the appraiser is an MLS participant, they are using that information under license and they are permitted to use it to support their valuation, but that is it, they cannot grant someone else the right to use that information and that is what’s happening with Certification 25,” he said.

It is concerns like these that lead appraisers to say the discussion around Certification 25 is not over yet.

“I don’t think it will sit well with a lot of people in real estate when they read or begin to understand how and where this data may be used,” Lundquist said.

In addition, Mehbod said Certification 25  is why she and other like-minded appraisers have chosen to stop doing appraisal work for the GSEs. If a homebuyer wants their loan to close they have no choice but to allow the appraiser to generate a report, which Mehbod said will create “massive animosity right at the front door.”

“It positions the appraiser as a forced data collector rather than an independent expert,” she said. “This friction damages public trust and opens a legal minefield for our profession, leaving appraisers highly vulnerable to consumer complaints and lawsuits from angry borrowers when transactions get messy over data harvesting policies they never wanted to participate in.”

With UAD 3.6 just beginning to go into effect, it remains to be seen if anything regarding Certification 25 will change or how consumers and real estate brokers, agents and MLSs will respond.

#5488. A $20M fine stalks Los Angeles over delay of a new housing project

A letter warns Los Angeles it has 60 days to act on a 398-home plan in Woodland Hills. The attorney cites Housing Accountability Act exposure of at least $19.9 million in fines, plus attorney fees, costs, and potential compensatory damages.  AI Summary

Blocking a Los Angeles housing development over a mountain lion could cost the city $20 million or more and still fail to stop the project.

L.A. has 60 days to approve 398 homes at Woodland Hills Country Club or face a lawsuit that could cost it that much, according to a letter from the club’s attorney, Dave Rand, sent to the city Friday. A judge could order the city to pay punitive damages for the delay and rule that the development still must proceed, Rand confirmed with HousingWire TBD.

If the club prevails in its case for damages provided under the Housing Accountability Act, the city would owe fines of at least $19.9 million. It would also owe attorney’s fees, costs and compensatory damages.

The letter says that exposure “could therefore cost the city well in excess of $20 million.” Rand wrote that he can’t imagine the risk to taxpayers “is worth it.”

Rand wrote that the city’s denial violated both Assembly Bill 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act. The letter invokes AB 712, which extends any limitation period by 60 days from the letter’s date. That keeps the club’s legal options open while the city weighs its response.

Rand explained the fine math on social media. The base fine is $10,000 per unit for a violation, and $50,000 per unit for a finding of bad faith.

AB 712 raises the fine to an automatic $50,000 per unit if the city has lost in court at least once in the same housing element cycle. At $50,000 a unit, 398 homes come to the $19.9 million cited in the letter.

The letter includes a claim for damages, which follows an Oct. 23 ruling from the Second Appellate District. It held that a homeowner could seek damages when a city misses a mandatory permit deadline.

That case involved an accessory dwelling unit, not AB 2011. Legal scholars have said its reasoning could reach other ministerial housing laws, including the one Rand cites.

The state housing department has set a Nov. 25 deadline for Los Angeles to respond to its own letter. The department said it could refer the matter to the state attorney general.

Other California cities have backed down when the cost of continuing to dig their heels in became clear. Glendale’s council voted 4-1 last October to reject Trammell Crow Residential’s 682-unit plan for a former Sears store. The project included 72 very low-income units.

The state housing department issued a notice of violation Dec. 30. It warned of fines up to $34 million if the city did not reverse course. Glendale’s council reversed its denial in late January, three months after rejecting the project. No lawsuit was filed, but the developer’s attorney had called the case a “slam dunk” under the Housing Accountability Act.

Morgan Hill in Silicon Valley took a similar path. City officials settled with High Street Residential, a builder’s remedy developer, to avoid costly litigation with the developer and the state.

The 105-home project had been hanging in legal limbo for three years. The city council unanimously approved it last week.

#5487. MazeBolt launches native RADAR deployment for Akamai DDoS protection customers

Distributed denial-of-service testing company MazeBolt Technologies Ltd. today launched a native deployment of its RADAR validation platform for customers of Akamai Technologies Inc.

Enterprises using Akamai’s DDoS protection can have continuous testing running within hours without taking services offline. The release targets the configuration gaps that open up as a company adds services, application programming interfaces and regions behind its DDoS protection.

Akamai setups are rarely tested independently against each of those changes, according to MazeBolt, and a gap can stay hidden until an attack reaches a login page or a payment flow. Founder and Chief Executive Matthew Andriani said testing “even a few times a year cannot keep pace” now that artificial intelligence projects keep adding new services and APIs.

Akamai’s own State of the Internet report, published in March, found that Layer 7 DDoS attacks rose 104% over two years, and the company blamed part of that growth on attack tools that use AI to make web applications and APIs easier to hit.

RADAR fires simulated attacks at Akamai-protected services from inside the customer’s own environment. The attack library covers known vectors as well as the AI-orchestrated and AI-generated attacks MazeBolt added with its VectorAI module in June. When RADAR first tests a production environment, about 37% of attack vectors get past the protection already in place, based on MazeBolt’s data from initial deployments.

Each run ends in a report with remediation guidance written for the specific protection vendor, and RADAR repeats the test once a fix is in place. “Deployed protection is not proven protection,” said Eyal Rahimi, vice president of engineering at MazeBolt. Customers also need to be able to prove which gaps they have closed, Rahimi said.

Most financial institutions test far less often. In a MazeBolt survey of 300 of their security leaders last year, 86% said they test their DDoS defenses once a year or less. Akamai reported in May that the median duration of Layers 3 and 4 DDoS attacks on the sector has risen 738% since 2024.

John Grady, chief analyst at Omdia, said misconfigurations and out-of-date rules remain the source of many security incidents. “DDoS is no different,” Grady said. “It is a critical area where security teams must ensure protection is current, because successful attacks impact availability and directly affect the bottom line.”

Native Layer 7 support for Akamai environments is available today to all RADAR customers. Cloudflare Inc., F5 Inc. and Radware Ltd. are among the other mitigation vendors whose products RADAR already tests across scrubbing centers, on-premises equipment and cloud services.

#5486. Global Industrial Automation Market to Hit US$ 410.3 Billion by 2031, Registering 9% CAGR: Wissen Research

SHERIDAN, Wyo., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global industrial automation market is valued at USD 266.7 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 410.3 billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 9% over the forecast period (2026â2031), according to a new study by Wissen Research.

The clearest evidence is on the factory floor. The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) reports that factories installed a record 603,000 industrial robots in 2025, up 11% from the year before, and that the global operational stock reached 5.079 million units. IFR forecasts installations to rise another 9% in 2026, to approximately 655,000 units.

Behind the robots is a broader shift. The market is moving from hardware-oriented, isolated machine control toward connected, software-based production that combines control hardware, robotics, industrial software, and real-time analytics. Demand is driven by labor shortages, rising quality standards, and the need to control complex processes in automotive, electronics, food, and pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Get a Free Sample of This Report to Explore Key Findings and Data: https://www.wissenresearch.com/request-a-sample/?report=industrial-automation-market

Industrial AI Has Moved From Pilot Projects Into Live Operations

Cisco's 2026 State of Industrial AI study found that 61% of surveyed organizations were using AI in live industrial operations, and 83% planned to increase their AI spending. The use cases already delivering results are practical ones: predictive maintenance, process automation, automated quality inspection, logistics, and energy forecasting. Machine vision systems powered by AI can spot defects and abnormal conditions, and AI can adjust process parameters as production conditions change.

Getting there is harder than buying software. AI has to be integrated with industrial control systems, edge computing, and data platforms, which depends on good machine data, working IT and operational technology (OT) connections, and the state of legacy systems. In the same Cisco study, 97% of respondents expected AI workloads to affect their industrial network requirements, 51% anticipated higher connectivity and reliability requirements, and 43% reported limited or no collaboration between IT and OT teams. The report sees opportunities in industrial networking, edge devices, and real-time data infrastructure alongside conventional automation hardware, and in digital twins, which let companies test production changes virtually before implementing them.

For years, industrial robotics meant automotive welding and material handling. The IFR data show a broader base. In 2025, robot installations in metal and machinery grew 22%, while automotive and electronics installations each rose 10%. Collaborative robots (cobots) accounted for 66,000 new installations, about 11% of the total, and autonomous mobile robots are taking on internal transport. The growth is concentrated geographically: China installed about 354,000 robots in 2025, roughly 59% of the global total and 20% more than the year before, while India installed nearly 10,500, up 15%, with annual installations growing an average of 27% between 2020 and 2025.

The competitive map is shifting with it. Chinese robot manufacturers supplied 55% of the industrial robots installed in China in 2025, up from approximately 28% a decade earlier, intensifying competition for established international vendors.
