#5464. What to do after a tornado: 10 steps for safety and insurance claims

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What to do after a tornado, from avoiding downed power lines and gas leaks to documenting damage, filing insurance claims and applying for FEMA aid

A tornado can pass in minutes, but the danger it leaves behind lasts much longer. Downed power lines, leaking gas, weakened walls and debris full of nails turn a damaged neighborhood into a hazard zone well after the sirens stop. The choices people make in those first hours shape two things at once. One is whether everyone stays safe. The other is how smoothly the insurance and recovery process goes in the weeks that follow.

Knowing what to do after a tornado means thinking in two tracks. The first is physical safety. That starts with waiting for an official all-clear before leaving shelter. After that comes moving carefully through a changed landscape. Live wires, gas leaks, generator exhaust, unstable structures and cleanup injuries each carry their own risks. Each one calls for a specific response.

The second track is financial. Insurers and government agencies run on documentation. Photos taken before cleanup, a written inventory of damaged belongings, receipts for emergency repairs and a claim number from the insurer together form the record that supports a payout. Missing pieces can slow a claim or leave costs uncovered.

This guide walks through 10 steps in roughly the order most households face them. The early slides cover immediate safety. That means waiting for the all-clear, avoiding downed lines and handling gas and carbon monoxide risks. It also means judging whether a building is safe to enter and treating debris injuries. The later slides turn to paperwork and money. They explain how to document damage, file a homeowners insurance claim, make temporary repairs, claim additional living expenses, apply for help from FEMA and file for vehicle damage. The final slide covers protecting a household from contractor fraud and finding support for the emotional toll a disaster can take.

One caution applies throughout. Insurance policies are not uniform. Deductibles, coverage limits and filing deadlines vary by insurer, by policy and by state. Federal disaster aid for individuals depends on whether the president has issued a disaster declaration for the area. The guidance here describes how these systems generally work. The policy documents and the agencies involved have the final word on any individual claim.

Each step below stands on its own, so readers can jump straight to the part that matters most right now.

Stay in shelter until local officials or the National Weather Service say the threat has passed. More storm cells can follow a tornado. A quiet sky or a sudden drop in the wind does not mean the danger is over.

The National Weather Service issues tornado warnings for specific areas, and each warning carries an expiration time. A warning can be extended, or a new one issued, as another storm moves in. Local emergency management offices, broadcasters and weather radios pass these updates along. A battery-powered radio or a charged phone lets people in a basement or interior room follow the updates without stepping outside to look.

One storm system can produce more than one tornado over several hours. The calm right after a funnel passes can therefore mislead people. Leaving shelter too early can put someone in the open just as the next cell arrives.

Once officials confirm the threat has ended, dress for the debris before moving through the area. Sturdy, closed-toe shoes protect feet from broken glass, exposed nails and splintered wood. Long sleeves and long pants shield the skin from cuts and scrapes. Gloves make it safer to push aside branches, shingles or torn sheet metal.

As soon as it is safe to move around, check everyone nearby for injuries. That includes family members, neighbors and anyone else who was caught outside when the storm hit. Give first aid to people who are hurt, starting with the most serious problems, such as heavy bleeding or trouble breathing.

Call 911 for anyone with a serious injury. Phone networks can be overloaded after a storm. A text message sometimes goes through when a voice call does not.

Do not move a badly injured person unless they face immediate danger, such as a fire or a collapsing structure. Moving someone with a neck or back injury can make that injury worse. Report anyone who is trapped to emergency responders, who have the equipment to reach them safely.

Treat every power line a tornado has brought down as live, and keep well clear of it. Report it to the local electric utility or to emergency services.

That caution applies to any fallen line, whatever it looks like. A wire lying still on the ground calls for the same distance as one that is sparking or moving. Treating every line as live removes the need to guess.

The danger can extend beyond the wire itself. A line touching a fence, a car or standing water should be treated as live. So should the object it touches. That means staying off a fence with a cable draped across it. It also means staying out of any puddle or flooded patch where a line has landed.

A car with a line lying across it falls into the same category. Anyone outside the vehicle should keep away from it rather than approach to help.

Keeping clear also means leaving the line where it is. Do not try to move it or anything it is resting on. Keep children and pets back from the area as well.

The same rule holds on a walk through the neighborhood to check on others. A fallen line may sit beside a driveway, across a sidewalk or under debris. Choose a route that stays well away from it.

The call to the utility or emergency services is what gets a downed line dealt with. Crews need to know where a line is before they can make it safe. A useful report gives the location and says whether the line is touching a fence, a car or water. Until crews arrive, the line should still be treated as live.

A rotten-egg smell after a tornado can signal a natural gas leak. Anyone who notices it should leave the building at once, avoid switches and open flames, and call for help only after getting outside.

Utilities add that odor to natural gas on purpose. It is there so people can notice a leak. That makes the smell a signal to act, not a puzzle to solve. A household should not wait to see whether it fades or try to trace where it is coming from.

Getting out comes first. Everyone in the building should leave, without stopping to open cabinets, inspect appliances or attempt a repair. Distance from the structure is the goal, not a closer look at the problem.

Light switches and other electrical controls should be left alone on the way out. The same goes for matches, lighters, candles and stoves. A spark or flame inside a building filled with leaking gas can ignite it.

The phone call belongs outside as well. Once everyone is clear of the building, the leak can be reported to the gas utility or to emergency services.

Portable generators bring a separate danger: carbon monoxide in their exhaust. A generator must never run inside a home or inside a garage. That rule holds even when the power has been out for a long stretch and an enclosed spot seems more convenient.

The CDC advises keeping a generator at least 20 feet from the house. Its guidance also calls for placing the unit away from windows and doors. Those openings are where exhaust can find its way back indoors.

Both parts of the guidance apply at once. A generator set 20 feet from the house still falls short if it sits beside an open window. No distance from windows makes it acceptable to run a generator in a garage.

Stay out of any building with leaning walls, a sagging roof or a shifted foundation until a qualified inspector has cleared it. Any one of those three signs is enough to keep everyone outside.

A tornado can leave a house standing while damaging the parts that hold it up. A home that looks mostly intact from the street is not necessarily safe to walk into.

Leaning walls are the first warning sign. A wall that tilts instead of standing straight is reason to wait outside.

A sagging roof is the second. A roofline that dips or bows in the middle suggests the structure beneath it may not be sound.

A shifted foundation is the third. A house that appears to have moved on its base, or no longer lines up with where it stood before the storm, should be treated as unsafe.

When any of these signs is present, the whole building stays off limits, not only the room where the damage shows. That applies to family members, neighbors and anyone who arrives offering to help.

The decision on reentry belongs to a qualified inspector, not to the homeowner or a neighbor. Until that clearance comes, any look at the damage happens from outside the building.

Belongings, documents and keepsakes left inside can wait until the building has been cleared.

Puncture wounds from nails, splintered wood and other tornado debris are common during cleanup. The CDC recommends a tetanus booster after an injury if the last shot was more than 10 years ago.

A tornado leaves broken lumber, exposed nails, shattered glass and twisted sheet metal across yards and inside damaged rooms. Injuries can happen in the days after the storm, as people sort through that wreckage by hand. A nail pushed through a shoe sole or a cut from a jagged edge can seem minor at first.

Tetanus is a serious infection risk with these wounds. The bacteria that cause it live in soil and dirt. A deep, narrow puncture gives them a place to grow. A wound that looks clean on the surface can still carry that risk.

Anyone hurt during cleanup should find out when they last had a tetanus shot. A person who cannot remember the date, or whose last dose was more than a decade ago, is due for a booster. A doctor, an urgent care clinic or a local health department can give it. A deep or dirty wound can change that timing. Describing how the injury happened helps a provider decide whether a shot is needed sooner.

Clean any wound with soap and clean water, then cover it. Redness, swelling, warmth or pus around a wound are signs to get medical care.

Chainsaws bring a separate set of hazards. Cutting fallen trees and limbs puts a fast-moving blade close to the body, often on uneven ground. Branches bent under tension by the storm can spring back when cut. People without chainsaw experience can leave large trees to trained crews.

Ladders add their own risk. Climbing onto a damaged roof or reaching gutters from soft, debris-strewn ground makes a fall more likely. A second person holding the base and stable, level footing reduce that danger. Working alone with a ladder or a chainsaw means no one is nearby to call for help after an accident.

Before moving a single piece of debris, take dated photos and video of every room in the home and of the exterior. Then start a written list of damaged items. Together, these records show what the tornado left behind before anyone began cleaning up.

The order matters. Once a fallen branch is dragged off a roof or a soaked rug is hauled to the curb, that scene no longer exists. Pictures taken first capture the damage as it was, not as it looked after hours of sorting and clearing.

Dates are a central part of the record. A date ties each image to the period right after the storm. Many phones store the date and time inside each image file. Checking that the device's clock is set correctly before recording keeps those timestamps accurate.

Coverage should be complete. That means every room, including rooms that appear untouched. It also means the roof, siding, windows, fences and outbuildings, photographed from wherever they can be seen safely. Wide shots show where damage sits within a room. Close shots show the detail, such as a cracked window frame or a hole punched through drywall.

Video adds context that still images can miss. A slow walk-through lets the camera follow damage from one space into the next. Speaking while recording, to name each room and describe what is broken, turns the footage into a narrated record.

The written list does a different job. Photos show damage, but they do not always identify what an object was or where it came from. A list can name each damaged item, note the room it was in and describe its condition. Brand names, model details and approximate age can be added where they are known.

Keeping the photos, video and list together, with backup copies stored in more than one place, protects the record if a phone is lost or broken. Organized copies are also easier to share later with an insurer, a landlord or an aid agency.

Personal safety still comes first. Stepping near an unstable wall or climbing onto a debris pile for a better camera angle puts the photographer at risk.

A standard homeowners insurance policy generally covers wind damage, and that includes damage caused by a tornado. The first step is to call the insurer or agent promptly, get a claim number and ask whether the policy sets a proof-of-loss deadline.

Is tornado damage covered by homeowners insurance? Under most standard policies, it is. A tornado is a windstorm. The damage it does to a roof, siding or interior usually falls under the wind coverage in the policy.

Flood is a different matter. Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage. Covering it requires a separate policy, such as one written through the National Flood Insurance Program. A storm system that produces a tornado can also bring heavy rain. Where both wind and rising water hit the same property, the two kinds of damage may fall under different policies.

The deductible is the next detail to check. Some states and some policies apply a separate wind or hail deductible instead of the standard one. That deductible is often set as a percentage of the insured value of the dwelling, not as a flat dollar amount. A percentage deductible rises with the home's insured value. The owner's out-of-pocket share therefore depends on how much the home is insured for. The declarations page and the policy wording show which deductible applies.

The claim number issued on the first call becomes the reference for every later conversation, estimate and payment. Recording it alongside the date and the name of the representative keeps the claim file in order.

Proof-of-loss requirements are worth raising directly. A proof of loss is a formal statement of what was damaged and what it is worth. Some policies set a deadline for submitting it. Asking on the first call avoids learning about a deadline after it has passed.

None of these rules is universal. Coverage terms, deductibles and deadlines vary by insurer and by state. The policy itself sets the terms that apply to any one claim.

Homeowners insurance policies generally expect the owner to take reasonable steps to keep a tornado-damaged house from getting worse. Tarping a torn roof and boarding up broken windows are the standard examples. Receipts for that work belong with the claim.

The purpose is to limit what happens next. A roof with a hole or missing shingles leaves the rooms below open to the next rain. A shattered window exposes the interior to weather and leaves the house unsecured. A tarp or a sheet of plywood closes those openings until permanent repairs can be arranged.

The word reasonable carries weight here. These are stopgap measures meant to protect what remains, not a rebuild. What a policy counts as reasonable is set out in its own wording. That wording differs by insurer and by state.

Every purchase tied to emergency protection is worth keeping a record of. That includes tarps, plywood, nails and any labor paid for. Receipts show the insurer what was spent on protecting the property. Keeping them in one place, alongside the claim number, makes them simpler to hand over.

A separate part of many policies addresses where a household stays while the house cannot be lived in. This is additional living expense coverage, often called Coverage D. It applies when a home is unlivable. It is meant for costs such as hotel stays and meals.

The trigger is the condition of the home. A house that is damaged but still livable may not meet that test. The limit on this coverage also varies from policy to policy. The policy document is the place to confirm how much is available.

Hotel bills and meal receipts from the displacement period should be saved the same way as receipts for tarps and plywood. Not every policy includes Coverage D. A household that is unsure whether its policy does can ask the insurer or agent directly.

FEMA individual assistance opens to tornado survivors only after the president issues a disaster declaration for the affected area. Once that declaration is in place, households can apply online at DisasterAssistance.gov or by phone at 1-800-621-3362.

The declaration is the trigger for everything else. Without one, the federal individual assistance program is not available to residents, however heavy the local damage. County emergency management offices and local news outlets generally announce when a declaration has been made and which counties it covers.

The clock starts on the date of that declaration. The usual application window runs 60 days from that point. Applying early leaves more time to gather paperwork and respond to any follow-up requests before the window closes.

People who carry homeowners or renters insurance should file with their insurer first. Federal disaster aid is meant to help with needs that insurance does not cover. It does not replace a policy that already applies to the loss.

Cars, trucks and SUVs follow a separate path from the house. Tornado damage to a vehicle is typically handled under the comprehensive portion of an auto insurance policy, not under a homeowners policy. Comprehensive is the part of an auto policy that applies to damage from causes other than a collision with another vehicle or object.

A driver who carries only liability coverage is in a different position. Liability coverage pays for harm the driver causes to other people and their property. It generally does not pay to repair the driver's own car.

The auto claim should be opened as its own claim, even when the same company insures both the home and the vehicle. Auto deductibles and filing rules differ from one insurer and state to the next. Reading the auto policy's declarations page shows whether comprehensive coverage is in force and what deductible applies to it.

Before hiring anyone to repair tornado damage, check the contractor's license, get written estimates and a written contract, and do not pay the full amount upfront.

Storm-chasing contractors are crews that travel into areas hit by severe weather to look for work. Some knock on doors in the first days after a tornado. At that point, homeowners are under pressure to close up roofs and walls. A fast handshake deal leaves little room to confirm who is actually doing the work.

A license check is the first filter. Licensing rules for contractors differ from state to state. The agency that issues contractor licenses where the home sits can confirm whether a contractor holds one. A contractor who cannot give a license number is a reason to keep looking.

Written estimates let a homeowner compare bids for the same job. A verbal quote cannot be checked later, and it gives an insurance adjuster nothing to review. Collecting more than one estimate also shows whether a single bid is far out of line with the others.

The contract should be on paper before work begins. It should spell out what work will be done, what it will cost and when it will be finished. A signed document gives the homeowner something to point to if the job is left incomplete or the price changes.

Payment terms carry as much weight as the price. Paying the full amount before work starts removes the homeowner's leverage. If the contractor disappears or does poor work, that money may be gone. Paying in stages as work is completed keeps that leverage in place.

The emotional toll of a tornado is a separate part of recovery. Losing a home, belongings or a sense of safety can bring stress, grief and trouble sleeping in the weeks that follow. Those reactions can show up in adults and children alike.

One place to turn is the Disaster Distress Helpline. It is run by SAMHSA, the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. The helpline number is 1-800-985-5990.

#5463. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5462. Where to take shelter in a tornado, from storm cellars to roadside ditches

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Knowing where to take shelter in a tornado saves time when a warning hits, and these 10 options run from storm cellars to roadside ditches

A tornado shelter is only as useful as the plan that gets you into it. The safest spot depends on where a person happens to be when the sky turns — at home, at work, in a car or on foot. That choice has to be settled long before sirens sound. Minutes matter, and they are easier to spend moving than deciding.

That is the practical answer to the question of where to take shelter in a tornado: it changes with the setting. A family with an underground cellar faces a different decision than someone in a third-floor apartment, a shopper in a big-box store or a driver on an open highway. Each place has its own safest corner and its own common mistakes.

The guidance behind all of these settings rests on one principle. Get low, get inside and put as much solid material as possible between your body and the wind. Much of the danger in a tornado comes from what the wind carries. Shattered glass, lumber, roofing and other debris can travel at high speed. Earth, concrete and interior walls stop that debris. Windows, wide roofs and thin exterior walls do not.

The U.S. National Weather Service, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the American Red Cross publish safety advice built around that idea. Their recommendations line up on the basics. Go to the lowest level available. Choose a small interior space without windows. Protect the head and neck. Leave structures that cannot hold up to tornado-force winds before the storm arrives, rather than after.

Some popular advice runs the other way. Several long-repeated tips about where to stand or what to do inside a house are myths, and a few can cost time. Knowing which ones to ignore is part of being prepared.

This slideshow walks through 10 shelter options and situations. It starts with purpose-built spaces such as storm cellars, safe rooms and community shelters. It moves through ordinary homes, apartment buildings and large public buildings. It ends with the hardest cases: mobile homes, vehicles and open ground with no structure in sight.

Each slide covers one setting on its own. Readers can go straight to the place that matches their home, workplace or daily commute. A shelter plan made on a calm day is ready when a storm appears in the forecast.

An underground storm cellar, dug into the ground and set apart from the house, is among the safest places to wait out a tornado. The earth around it shields the people inside from the wind and from flying debris.

That protection comes from the cellar's design, not from the home nearby. A cellar sits below ground level. Wind moves across the top of it instead of striking tall walls head-on. The structure also stands apart from the house. Its safety does not depend on the home's walls, roof or floors staying intact. No upper story sits overhead that could come down on the people inside.

The separation has a cost. Reaching a detached cellar means going outdoors, crossing a yard and opening a door, often in rain, hail or strong wind. Shelter guidance from the U.S. National Weather Service, FEMA and the American Red Cross calls for getting to safety before a storm arrives. Once debris is already in the air, a short walk to the cellar becomes an exposed one.

After everyone is inside, the door should be latched from the inside. Wind can pull an unsecured door open. An open door also lets debris into the space. A secure latch keeps the entrance closed while the storm passes over.

Head protection still matters below ground. The entrance is the weak point of any cellar, and debris can strike near it. A bicycle or sports helmet adds a layer of cover. Thick blankets wrapped around the head and shoulders serve the same purpose when no helmet is at hand.

A cellar works best when it is ready before tornado season. That means a clear path from the house to the door. It also means a door that opens and latches without a struggle, and a floor free of clutter. A flashlight stored inside is useful. The space goes dark once the door shuts.

After the storm, debris from nearby buildings or trees can pile up on top of a cellar door. Family members or neighbors who know the cellar's location can check on anyone who sheltered there.

A safe room is a reinforced room or small structure built specifically to protect people from extreme winds. When it follows FEMA and ICC 500 standards, it is designed for winds of 250 mph. That makes it a purpose-built refuge rather than an ordinary room pressed into service.

Two documents define what counts as a safe room. FEMA publication P-361 sets out the design guidance. The ICC 500 standard, issued by the International Code Council, covers how storm shelters are constructed. Architects, engineers, builders and local code officials use the two together when planning a room.

The 250 mph design figure applies only to rooms built to these standards. A closet lined with extra drywall does not meet it. Neither does a prefabricated shelter with no documentation showing it follows the standards. Anyone buying or building a safe room can ask the builder or manufacturer to confirm in writing that the design follows P-361 and ICC 500.

A safe room can take two basic forms. One sits inside the house and is often built into a basement, an interior closet, a bathroom or a garage. The other stands alone as a separate small structure on the property. An in-home room can be reached without stepping outside during a storm. A standalone unit needs a short, clear path from the house that the household can cover quickly.

Either version depends on its connection to the ground. The room has to be properly anchored to its foundation so the structure stays in place under extreme wind. The walls, ceiling, door and anchoring are designed to work as one system. A room with strong walls but poor anchoring does not meet the standard.

A safe room also gives a household a fixed destination. Instead of choosing a room on the spot when a warning is issued, everyone already knows where to go. Keeping the path to the room clear of stored items saves time. So does making sure every member of the household, including children and regular guests, knows how to reach the room and close its door securely.

A public community shelter gives people a sturdy place to go during a tornado when their own home offers little protection. Some towns, schools, parks and manufactured-home communities maintain these shelters. The local emergency management office can tell residents where the nearest one is.

These shelters matter most for households without a basement, storm cellar or safe room. They also serve people who live in structures that cannot stand up to tornado winds. For those residents, the nearest public shelter may be the only purpose-built option within reach.

The first step is to find out whether one exists nearby. County or city emergency management offices keep track of public shelter locations. A phone call or a visit to the office's website can settle the question long before storm season begins. Not every community has a public shelter. In some places the answer will be no, and the household will need a different plan.

The location alone is not enough. Residents should also confirm when the shelter opens. Some public shelters are not staffed or unlocked around the clock. A shelter that is closed when a storm hits offers no protection. Finding that out at the door wastes time that cannot be recovered.

Other practical questions are worth asking in advance. Who opens the doors, and what triggers the opening? Are pets allowed? Is the building accessible for people who use wheelchairs or walkers? Rules on these points differ from one shelter to the next. The local emergency management office is the place to get answers.

Travel time is part of the plan as well. A shelter several miles away is useful only if the household can reach it before the storm arrives. Driving the route once in calm weather shows how long the trip actually takes, including stoplights and traffic.

The details belong in writing. A note on the refrigerator or a saved entry in each family member's phone keeps the plan from depending on one person's memory. That record should list the shelter's address, hours and route.

In a house with a basement, go down to the lowest level and move away from any windows. Get under a sturdy workbench, a heavy table or the staircase, and cover your head and neck.

A basement works as a tornado shelter because most of it sits below ground. Soil packed against the foundation walls helps block wind and debris that could punch through walls above grade. The floor overhead adds another layer between the people inside and the storm.

Basement windows are the weak point. Many basements have small windows set high in the wall or window wells at ground level. Glass in those openings can shatter, and debris can blow through the gap. The better position is along a wall or in a corner away from them, ideally in the part of the basement farthest from any window.

Overhead cover matters too. A sturdy workbench or heavy table acts as a shield against anything that drops from the ceiling. That can include ductwork, light fixtures or pieces of the floor above. The space under a basement staircase offers similar protection. The stair structure stands between the people beneath it and falling material.

What sits on the floor above should shape where you crouch. A piano, refrigerator, washing machine, chest freezer or other heavy appliance can crash through if a tornado damages the house and the floor gives way. Tornado guidance from the National Weather Service warns against sheltering directly beneath heavy objects like these. Noting where they stand before storm season makes it faster to pick a safe spot when a warning arrives.

Once in position, crouch low and use your arms and hands to cover your head and neck.

A little preparation shortens the trip downstairs. Keep the stairs and the route to the basement clear of boxes and clutter. Leave the space under the workbench, table or stairs empty so people can get into it without moving anything. A flashlight stored near that spot helps if the power goes out. Everyone in the household should know in advance which corner of the basement to use.

In a house without a basement, the safest choice is a small, windowless room on the lowest floor, such as a closet, bathroom or interior hallway. The aim is to put as many walls as possible between the people sheltering and the outside of the house.

Each wall acts as a separate barrier. Tornado winds carry branches, roof shingles, glass and pieces of other structures. That debris hits the exterior walls first. A room at the center of the house makes debris pass through several layers before it reaches anyone inside. A room along an outside wall gives up that buffer.

Windows are the weakest point in most homes. Glass can shatter from wind pressure or a debris strike. The broken shards then become projectiles. A room with no windows removes that hazard. That is why a center closet or a hall bathroom with no exterior glass is usually a better pick than a bedroom, even a large one.

Floor level matters too. In a two-story house, that means a closet or bathroom on the ground floor rather than one upstairs. If the only windowless space is a hallway, stay near its middle. Keep away from doors that open onto rooms with windows.

Padding adds another layer of protection. Pull a mattress over the group if there is time to drag one in. Pillows, couch cushions and thick blankets also help shield against falling debris and broken ceiling material.

Two pieces of older advice should be ignored. The first is to shelter in the southwest corner of the house. That idea rested on the assumption that debris would blow away from that side. It is a myth. Tornado winds rotate and shift. Debris can come from any direction.

The second is to open windows to equalize air pressure, on the theory that this keeps the house from bursting. That is also a myth. Wind and flying debris do the damage, not a pressure difference. Crossing the house to open windows wastes time that should go toward reaching shelter. It also puts people next to glass just as the storm arrives.

Picking the room ahead of time makes the move faster. A closet packed with boxes or a bathroom cluttered with stored items may not hold everyone. Clearing that floor space before storm season means a household can get in, close the door and get down without delay.

In an apartment or multistory building, the safest place during a tornado is an interior hallway or room on the lowest floor you can reach. Stay away from exterior walls and windows. Windows facing the storm can break, and the glass becomes part of the debris the wind carries.

Height adds risk. Upper floors face stronger winds than floors near the ground. A resident on the 12th floor is more exposed than a resident at street level. People who live high in a building should plan to move down when a tornado threatens instead of staying in their own unit.

The stairs are the way down. Elevators can stop if the power fails, and that can trap people between floors while the storm passes. An enclosed stairwell near the center of the building also keeps people away from windows while they descend.

Position within a floor also counts. Sometimes there is no time to reach the ground floor. In that case, a windowless corridor near the middle of the current floor offers more protection than a room along the outer edge. When the hallway itself is lined with windows, a small bathroom or closet in the center of the unit is the better choice.

Planning should happen well before a storm. Residents should ask the building manager whether there is a designated shelter area on the ground floor or below, such as a basement corridor or an interior room. It also helps to know which stairwell leads there and whether those doors stay unlocked.

Shoes are part of the plan. Sturdy, closed-toe shoes protect feet from broken glass, nails and other debris in hallways and stairwells. They also help if residents have to leave the building on foot after the storm, possibly in the dark if the power is out.

Time is a factor in tall buildings. Walking down many flights of stairs takes minutes, not seconds. Residents with limited mobility, young children or pets need even longer. They should start moving to the lower floor as soon as a threat develops.

In a school, office, hospital, mall or large store, follow the building's tornado plan and go to its designated shelter area. That area is usually an interior hallway or room on the lowest level.

Large public buildings are laid out differently from houses. Many people inside them do not know the floor plan well. They depend on a plan someone else has already prepared. Staff who know that plan can direct visitors, students and patients who do not. Following those directions saves the time it would take to hunt for a hiding spot in an unfamiliar building.

Rooms with wide-span roofs are the places to stay out of. Gymnasiums, auditoriums and cafeterias have large roofs that are more likely to fail in a tornado. Those roofs stretch across a broad open space with few or no interior supports. If the wind lifts or breaks part of the structure, no inner walls stand in the way of debris falling on the people below.

Schools face this risk directly. Many have a gym, an auditorium and a cafeteria in the same building. Each of these rooms can hold a large group at once. Moving students out of them and into lower-level interior hallways puts shorter roof spans overhead and more walls between them and the outside.

In multistory offices and hospitals, the designated area is usually an interior corridor or room on a lower floor. It should be away from windows, glass doors and glass-walled lobbies. Elevators are a poor choice once a tornado threatens. The power can fail and leave people trapped between floors.

In large retail stores, the place to go is the designated shelter area, not the open sales floor. A sales floor sits under the same kind of wide roof as a gym. It is also lined with tall shelving and stacked merchandise that can topple or turn into debris. Malls add skylights, glass storefronts and open atriums. All of them can shatter and send glass across the space below.

Anyone who spends regular time in one of these buildings can find out where its shelter area is on an ordinary day. That way the route is already familiar when a tornado threatens.

A mobile or manufactured home is not a safe place to ride out a tornado, even when it is tied down. The safer move is to leave before the storm arrives and go to a sturdy building or community shelter chosen in advance.

Guidance from the National Weather Service, FEMA and the American Red Cross is consistent on this point. Tie-downs and anchors do not turn a manufactured home into a tornado shelter. No space inside one offers the protection of an interior room in a sturdy building. That includes the bathroom, the hallway and the closet.

That fact changes the whole plan. People in a sturdy house can wait for a warning and move to a lower floor or an inner room. People in a mobile home have to travel somewhere else, and travel takes time. The destination has to be chosen on a calm day, not in the middle of a storm.

A workable plan names a specific place. It might be a relative's house with a basement or a neighbor's sturdy home. It might also be a public building that opens as a shelter, or a shelter run by the manufactured-home community itself. Households should know the route and how long the trip takes. They should also decide who is responsible for getting children, older relatives and pets out the door.

Timing depends on knowing the difference between two alerts. A tornado watch means conditions are favorable for tornadoes in and near the watch area. A tornado warning means a tornado has been seen or indicated by weather radar. For people in a mobile home, the watch is the signal to get ready to move. If a watch is in effect and a shelter is nearby, the guidance is to go then. Waiting for a warning may leave only minutes to make the trip.

Acting on a watch requires hearing about it promptly. A NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts National Weather Service alerts directly. Models with an alarm feature can sound when an alert is issued. Emergency alerts turned on in a mobile phone add a second way to get the message. Having both matters most during nighttime storms, when a household may be asleep as a watch goes into effect.

A car, truck or SUV is not a safe place to ride out a tornado. Tornado winds can lift or toss a vehicle, and the metal shell does little to stop flying debris.

A driver's best option depends on how much distance separates the car from the storm. If the tornado is far enough away to reach a sturdy building safely, drive there and go inside. The target is a solid structure such as a store, school or office. A carport or open canopy does not count. Once inside, head to the lowest floor and an interior space away from glass.

That judgment has limits. A tornado's distance and direction are hard to gauge from behind a windshield. Heavy rain and hail can hide a funnel entirely. At night, darkness can do the same. Tornadoes can also change direction. A driver who cannot see the storm clearly should not assume there is time to spare.

Do not try to outrun a tornado through traffic. Congested roads, stoplights and other drivers making sudden decisions can leave a car stuck in place as the storm closes in. A vehicle that cannot move offers the same weak protection as a parked one, with the added risk of collisions on every side.

Advance planning gives drivers more options. People who travel regularly through tornado-prone areas can note sturdy buildings along familiar roads before storm season begins. On days when severe weather is in the forecast, a driver can also check conditions before a long trip and delay it if storms are expected along the route.

If flying debris arrives and no building is within reach, the National Weather Service describes staying in the vehicle as a last resort. Pull over out of the traffic lanes. Keep the seat belt fastened. Lower the head below the level of the windows and shield it with a coat or cushion if one is handy.

Anyone caught outdoors with no sturdy building or shelter within reach should find a ditch or other low spot, lie flat and cover the head and neck with both hands. The U.S. National Weather Service presents this as a last resort, not a plan.

A ditch offers far less protection than a cellar, a basement or an interior room. It fits a narrow situation. A tornado is close, there is no time to get indoors, and standing in the open is the only other choice.

The reasoning comes down to height. Wind and flying debris do their damage above ground level. The lower a person lies, the less of the body is exposed to objects in the air. A roadside ditch, a ravine or a dip in a field can all work. Lying face down with the hands clasped over the back of the head and neck shields the area where an injury can be most serious.

Flooding is the second hazard to watch. The thunderstorms that produce tornadoes often bring heavy rain. Ditches and low ground are where that water drains. A spot that is already holding water or carrying a fast current is not a safe place to lie down. Watch for rising water and move if it starts to collect.

A highway overpass is not a substitute for a ditch. The NWS advises against sheltering beneath one. The gap under a bridge can funnel wind and debris through a narrow space. The concrete deck overhead does nothing to stop objects flying in from the side. A person who stops there gains no real protection and may also block traffic for others trying to reach safety.

Trees and other tall objects are poor places to be near as well. Power poles, signs and large branches can snap or topple in strong winds. Anything that falls lands on whoever is beneath it. Moving away from them toward open, low ground lowers that risk.

None of these steps makes the open a safe place to ride out a tornado. They are ways to reduce exposure when every better option has run out.

#5461. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

#5460. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

The pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.
