#5459. Tornado watch vs. warning vs. emergency: what each alert means and what to do

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tornado watch vs. warning vs. emergency: a guide to what each National Weather Service alert means, where to shelter and what to do before and after a tornado

The difference between a tornado watch and a tornado warning comes down to one question: has a tornado formed yet? A watch means the atmosphere could produce one. A warning means one is happening now or is about to. A tornado emergency means a severe, confirmed tornado is moving into a populated area.

Each step up adds certainty and leaves less time to act. That is why the labels matter. Treating a warning like a watch costs minutes that should go toward reaching shelter. Treating a watch like a warning skips the preparation a watch exists to allow.

In the U.S., the system belongs to the National Weather Service, part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The Storm Prediction Center in Norman, Oklahoma, issues tornado watches. Those watches usually span many counties and last several hours. Local National Weather Service forecast offices issue tornado warnings for a much smaller area. A warning rests on a tornado spotted by observers or one indicated by radar. The same local offices add tornado emergency wording to a warning when a catastrophic threat to life exists. That wording is not a separate tier of alert. It is language inside a warning that marks an extreme, immediate danger to people in the storm's path.

The tornado watch vs. warning distinction is only part of the picture. Each alert also calls for a different response. A watch is time to prepare by reviewing the plan, charging phones and confirming where to shelter. A warning means moving to that shelter right away. A tornado emergency means the threat is direct. Protecting the head and neck in the safest available spot comes first.

Alerts travel through several channels. Wireless Emergency Alerts push warnings to phones in the affected area. NOAA Weather Radio, TV and local radio carry them as well. Outdoor sirens are meant for people outside and may not be heard indoors.

The 10 slides below cover what each alert means, who issues it, what to do during a watch and a warning, and where to shelter at home. They also explain why mobile homes, cars and highway overpasses fail as shelter, how alerts arrive and what to do once the storm has passed.

A tornado watch means atmospheric conditions over a region favor the development of tornadoes. It does not mean a tornado has been spotted or detected on radar. It signals that the ingredients are in place and that storms forming in the area could produce one.

The word "watch" describes possibility, not an event under way. A tornado that is occurring or imminent triggers a different alert, the tornado warning. A watch can stay in effect from start to finish without any tornado forming inside it.

The conditions behind a watch follow a familiar pattern. Tornadoes typically come from thunderstorms that form in warm, moist, unstable air. Winds that change speed and direction with height, known as wind shear, can make those storms rotate. A thunderstorm with a persistent rotating updraft is called a supercell. Supercells produce many of the strongest tornadoes. A trigger such as a cold front or a dry line can set the storms off. When forecasters see these factors lining up, a watch goes out.

A tornado watch covers a broad area. The counties it lists can cross state lines. Its timeframe is also long, covering the hours when storms are expected to develop. That scale reflects the limits of forecasting at this stage. Meteorologists can identify a region at risk well before they can say which town, if any, a tornado will reach.

A watch is not fixed once it is issued. It can be extended in time, expanded to more counties or canceled early as the forecast changes.

The sky under a watch may look calm. Watches are often issued before storms have formed at all. Clear or partly cloudy conditions at the moment a watch appears do not mean the threat has passed.

A tornado watch also points to a broader severe weather risk. Storms in the watch area can bring large hail and damaging straight-line winds even if no tornado forms. A separate product, the severe thunderstorm watch, is used when those hazards are expected but tornadoes are considered less likely.

Tornadoes can also develop outside any watch area. A tornado warning can be issued for a place with no watch in effect.

Some tornado watches carry the phrase "particularly dangerous situation." That wording flags an unusually high risk of strong, long-lived tornadoes within the watch area.

A tornado warning means a tornado is happening now or is about to happen in the warned area. Anyone in the storm's path should take shelter immediately.

A warning marks the point where preparation ends and action begins. A watch asks people to get ready and keep monitoring. A warning asks them to move. It points to a specific storm that is producing a tornado or close to producing one.

Forecasters issue a warning based on one of two kinds of evidence. The first is a sighting, such as a report from a trained storm spotter, a local emergency official or a member of the public. The second is radar indication. In that case, Doppler radar shows rotation in a storm that suggests a tornado is forming or already on the ground.

Dual-polarization radar can also pick up debris lofted into the air by a tornado. That signature indicates a tornado is already on the ground and causing damage, even if no one has seen it.

Warning text states which basis applies. It labels the tornado as either radar indicated or observed. It also typically gives the storm's location, its direction and speed of movement, and the towns in its path.

Both kinds call for the same response. A radar-indicated warning does not signal a smaller threat. Heavy rain or darkness can hide a tornado from view. Radar may detect one before anyone can see it. Waiting for visual confirmation uses up time that could be spent reaching shelter.

The area under a warning is drawn around the storm itself. The National Weather Service outlines a polygon covering the storm's current position and its expected track. People inside that shape face the threat. People in the same county but outside the polygon may not be under the warning.

Each warning is tied to a particular storm and carries a set expiration time. It can be canceled early if the storm weakens or moves away. A new warning can follow if the same storm or another one threatens the area again. Between those points, forecasters issue severe weather statements that update the warning, and these can trim the warned area as the storm passes.

A tornado emergency is enhanced wording that the National Weather Service adds to a tornado warning in the gravest cases. It is used when a severe, confirmed tornado is moving into a populated area and poses a catastrophic threat to life.

The phrase does not create a separate alert category. A tornado emergency sits inside a tornado warning and is not a third rung above it. What changes is the language of the alert. That language tells people the danger has moved from serious to potentially catastrophic.

The local NWS forecast office covering the area at risk makes that call. It is the same office that issued the warning in the first place. The NWS is part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The decision to use the stronger wording does not come from a national center.

Two conditions sit at the center of the decision. The first is confirmation. A standard warning can rest on radar indication alone, when forecasters see a storm signature that suggests a tornado. A tornado emergency requires a severe tornado that is confirmed, not just suspected. The second condition is location. The tornado must be moving into a populated area, such as a city or town, where many people are in its path.

For anyone under one, the message is direct. The threat is real, close and severe. There is no time to wait for more information, step outside to look or check with a neighbor. The response is to reach the strongest shelter available at once and protect the head and neck.

The wording can also change how the alert arrives. A tornado emergency can trigger a more urgent phone alert than a standard tornado warning. That stronger notification sets the situation apart from a routine warning.

Knowing the term ahead of time saves time later. A person who hears "tornado emergency" for the first time during a storm may lose seconds working out what it means. A person who already knows it signals a confirmed, severe tornado headed toward a populated place can act on it right away.

The Storm Prediction Center in Norman, Oklahoma, issues tornado watches for the U.S. Local National Weather Service forecast offices issue tornado warnings. Those local offices also decide when a warning carries tornado emergency wording.

Both alerts come out of the same system. The National Weather Service, or NWS, is part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the federal agency abbreviated as NOAA. The Storm Prediction Center is one of the national centers within the weather service. The local forecast offices are spread across the country. Each one is responsible for its own group of counties.

The division of labor follows the scale of the threat. A watch is a regional judgment that the atmosphere is primed for tornadoes. A national center that monitors the whole country is suited to spotting where those broad conditions are lining up. Before a watch goes out, the Storm Prediction Center coordinates with the local offices in the affected area.

A warning is a storm-scale call. It responds to a specific storm that has produced a tornado or appears about to. Local forecasters track individual storms across their own territory. That focus on a limited territory lets them outline a warning around the communities in a particular storm's path.

One person can be under both alerts at once. The watch comes from the national center in Norman. The warning comes from the forecast office responsible for that person's county. That office also produces the routine daily forecasts for the same area.

A third label enters the picture later, and it is separate from every alert. Tornado strength is rated on the Enhanced Fujita scale, which runs from EF0 to EF5. That rating is assigned after the tornado has passed, based on the damage it left behind. NWS survey teams examine the damage to set the rating. Watches, warnings and tornado emergencies are not tied to an EF number.

A tornado watch is the time to prepare, not to take shelter. Review your household plan, charge your phone and confirm where you will take cover. Then keep checking the forecast. If a warning follows, you will need to move quickly.

No tornado has to exist when a watch is issued. A watch gives a household time to get organized before any storm is close.

Start with the plan itself. Everyone in the household needs to know which room or space they will go to and how to get there. Walk through the route once, especially with children or guests who may not know the layout of the home. Decide in advance who will help anyone with limited mobility and who will bring the pets. Settling those questions during a watch means nobody has to work them out after a warning is issued.

Charge phones, tablets and any backup battery packs. A tornado can knock out electricity. A charged phone remains a way to receive alerts, check on family and call for help afterward. A flashlight with working batteries belongs in or near the shelter space for the same reason.

Make sure the shelter location is ready to use. A basement or storage room that is cluttered or locked can slow people down when there is little time. Clearing a path to it during a watch removes that problem before it matters.

Keep monitoring conditions. The weather during a watch can change, and a warning may be issued for part of the watch area. Follow local forecasts and keep phone alerts switched on rather than silenced.

For people who live in mobile homes, a watch is the signal to leave for a sturdy building or designated shelter before storms arrive.

Stay ready to move on short notice. Keep shoes on or nearby. Keep keys and essential medications within reach. Hold off on plans that would be hard to interrupt, such as a long drive toward the storms.

When a tornado warning covers your area, go to a basement or storm cellar. If the home has neither, move to a small interior room without windows on the lowest floor, such as a bathroom or closet, and stay away from exterior walls.

The order of those choices follows a single idea: put as much of the building as possible between you and the storm. A basement or storm cellar sits below ground level, out of the direct path of the wind and the debris it carries. That is why the National Weather Service lists it as the first choice.

Many houses have no basement. In that case, the lowest floor is the next option. Upper stories stand higher and are more exposed to the wind. Moving downstairs reduces that exposure before the tornado arrives.

The room chosen on that floor is the next decision. An interior room is surrounded by other parts of the house rather than sharing a wall with the outdoors. Every wall between you and the outside is another barrier that debris has to get through. In many homes, a bathroom or a closet near the center of the floor fits that description.

Windows are the hazard to avoid. Glass can break under the force of the wind or the impact of flying objects. The broken pieces can then be thrown across a room. A space with no windows removes that danger. Exterior walls carry a related risk. They face the wind and anything it picks up before the rest of the house does.

Reaching the right room is only part of the protection. Once there, cover your head and neck, the parts of the body where an injury from falling or flying debris can do the most harm. A mattress pulled over the people sheltering offers a wide, padded layer. A helmet, such as one used for biking or other sports, shields the head directly. Heavy blankets serve as cover when nothing else is at hand.

Stay in the shelter room until the warning ends or local officials say the threat has passed.

Mobile homes and vehicles do not provide safe shelter during a tornado, even when a mobile home is tied down. Anyone in either should move to a sturdy building or a designated storm shelter before the storm arrives.

A mobile home is built to be light enough to transport. That design leaves it with little mass to resist tornado winds. Tie-downs help anchor a unit to the ground. They still do not make a mobile home safe in a tornado. Residents should plan to leave rather than wait out a storm inside.

Timing matters more for mobile home residents than for most people. Someone in a house with a basement can wait for a warning and then walk downstairs. Someone in a mobile home has to travel to reach protection. By the time a warning is issued, a tornado is already occurring or imminent. The safer moment to go is when a tornado watch is issued. At that stage, conditions favor tornadoes, but no tornado is bearing down on the area.

That move works only if the destination is chosen ahead of time. Options include a friend or relative's house with a basement, a community storm shelter or a sturdy public building. Some mobile home communities have their own designated shelter. Residents can ask the park manager whether one exists and how to get inside. Knowing the route and the length of the trip removes guesswork on a stormy day.

A car or truck carries similar risks. A vehicle's thin metal body and glass windows offer little protection from flying debris. Tornado winds can also lift, roll or toss a vehicle. Sitting inside one is not a form of shelter, however solid the vehicle feels.

Drivers who learn of a tornado warning should get into a sturdy building as quickly as they safely can. On a day when a tornado watch is in effect, checking the forecast before a trip makes it easier to postpone travel. It also gives drivers a chance to plan stops near solid structures along the way.

A highway overpass is not a safe place to wait out a tornado. The National Weather Service advises against sheltering beneath one. Wind and flying debris can be concentrated there.

From the driver's seat, a concrete span can look solid, and on many stretches of highway it is the only structure in sight. A deck overhead, however, is not the same as walls on every side.

The space under an overpass is open at both ends. That opening can channel wind through the gap beneath the deck. Nothing stands between a person there and the debris a tornado throws through the air, such as broken wood, sheet metal and glass. Walls block that debris, and an overpass has none around the space beneath it.

Getting into that space often means climbing a sloped embankment toward the underside of the deck. That moves a person higher off the ground rather than lower. Wind speeds generally increase with height above the ground. Tornado shelter guidance points the other way, toward the lowest available level.

A stopped car creates a second problem. Vehicles pulled over beneath a bridge can block lanes that other drivers need to escape the storm. They can also block emergency crews once it has passed.

For anyone caught outdoors with no sturdy building in reach, the National Weather Service describes one fallback. It is a last resort. Lie flat in a ditch or other low spot. Cover your head with your arms or anything sturdy at hand.

A low spot reduces exposure to wind and debris passing overhead. It does not match the protection of a basement or interior room. That is why it ranks at the bottom of the options.

When a tornado is close and no building is within reach, the goal is the lowest ground nearby. A raised concrete span is the opposite of that.

Tornado warnings reach the public through several channels at once. Phones, weather radios, broadcast stations and outdoor sirens each carry the same alert in a different way. Each one has gaps the others can cover.

Wireless Emergency Alerts send a short message to compatible phones in the warned area. The message arrives with a distinctive tone and vibration. Delivery depends on where the phone is, not where its owner lives. A driver passing through a warned county can receive the alert. A resident traveling elsewhere will not get one for their home county. No app or sign-up is needed.

A phone alert only works if the phone is powered on and within range of a cell network. Phone settings also let users switch off some categories of emergency alerts. Anyone relying on a phone during storm season should check that those alerts are turned on.

NOAA Weather Radio is a network of stations, operated by NOAA, that broadcasts National Weather Service forecasts and warnings around the clock. Dedicated receivers can sound an alarm when a warning is issued. That alarm can wake a household overnight, when a phone may be silenced or out of reach. Many receivers let owners program the specific county they want alerts for. That setting cuts down on alarms for storms elsewhere in the region. Many receivers also run on batteries if the power fails.

Television and local radio stations relay warnings as well, frequently with maps or descriptions of the storm's location and direction. That context helps people judge where a storm is heading relative to their own neighborhood. A short phone message cannot carry the same level of detail.

Outdoor warning sirens serve a narrower purpose. They are meant to alert people who are outside — at a park, on a farm or at a sports field — to get indoors and seek more information. Sirens are owned and activated by local governments rather than the National Weather Service. Testing schedules and activation rules differ from one community to the next.

Sirens are not designed to be heard inside a home. Closed windows, running appliances and the noise of the storm itself can drown them out. The absence of a siren does not mean no warning is in effect.

Each channel can fail in its own way. A dead battery, a dropped signal or a power outage that knocks out the television can each cut off one source. Keeping at least two channels active lowers the chance that a single failure leaves a household without notice.

After a tornado passes, stay clear of downed power lines, wear sturdy shoes against broken glass and debris, and check everyone for injuries. Call 911 for emergencies, and send texts rather than calls for everything else.

The period right after a storm carries its own hazards. Damage that could not be seen from a shelter becomes visible only when people step outside. Much of it sits at ground level or hangs overhead.

Downed power lines are a major hazard. A line lying across a yard, a fence or a puddle can still carry current, and there is no reliable way to tell by looking at it. Treat every fallen wire as live. Keep well away from it, and keep children and pets back too. Report it to the local utility, or to 911 if it poses an immediate danger.

Broken glass, splintered wood, exposed nails and torn sheet metal often cover the ground after a tornado. Sturdy, closed-toe shoes or boots offer protection that sandals or bare feet cannot. Long sleeves, long pants and work gloves add another layer for anyone moving through debris.

Check for injuries before looking at property damage. Look over everyone in the household first. Then check on neighbors if it is safe to reach them. A person who seems fine at first may have cuts or other injuries that become apparent later. For serious injuries, call 911.

Phone networks can come under heavy strain after a major storm, as many people try to reach family at the same time. A text message uses less network capacity than a voice call. It can sometimes go through when a call fails. Texting relatives leaves voice lines open for people trying to reach emergency services.

Gas leaks are another risk once the wind dies down. A tornado can damage gas lines inside and outside a building. If you smell gas, do not light matches, candles or lighters, and avoid any open flame. Leave the building and report the leak to the gas utility or 911 from a safe distance. A battery-powered flashlight is a safer light source in the dark than a candle.

Damaged buildings can also shift or collapse after the storm has passed. Stay out of any structure with visible structural damage until local officials say it is safe to enter.

#5458. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

— Lattice Semiconductor, a Hillsboro, Ore.-based company, has added two directors to its board:

Editor’s note: Story updated Nov. 2 with information from Helen Chiang’s LinkedIn post.

Hiring elite engineers or proven revenue leaders in 2026?

Great teams still win, and finding them is harder than ever. That’s why GeekWire teamed up with Prime Team Partners on GeekWork, a hiring initiative built to help companies connect with exceptional talent.

Prime Team Partners blends AI-powered recruiting with deep human expertise. GeekWire brings unmatched reach across the tech community. Together, we help employers cut through the noise and hire smarter, faster.

#5457. What to do in a tornado, and 10 common beliefs to drop before a warning

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tornado myths debunked, from opening windows to sheltering under highway overpasses — 10 common beliefs that waste precious minutes or put people in danger when a storm hits

A tornado rarely gives anyone much time to think. The decisions people make in the minutes before it arrives often come from habits learned years earlier, from a parent, a teacher or a post shared online. Some of those habits are sound. Others are folklore that can cost time or steer people toward the wrong place.

Flying debris is the leading cause of tornado deaths and injuries, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That single fact undercuts several popular beliefs. Opening windows, choosing a particular corner of the basement or sheltering under a highway overpass all assume a different kind of threat. Each one either wastes the seconds people need to reach shelter or leaves them exposed to wind-driven objects. Mobile homes and cars pose a related problem. Neither offers reliable protection from tornado winds.

Other myths concern geography. Many people assume rivers, hills or big cities offer protection, or that tornadoes belong mainly to the Great Plains. The historical record says otherwise. Tornadoes have been recorded in all 50 states and in every month of the year. They have crossed rivers, climbed into mountains and torn through downtown districts.

A third group of myths concerns judgment. People try to size up a tornado by how it looks, decide a weak one poses little risk, or wait for a siren before moving. Ratings on the Enhanced Fujita Scale are assigned after a storm, based on the damage it left. Low-rated tornadoes still produce winds strong enough to turn debris into projectiles. Outdoor sirens are designed for people outside. A tornado can also be hidden by rain or darkness.

This guide to tornado myths debunked covers 10 beliefs that circulate widely in the U.S. It is a selection, not a complete catalog. Each slide states the correction first, then explains what the NWS and the storm record show instead. The aim is to settle what to do in a tornado, and what to skip, before a warning is ever issued.

Opening windows will not keep a house from bursting as a tornado passes. Homes fail because of extreme wind and the debris it carries. The minutes spent at a window are better used getting to shelter.

The myth rests on a real piece of science. Air pressure inside a tornado's core is lower than the air around it. The old reasoning held that a sealed house would keep its normal pressure while the storm's low pressure passed overhead. In this telling, the difference would push the walls and roof outward until the building exploded.

The explanation sounds tidy, but it does not match what happens to buildings. Damage surveys after tornadoes show structures torn apart by wind forces acting on roofs, walls and the connections between them. Flying debris then punches through whatever the wind has not already broken. A pressure difference is not what brings a house down.

An open window can also work against the structure. When wind pushes into a building through an opening on the side facing the storm, pressure builds inside. That trapped air adds to the lifting force on the roof from below. This internal pressure is why a broken window or open garage door matters in high winds.

The larger danger is to the person doing the opening. Windows are the most fragile part of a house's outer shell. In a tornado, glass can shatter into fast-moving shards with almost no warning. Anyone standing beside a window is in the spot where injuries from broken glass and airborne debris are most likely.

Time is the other cost. A tornado warning may leave only minutes before a storm arrives. Walking from room to room to open windows uses up part of that margin. If a tornado hits the house directly, debris is likely to break the windows regardless.

The National Weather Service (NWS) advises against opening windows and tells people to stay away from them. The next step is to head straight for a basement, storm shelter or interior room on the lowest floor.

No corner of a basement is reliably safer than another during a tornado. What protects you is solid cover overhead and shielding for your head and neck.

The southwest-corner advice grew out of a pattern in U.S. storms. Many tornadoes in the U.S. travel from the southwest toward the northeast. The reasoning held that a house struck from that direction would throw its walls and wreckage toward the far side. The southwest corner, in theory, would stay clear.

That logic fails in several places. Tornadoes do not always follow a southwest-to-northeast track. They can approach from the northwest, the south or other directions. Some also shift course along their path. Someone heading to one fixed corner has no way of knowing which way a particular storm is moving.

The wind inside a tornado also rotates. As the vortex passes over a house, the damaging wind can strike from one direction and then from others within seconds. Walls and floors can give way on any side of the structure. The resulting debris does not land in a predictable pattern.

In a basement, the main danger usually comes from above. When a house is torn apart, the floor overhead can collapse. Heavy objects on that floor can fall through with it. The National Weather Service advises people sheltering in a basement to avoid spots directly beneath heavy items upstairs, such as a piano or refrigerator.

The practical goal is to put something solid between your body and anything that falls. A heavy workbench or sturdy table can absorb the impact of collapsing material. A mattress, sleeping bag or thick blanket adds another layer against smaller debris. Crouching low and covering your head and neck with your arms guards against the injuries most likely to be fatal. A bicycle or sports helmet offers further protection for the head.

An underground storm shelter or safe room offers more protection than an ordinary basement. Homes with neither a shelter nor a basement still have a reasonable option. The next choice is a small interior room on the lowest floor, such as a closet, bathroom or hallway. The more walls between you and the outside, the better.

A highway overpass is not a tornado shelter, and the National Weather Service (NWS) tells people not to use one. The span gives little protection from flying debris and leaves anyone beneath it exposed to the storm.

The belief spread after a 1991 video showed a television news crew sheltering under a Kansas Turnpike overpass as a tornado passed. The crew survived, and the footage was replayed for years. It did not show what a direct hit from a strong tornado would do to people in the same spot.

A bridge deck blocks only what falls from above. Tornado winds move sideways and rotate around the storm's center. Boards, broken glass, sheet metal and gravel can fly horizontally into the open space under the span. Nothing about the structure stops them.

The shape of an overpass can make conditions worse. The gap beneath the deck can channel the wind and speed it up as air is forced through the opening. A spot that looks sheltered on a calm day can become one of the windiest places on the road.

Many people who stop under an overpass climb the sloped embankment toward the girders to get out of the rain. That move lifts them higher off the ground. Friction with the surface slows wind near ground level. Wind speeds tend to increase with height. The climb puts a person into stronger winds and greater exposure to debris.

The design of overpasses also varies widely. Some have a narrow ledge under the girders. Many have no crawl space at all, only a solid wall or an open shoulder. A driver who pulls over expecting cover may find none.

Stopped vehicles create a separate danger. Cars and trucks parked in travel lanes block traffic. That can trap other drivers in the tornado's path and delay emergency crews trying to reach the area afterward. Parked vehicles can also be struck by traffic moving at highway speed through heavy rain and poor visibility.

No river, valley, hill or mountain range protects a town from a tornado. Local terrain is never a reason to put off taking shelter.

The belief takes many local forms. Some towns hold that a nearby river splits storms apart. Others trust a ridge, a bluff or a valley floor to steer a funnel away. A town that goes years without a direct hit can come to credit its landscape for what was chance.

The historical record does not support these ideas. The Tri-State tornado of March 18, 1925, began in Missouri and tracked through Illinois into Indiana. Along the way, it crossed the Mississippi River at the Missouri–Illinois line and the Wabash River at the Illinois–Indiana line. Its recorded path ran about 219 miles.

The tornado killed 695 people, the highest toll of any tornado in U.S. history. Neither river broke up the storm or shielded the communities on the far bank.

Mountains offer no guarantee either. On July 21, 1987, a tornado struck the high country of northwest Wyoming. It is known as the Teton–Yellowstone tornado, after the area it crossed. The storm cut through remote, forested wilderness at elevations where many people assume tornadoes cannot form.

Tornadoes are far less common in mountainous terrain than on the Plains. Less common is not the same as impossible. The Wyoming storm shows that rugged, high ground does not rule a tornado out.

A tornado forms beneath a thunderstorm that can tower thousands of feet above the ground. A riverbank or hillside is small by comparison. Neither one cuts the storm off from the energy that feeds it.

The practical response is the same in every setting. When a tornado warning is issued, people in a river valley, on a hilltop or in the mountains should move to shelter right away. Waiting to see whether geography intervenes costs time that a fast-moving storm does not give back.

Cities offer no built-in protection from tornadoes. Urban neighborhoods, suburbs and downtown business districts in the U.S. have all taken direct hits, some of them deadly.

The Joplin, Missouri, tornado of May 22, 2011, shows how deadly a city strike can be. Rated EF5, the highest category on the Enhanced Fujita Scale, it tore through the city and killed 158 people.

Downtown cores have been struck as well. A tornado crossed downtown Nashville, Tennessee's capital, on March 3, 2020. It arrived in the early-morning hours, when many residents were asleep.

Moore, Oklahoma, a suburb south of Oklahoma City, shows that the same community can be hit more than once. Violent tornadoes struck Moore in 1999 and again in 2013.

The belief that cities are protected often rests on a misreading of the record. Built-up areas cover a small share of the land in tornado-prone states. Most tornadoes therefore pass over farmland, forest or open country. That makes urban strikes less frequent, not impossible. Whether a particular block is hit comes down largely to chance.

Tall buildings do not shield a downtown either. A tornado is the lower end of a rotating column connected to a thunderstorm that towers far above any building. A cluster of high-rises is small by comparison and does not break up or steer the circulation.

When a tornado does reach a city, density works against residents. More buildings mean more material that can be torn loose and thrown. Large panes of glass on office towers and storefronts can shatter into the streets below.

For people caught downtown, the National Weather Service advises getting to an interior hallway or stairwell on the lowest floor of a sturdy building. Large open-span rooms such as auditoriums, gyms and big-box stores are poor choices. Their wide roofs are more prone to collapse. Lobbies and atriums walled with glass are also places to leave quickly.

Every U.S. state has recorded at least one tornado. Living outside Tornado Alley does not mean living outside tornado risk.

"Tornado Alley" is an informal name for a stretch of the Great Plains where tornadoes are frequent. It has no official borders, and different maps include different states. Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska are the states most often placed inside it. The label describes a loose region, not a line that storms respect.

The trouble with the name is what it suggests about everywhere else. A household in Georgia or Ohio may treat tornado planning as something meant for people elsewhere. That assumption can slow the response when a warning arrives.

The Southeast is the clearest counterexample. The region, sometimes called Dixie Alley, sees a large number of tornadoes. Mississippi, Alabama and Tennessee are among the states most often associated with that name. The April 2011 Super Outbreak, centered on April 27, tore across Alabama, Mississippi and Tennessee. Tuscaloosa and Birmingham were among the cities struck.

Southeastern tornadoes can carry hazards that open-country storms often do not. Some strike at night, when people are asleep and less likely to notice a warning. Dense trees and rolling hills also block the view of the sky. A tornado that might be visible for miles across flat prairie can stay hidden until it is close.

Timing is another part of the myth. Spring is the peak tornado season in the U.S., but the risk does not end when spring does. On the night of December 10, 2021, a violent tornado struck Mayfield, Kentucky. That town sits far from the Plains, and the storm came months past the spring peak. A household that stops paying attention once spring ends is relying on the calendar instead of the forecast.

The correction applies in every part of the country. Local forecasts and warnings, not a regional nickname, are the measure of risk on a given day. A tornado warning in Pennsylvania calls for the same urgency as a warning in Oklahoma.

A car is not a dependable escape from a tornado. Some tornadoes travel faster than 60 mph, roads can quickly become blocked, and a vehicle offers little protection once the wind arrives.

The myth rests on an idea that sounds reasonable. Cars are fast, and many tornadoes move at a modest pace. The problem is that forward speed varies widely from storm to storm. One tornado may crawl along. Another may cross open country at highway speed. A driver has no reliable way to tell which kind is approaching.

Direction is just as hard to judge from behind the wheel. Tornadoes can shift course, and a storm's track may cut across the very road a driver planned to use. A funnel that looks distant can be closer than it appears. The parent thunderstorm often brings heavy rain and hail as well. That combination limits how far a driver can see and how well tires grip the pavement.

Roads add another set of problems. Many drivers may try to leave at the same moment once a warning is issued, and highways can jam fast. A car stuck in traffic sits in the open, with no way forward and no shelter nearby. Downed trees, power lines and wreckage can also close a route ahead of the storm.

Vehicles themselves offer limited protection. Tornado winds can roll, lift or throw a car. Flying debris can shatter windows and enter the cabin. A car's thin metal shell is not built to withstand the forces that tear apart well-built houses.

The safer approach is to avoid ending up on the road at all. A tornado watch is a cue to delay a trip or plan a route that passes sturdy public buildings. When a warning arrives and a solid structure is close, such as a store, school or office building, the National Weather Service (NWS) advises driving there and getting inside.

Drivers caught with no building in reach face only poor options. Guidance on what to do in that situation has changed over the years, and no choice is considered safe. Every remaining option carries a serious risk of injury.

A mobile or manufactured home offers little protection from a tornado, even when tie-downs anchor it. The National Weather Service (NWS) advises residents to leave for a sturdy building or storm shelter before the storm arrives.

The belief that tie-downs make a mobile home safe comes from what they are built to do. Straps and ground anchors help keep a home from sliding or overturning in strong wind. That protection has limits. A tornado can tear the structure apart around its anchors or pull the anchors out of the ground.

Manufactured homes use lighter materials than most site-built houses. Their walls and roofs give the wind a large surface to push against. Once the shell fails, there is no interior room or lower floor left to retreat to. Anyone inside is then exposed to the same flying debris that broke the home apart.

That makes timing the central issue for mobile home residents. Sheltering in place is not a workable option. The decision to move has to come early. Waiting until a tornado is visible or close leaves too little time to reach a safer building.

Planning ahead closes that gap. Some mobile home parks have a community storm shelter. Residents can ask park management where it is and when it opens. Other households arrange to go to a relative's or neighbor's house with a basement, or to a nearby public building. Knowing the route in advance saves minutes on the day of a storm.

A ditch is the fallback when no sturdy building can be reached in time. It is a last resort, not a safe place. The NWS advises lying flat in a nearby ditch or low spot and covering your head with your hands. Getting below the level of the surrounding ground reduces exposure to some flying debris.

Ditches carry their own risks. Heavy rain from the same storm can flood them quickly. Debris can still land on a person lying in one. Choosing a spot away from trees, vehicles and the mobile home itself limits what can fall or roll on top of you.

A tornado rated EF0 or EF1 is not a harmless tornado. The lowest rating on the Enhanced Fujita Scale still covers estimated winds of 65 to 85 mph, enough to snap tree branches and push over shallow-rooted trees.

The Enhanced Fujita Scale, or EF Scale, rates tornadoes from EF0 to EF5. It replaced the original Fujita Scale in February 2007. That earlier system was introduced in 1971 by T. Theodore Fujita, a meteorologist at the University of Chicago. At the top of the newer scale, an EF5 rating means estimated winds above 200 mph.

An EF1 tornado carries estimated winds of 86 to 110 mph. That range overlaps the sustained-wind ranges of Category 1 and Category 2 hurricanes on the Saffir-Simpson scale. Tornado ratings are based on three-second gusts rather than sustained winds. That makes the comparison loose. It still shows the force behind a storm with a low number attached.

Much of the danger at the low end comes from what the wind lifts. Shingles, lumber, tree limbs, patio furniture and sheet metal can all go airborne. A piece of wood moving at those speeds can shatter a window and keep going. People caught outdoors or near glass face the greatest exposure.

National Weather Service survey teams set the rating by walking the damage path once the tornado has lifted. They compare what they find against 28 damage indicators. Those indicators include structures such as homes, schools and barns, along with trees and power poles. Each indicator has degrees of damage tied to an estimated wind speed.

That process matters for anyone weighing whether to take cover. Nobody can know a tornado's final rating while it is still on the ground. A tornado's width or shape also says little about its strength. Some narrow tornadoes have caused violent damage, and some wide ones have been rated weak.

A rating can also understate a storm. The scale depends on what the tornado damaged. A tornado crossing open fields with few buildings may receive a low rating even if its winds were stronger. The EF number records the damage found, not necessarily the peak wind.

Most tornadoes recorded in the U.S. are rated EF0 or EF1. Those storms still peel off roofs, drop trees onto houses and cars, and bring down power lines.

A tornado warning is the signal to take shelter, whether or not a siren sounds or a funnel is in sight. Outdoor sirens are built to alert people who are outside, and many tornadoes are hard or impossible to see before they arrive.

Outdoor warning sirens are generally owned and operated by local governments, not by the National Weather Service (NWS). Their purpose is to reach people in parks, on ball fields, on farms and on streets. Inside a home or office, the sound can be lost behind closed windows, running air conditioners, televisions or the noise of the storm itself. A person who is asleep may not hear one at all. Silence from a siren does not mean a storm has passed or missed.

Waiting to spot the funnel carries its own danger. Some tornadoes are wrapped in heavy rain, which can hide the circulation until it is close. Others arrive after dark, when lightning offers only brief glimpses of the sky. Low clouds, hills and trees can block the view as well. By the time a tornado is visible from a window, the time to reach shelter may be gone.

The two official alert terms mean different things. A tornado watch means conditions are favorable for tornadoes to develop in and near the watch area. The Storm Prediction Center issues watches, and they usually cover a large region for several hours. A watch is a cue to review a safety plan, charge phones and confirm where to go.

A tornado warning means a tornado has been spotted or indicated by weather radar. Local NWS offices issue warnings for smaller areas. When a warning covers your location, the NWS advises moving to shelter immediately rather than stepping outside to look for the storm.

Alerts come through more than one channel. NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts NWS warnings around the clock. Many receivers can sound an alarm when a warning is issued for a selected county. Wireless Emergency Alerts push tornado warnings to compatible mobile phones in the affected area without requiring a sign-up. Local broadcast meteorologists and weather apps add further backup. A second alert source matters most at night, when an outdoor siren alone may not wake anyone inside.

Anthropic’s bankers are reportedly valuing Anthropic between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. Below is a simple, interactive tool to help you form your own opinion of what’s an appropriate valuation for Anthropic.

Disclaimer: this is highly simplified, and I’m not an investment advisor.

The whole IPO debate comes down to two numbers nobody knows: how much revenue Anthropic will have in 2028, and how much of it will be profit. Pick yours.

The arithmetic ignores two things that roughly cancel: a 2028 profit is worth about 17% less today than the same profit earned now, and Anthropic’s $132 billion in cash adds about 7% to any result. Big Tech multiples are market value divided by the latest quarter’s operating profit, annualized; margins are operating margins from the latest quarter. Anthropic’s figures are from its S-1 and the forecast it gave investors. This is arithmetic, not investment advice.

#5455. Tornadoes strike in every month: a 12-month U.S. calendar of where and why

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tornado season by month runs well beyond spring, and this 12-month calendar shows where twisters strike, why the peak shifts and which historic storms marked each month

Tornadoes are not confined to spring. They can strike the U.S. in any month, including the depths of winter. The country records roughly 1,200 tornadoes in an average year, according to NOAA. That total is spread across a calendar far longer than the April and May storms most people picture.

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that touches the ground and is attached to a cloud base. The setup behind most tornadoes pairs warm, moist air near the surface with cooler, drier air above. Winds that change speed and direction with height add the spin. Where those ingredients line up shifts as the seasons turn.

That is why tornado season by month looks less like a single spike than a band of risk moving across the country. The Gulf Coast and Deep South are most active in the cooler months. The Southern Plains peak in late spring. May is the most active month on average across the U.S., per NOAA Storm Prediction Center climatology. By early to mid summer, the peak has moved to the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest. In autumn, a secondary season develops across the South and the Mississippi Valley.

Two regional nicknames describe this geography, though neither has official boundaries. Tornado Alley generally refers to the Great Plains, where late-spring storms build over open, flat country. Dixie Alley covers parts of the Deep South, where many tornadoes arrive in the cool season. Storms there can move quickly, and rain or trees can block the view of an approaching funnel.

Tornado strength is rated after the fact, based largely on the damage left behind. The Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale runs from EF0 to EF5. It replaced the original Fujita scale in the U.S. on Feb. 1, 2007. Tornadoes before that date carry F ratings. Older storms in this guide that have a rating are listed on the F scale, while storms since 2007 use the EF scale.

The 12 slides that follow move through the year in order, from January to December. The sequence is a calendar, not a ranking. Each slide explains where tornadoes tend to form that month, the weather patterns behind them and at least one documented storm that shows the risk in practice.

January tornadoes concentrate in the Deep South and along the Gulf Coast. Warm, humid air from the Gulf of Mexico can surge north there and collide with strong winter storm systems.

Most of the rest of the country is usually too cold and dry in midwinter to support tornadoes. Tornado-producing thunderstorms need plenty of moisture near the ground. Northern states rarely have it in January. Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and their neighbors sit close enough to the Gulf to draw on that moisture quickly.

The setup typically begins when a low-pressure system crosses the central U.S. Southerly winds ahead of it pull Gulf air inland. A band of strong winds a few thousand feet above the ground, known as the low-level jet, often speeds that flow. Temperatures and dew points climb across the South, sometimes within a day. A cold front then pushes in from the west, and thunderstorms form along and ahead of that boundary.

The winter jet stream supplies another key ingredient. In January, the jet stream often dips far south, placing its fast upper-level winds over the Gulf states. Those winds create strong wind shear across the region. Shear helps thunderstorms rotate. Rotating thunderstorms, called supercells, produce most strong tornadoes.

Selma, Alabama, showed how serious a January tornado can be. An EF3 tornado struck the city on Jan. 12, 2023. Selma sits on the Alabama River in the state's Black Belt region, far from the Great Plains that many people associate with twisters.

Dixie Alley is the informal name for the tornado-prone stretch of the lower Mississippi Valley and the Southeast. Alabama and Mississippi sit near its center. The same winter low-pressure systems that fuel these storms can bring snow and ice to states farther north at the same time.

The National Weather Service uses Doppler radar to detect rotation inside thunderstorms. Forecasters can issue a tornado warning from that radar signature before anyone confirms a funnel on the ground.

February tornado risk stays centered on the South and the lower Mississippi and Tennessee valleys. The Super Tuesday outbreak of Feb. 5–6, 2008, showed how widely late-winter storms can spread that danger.

The outbreak hit Tennessee, Arkansas, Kentucky and Alabama over two days. It shares its name with Super Tuesday, the Feb. 5, 2008, date when many states held presidential primary contests. The storms came after the U.S. adopted the Enhanced Fujita Scale, so they carry EF ratings.

February sits in the heart of the cool season. Across much of the central and northern U.S., the ground and air remain cold. Farther south, mild and humid air can return quickly whenever winds shift to blow from the south.

The trigger is usually a strong cold front. These fronts sweep out of the Plains behind powerful low-pressure systems. Ahead of them, warmer air surges north. Where the two air masses collide, the colder, denser air forces the warm air upward. Thunderstorms can then build fast.

Winter fronts often travel at high speed, and that shapes the storms they produce. Many February events feature a squall line, a long, narrow band of storms along or just ahead of the front. Tornadoes in a squall line tend to spin up quickly and can be brief. Heavy rain often surrounds them and hides them from view.

Other setups produce discrete supercells. These are isolated, rotating thunderstorms that form ahead of the main line. Supercells are responsible for most strong, long-lived tornadoes. When supercells and a squall line develop in the same system, tornadoes can touch down across several states.

Timing adds to the risk. Late-winter systems can arrive during busy daytime and evening hours, when people are at work, at school or on the road. Fast-moving storms leave little time between an alert and the storm's arrival.

The two main alerts mean different things. A tornado watch means conditions favor tornadoes across a broad area. A tornado warning means a tornado is occurring or has been indicated by radar nearby. During a warning, the standard guidance is to move to an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows.

March is when tornado risk starts spreading north from the Gulf Coast into the Mississippi and Ohio valleys and the lower Midwest. On March 18, 1925, the Tri-State Tornado killed 695 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, making it the deadliest tornado in U.S. history.

The month sits at the turn of the seasons. The sun climbs higher each week, and the spring equinox arrives around March 20. Ground across the South warms quickly under that stronger sunlight. Farther north, snow cover and cold air can hang on well into the month.

That gap produces sharp temperature contrasts across the middle of the country. Storm systems draw energy from those contrasts. A strong low-pressure system crossing the central U.S. can pull warm, humid air north on its eastern side while colder air pushes in behind it. Severe thunderstorms tend to form along the boundary between the two.

The jet stream adds another ingredient. In March it still carries much of its winter strength and often runs across the central and southern states. Strong winds aloft help a thunderstorm organize and rotate, the setup that can produce a tornado.

The Deep South stays in its active cool-season pattern through the month. As March goes on, the zone where warm and cold air collide reaches farther into the Mississippi and Ohio valleys.

The Tri-State Tornado crossed parts of all three states in a single day. People in its path had no weather radar, no television and no public tornado warnings to rely on. Commercial radio broadcasting was only a few years old. Residents had no organized way to learn a tornado was approaching before it reached them.

The National Weather Service now issues tornado watches when conditions favor tornadoes and warnings when one is spotted or indicated by radar. Doppler radar can detect rotation inside a storm before a tornado touches down. Those tools give people time to reach shelter, ideally a basement or a windowless interior room on the lowest floor.

That shelter guidance applies in March as much as in any other month. Warm spells this time of year can bring severe storms to communities that saw little of them over the winter.

April is a month of large tornado outbreaks across the central and eastern U.S. The Super Outbreak of April 3–4, 1974, produced 148 tornadoes across 13 states and killed 315 people.

The outbreak came before the Enhanced Fujita Scale took effect. Its tornadoes therefore carry ratings on the original Fujita scale. They are written as F ratings, not EF ratings.

A tornado outbreak is a cluster of tornadoes produced by one large weather system. In April, a deep low-pressure system can drag a cold front across several states at once. Thunderstorms then form along and ahead of that front over a wide area. Many of them can rotate at the same time.

Mid-spring sets up the sharp contrasts that feed these systems. Cold, dry air from Canada still pushes south as winter fades. Warm, humid air from the Gulf of Mexico flows north as the season warms. Where the two meet, the lower atmosphere becomes unstable and air rises quickly.

The jet stream supplies the other key ingredient. In April it remains strong and often runs across the middle of the country. Fast winds high overhead, paired with southerly winds near the ground, give a storm's updraft the twist it needs to start rotating.

An outbreak can unfold over many hours. Storms often begin in the afternoon, when daytime heating adds energy to the lower atmosphere. As the low-pressure system tracks east, new storms can keep forming after dark. They can reach communities far from where the first tornadoes touched down.

When instability and wind shear overlap across several states, one weather system can produce tornadoes in places hundreds of miles apart. That is how a single event can reach 13 states. On a major outbreak day, tornado watches can stretch across several states at the same time.

April sits between the cool-season activity of the Deep South and the late-spring peak on the Southern Plains. Tornado risk this month covers a broad stretch of the country, from the Gulf Coast north into the Ohio Valley and the Midwest.

May is the most active tornado month in the U.S. on average, according to NOAA Storm Prediction Center climatology. It is also when the Southern Plains, the heart of Tornado Alley, reach their late-spring peak.

The May setup depends on three ingredients lining up over the same ground. Warm, humid air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico near the surface. Hot, dry air from the desert Southwest and the high terrain of northern Mexico rides over the top of it.

The third ingredient is the jet stream. In late spring it still crosses the Plains with considerable strength. That supplies wind shear, the change in wind speed and direction with height that lets a storm rotate.

The boundary where moist and dry air meet near the ground is called the dryline. On many spring afternoons it sits across western Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas. Storms often form along or just east of it as the day heats up.

The layer of warm, dry air aloft acts as a lid, which forecasters call a cap. It can hold back storms for hours while heat and moisture build underneath. When the cap weakens in one spot, a single storm can grow quickly.

Those isolated storms are often supercells. A supercell is a thunderstorm with a deep, persistently rotating updraft known as a mesocyclone. Supercells produce most of the strongest tornadoes. The open, relatively flat Plains give them long stretches of ground to cross with little to break them up.

Two EF5 tornadoes from the past two decades show what a May storm can do. On May 22, 2011, an EF5 tornado hit Joplin, Missouri, and killed 158 people. On May 20, 2013, another EF5 tornado struck Moore, Oklahoma, a suburb of Oklahoma City.

Joplin lies in the far southwest corner of Missouri, near the Kansas and Oklahoma borders. Its location shows that May tornado risk is not limited to Oklahoma and Kansas. Moore sits in central Oklahoma, squarely inside the region most associated with Tornado Alley.

The Storm Prediction Center, based in Norman, Oklahoma, issues daily convective outlooks and tornado watches for the whole country. Local National Weather Service offices issue the tornado warnings that tell residents a storm is imminent.

In June, tornado activity moves north into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest, the regions that peak in early to mid summer. On June 16, 2014, two EF4 tornadoes struck near Pilger, Nebraska.

The northward move follows the jet stream. In spring, this band of strong upper-level winds often dips across the Southern Plains and the South. By June, it usually tracks across the northern U.S. and southern Canada. The wind shear that helps organize rotating storms travels north with it.

Moisture follows a similar path. Warm, humid air from the Gulf of Mexico pushes farther inland as summer builds. It can reach Nebraska, the Dakotas, Minnesota and Iowa. That moisture feeds storms well north of the Oklahoma and Texas stretch of Tornado Alley.

Daylight adds more fuel. The summer solstice falls around June 21. It gives the northern states their longest days of the year. Long hours of sunshine heat the ground and the air just above it. Warm air near the surface rises quickly once a storm begins to form.

When that heating overlaps with enough shear, supercells can develop. A supercell is a thunderstorm with a deep, rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Most strong and violent tornadoes come from supercells.

The Pilger tornadoes touched down near the small town in northeastern Nebraska on the same afternoon. Both earned EF4 ratings, the second-highest category on the Enhanced Fujita Scale.

A powerful supercell can sometimes produce more than one tornado at the same time. Separate funnels may form under different parts of the storm's rotating circulation. Paired tornadoes like these are uncommon. They force forecasters and storm spotters to track more than one threat at once.

Timing shapes the June risk as well. Plains tornadoes tend to form in the late afternoon and early evening, after the day's heating has peaked. Long June evenings mean many of these storms arrive while some daylight remains.

Geography matters too. Much of the Northern Plains is open farmland, with small towns spread far apart. A tornado can cross miles of fields before reaching a community. For residents of these states, the most active part of the year arrives weeks after the Southern Plains peak has passed.

July tornado activity concentrates across the northern tier of the U.S. and the Great Lakes region. By then the Southern Plains have usually passed their late-spring peak. The Northern Plains and Upper Midwest are in their early to mid summer season.

That shift follows the jet stream. In midsummer, the strongest upper-level winds typically run far to the north, often near the Canadian border. Storms need both instability and wind shear to rotate. Heat and humidity supply plenty of instability across much of the country in July. Strong shear is harder to find, and it tends to stay close to the jet.

States such as North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan sit near that band of stronger winds. Across the southern half of the country, shear is usually too weak in July to support many rotating storms.

Midsummer thunderstorms often organize into large clusters or lines that can travel hundreds of miles. Tornadoes can form along the leading edge of these systems. They tend to be brief. Heavy rain often hides them from view. The main hazard from these storm complexes is frequently damaging straight-line wind rather than tornadoes.

The Teton–Yellowstone tornado of July 21, 1987, showed that elevation offers no guaranteed protection. It struck the mountains of northwestern Wyoming and climbed above 10,000 feet. That makes it a rare high-elevation tornado. It was rated F4 on the original Fujita scale, which was still the U.S. standard in 1987.

Mountain tornadoes are uncommon. Cooler, thinner air at altitude usually limits the warm, moist conditions that storms feed on. The 1987 event is a reminder that the pattern has exceptions. Rivers, lakes, valleys and hills do not reliably deflect tornadoes either.

July also puts more people outdoors. Campers, hikers and boaters in parks and on lakes can be far from sturdy shelter when storms develop. For travelers in the northern U.S., checking the forecast before heading into remote areas is a practical step during this month.

August tornadoes are generally less frequent than spring twisters, and they can occur well outside the Plains. On Aug. 8, 2007, an EF2 tornado struck Brooklyn, New York, showing that late-summer storms can bring damaging tornadoes to dense urban areas.

The atmosphere in August works differently than it does in April or May. The jet stream typically sits far to the north in late summer. That position removes much of the strong wind shear that helps spring storms rotate. Heat and humidity remain plentiful, but the twisting ingredient is often weaker.

Many August thunderstorms are driven mostly by daytime heating instead. They tend to build in the afternoon and bring heavy rain, lightning and gusty winds. They often fade by evening. Tornadoes from these storms are often brief and weak. Some form along boundaries left by earlier storms, where colliding pools of air can spin up short-lived rotation.

The Brooklyn tornado also shows that a city offers no built-in protection. A common myth holds that tall buildings, rivers or urban heat keep tornadoes away. Large cities cover a small share of the land. Direct hits are therefore less frequent, but not impossible. When a tornado does cross a dense neighborhood, far more homes, cars and people sit in its path.

August falls within the Atlantic hurricane season, which runs from June 1 to Nov. 30. Landfalling tropical systems can add tornado risk near the coast in late summer.

The basic precautions do not change by season. A tornado watch means conditions are favorable for tornadoes to develop. A watch usually covers a broad area for several hours. A tornado warning means one has been spotted or indicated on radar. A warning targets a much smaller area and calls for immediate action.

People under a warning should move to a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. In apartment buildings without basements, an interior hallway or stairwell on a low floor offers more protection than upper stories.

September tornadoes often come from landfalling hurricanes and tropical storms rather than from classic Plains supercells. On Sept. 1, 2021, the remnants of Hurricane Ida produced an EF3 tornado in Mullica Hill, New Jersey, far from where the storm first came ashore.

Tropical systems are a recognized source of tornadoes. September also falls in the busiest stretch of the Atlantic hurricane season. Together, those two facts give the month a tornado pattern unlike spring's. The threat follows the track of each storm instead of staying in a fixed alley on the map.

The process starts with wind shear near the ground. As a hurricane moves over land, friction slows the winds at the surface. Winds a few thousand feet up stay much stronger. That sharp change in speed and direction over a short height creates the low-level spin a tornado needs.

The rotation usually develops in the outer rain bands, not near the eye. Small, shallow thunderstorms within those bands can become miniature supercells. The right-front quadrant of a tropical system, relative to its direction of travel, is the area most associated with tornadoes. For a storm moving north, that zone sits northeast of the center.

These tornadoes tend to differ from Plains tornadoes in several ways. Many are brief and rate low on the EF Scale, though the Mullica Hill tornado shows that stronger ones do occur. They are often wrapped in heavy rain, which can hide them from view. Their parent storms are low-topped. That can make the rotation harder to detect on radar, and warnings may come with little lead time.

The risk does not end when a hurricane loses strength. A weakening tropical system can carry moisture and shear hundreds of miles inland. Ida had weakened well below hurricane strength by the time its remnants reached New Jersey.

Tropical tornado threats often arrive alongside flash flooding and damaging straight-line wind. That mix can complicate decisions about shelter. A basement offers protection from a tornado, but low-lying spaces can also take on floodwater.

September tornadoes are not exclusively tropical. Cold fronts crossing the Plains and Midwest can still trigger ordinary severe thunderstorms. But storms tied to tropical systems make the month's risk highly mobile, with potential reach from the Gulf Coast to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

October opens the autumn secondary tornado season across the South and the Mississippi Valley. An EF3 tornado that hit Dallas on Oct. 20, 2019, showed that a major city can face a strong twister months after the spring peak has passed.

A secondary season is a second, smaller rise in tornado activity that follows the summer lull. It does not match spring in scale. It does bring the threat back to southern states that see relatively few tornadoes in July and August.

The jet stream drives the shift. In summer, the strongest upper-level winds sit far to the north, near the Canadian border. As autumn arrives and northern latitudes cool, the temperature contrast between polar and tropical air sharpens. The jet stream strengthens and drifts back south over the central and southern U.S.

That southward move matters because the jet stream supplies the wind shear storms need. Strong shear lets a thunderstorm organize and rotate. Without it, a storm's rain-cooled downdraft tends to choke off the warm air feeding it, and the storm collapses.

Cold fronts return in October as well. Through much of the summer, fronts tend to stall or weaken before reaching the Gulf Coast. In the fall, stronger fronts push south out of Canada. They run into air near the ground that is still warm and humid.

The Gulf of Mexico helps keep that air humid. Its waters hold summer heat into the autumn. Southerly winds flowing off the Gulf can carry that moisture inland ahead of an approaching front.

When a vigorous jet stream and a sharp front arrive over that moisture, the ingredients for severe storms come together again. The pattern resembles a smaller version of spring, arriving at the other end of the year.

North Texas lies at the southern edge of the Plains, a region usually associated with spring tornadoes. The 2019 Dallas tornado shows that the same area can see significant tornadoes in the fall. A tornado in a dense metro area also puts far more homes, businesses and roads in its potential path than one crossing open farmland.

November tornadoes can reach well north of the Gulf Coast. Strong cool-season storm systems can push severe weather into the Midwest and Ohio Valley, as an EF4 tornado showed when it struck Washington, Illinois, on Nov. 17, 2013.

EF4 is the second-highest rating on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. A tornado that strong in mid-November shows that a late-autumn setup can produce a violent twister far from the Southern Plains, where spring activity peaks.

The fuel for these storms comes from contrast. By November, cold air pushing south from Canada grows sharper. Warm, humid air can still linger over the South. When a deep low-pressure system forms between the two, its winds can draw that moisture north into states such as Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky.

The atmosphere in these setups usually looks different from a classic spring day. Shorter days and a lower sun limit surface heating, so instability tends to be modest. Wind shear, the change in wind speed and direction with height, can be very strong. Meteorologists call this a high-shear, low-instability environment, often shortened to HSLC. In spring, the balance often tips the other way, with plentiful instability supplying the energy.

Strong shear helps storms rotate even when they lack the explosive updrafts of a May afternoon. That combination makes forecasting harder. Storms may look less imposing on radar or in the sky, yet still organize enough to produce tornadoes. Forecasters weigh shear, moisture and the strength of the lifting mechanism, such as a cold front, to judge the threat.

The same powerful winds aloft move storms quickly. A fast-moving cell can cover a long distance in a short time. That shrinks the window between a warning and a tornado's arrival for anyone in its path.

Severe weather in the Midwest is most often associated with spring and summer. A November tornado falls outside that window. Shelter plans and alert sources, such as weather radios and phone warnings, apply in every month of the year.

December tornadoes are less common than spring twisters, but they can be deadly, and they often strike at night. An EF4 tornado struck Mayfield, Kentucky, on Dec. 10, 2021. That storm showed a December system can produce a violent tornado.

Winter tornadoes form under different conditions than late-spring storms over the Plains. Short days limit how much the sun warms the ground. That leaves the atmosphere with less of the buoyant energy that builds towering thunderstorms.

December often makes up for it with wind. The jet stream sits farther south in winter and blows harder. Strong low-pressure systems riding along it can pull warm, humid air north from the Gulf of Mexico ahead of a cold front.

When that moisture arrives beneath winds that change direction with height, storms can rotate even without intense heating. That rotation does not depend on daytime sunshine. The threat can last well after dark.

Overnight, a band of fast winds a few thousand feet above the ground, known as the low-level jet, often strengthens over the southern and central U.S. It can feed more Gulf moisture north and increase the turning of winds near the surface. Both help sustain rotating storms at night.

The Mayfield tornado hit Kentucky, hundreds of miles from the Gulf Coast. Strong December systems can push warm, unstable air well inland, carrying tornado risk beyond the Deep South.

Darkness adds a separate layer of risk. At night, a tornado may be visible only in flashes of lightning. Many people are asleep when overnight storms arrive.

Outdoor warning sirens are built to alert people who are outside. They are not designed to wake someone in a closed house. A NOAA Weather Radio with an alarm, or emergency alerts on a phone, can reach people that sirens miss.

Shelter guidance does not change with the season. The safest spot in a house is an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Mobile and manufactured homes offer little protection. Residents of those homes need a plan to reach a sturdier building before storms arrive.

December also bridges two calendar years. The same cool-season pattern carries into January. Tornado risk across the South does not pause for the holidays.
