#5454. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5453. 20 best places to visit in Europe in 2026, according to Lonely Planet

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Lonely Planet's 2026 Europe list pairs famous landmarks with quieter alternatives, from Paris to Bruges, as overtourism reshapes travel planning.

Planning a European trip now begins with a scroll and ends in a stall. Europe holds 44 countries, and any one of them could fill a two-week itinerary without repeating itself. A traveler weighing a famous capital against a medieval town nobody back home has heard of faces a problem of abundance. Open borders and short-haul rail deepen the dilemma, since a single trip can absorb three or four stops without much added effort. The hard part is no longer finding somewhere worth going. It is choosing which version of the continent matches the trip you want to take.

Crowds shape the itinerary as much as the sights do. Europe's biggest-draw cities absorb enormous summer volumes, and the pressure shows up in packed squares, long entry lines, and monuments that lose their atmosphere when too many people stand inside them at once. Money pulls in the same direction. A few days in an expensive northern capital can drain a budget at a speed a smaller town never will, and the cheaper alternative asks for patience, research, and a willingness to visit places no travel feed has catalogued. Travelers $TRV who want the landmarks without the crush have started treating the calendar as part of the decision, weighing months, weekdays, and districts before they book anything.

Lonely Planet built its 2026 European roundup around the same tension. Its editors made the picks themselves, drawing on firsthand knowledge instead of a survey, an index, or a numeric score. They set household-name cities beside little-known corners their staff return to on their own time, and they weighed glossy, big-ticket choices against modest, wallet-friendly ones. Overtourism shaped the mix, since several of the continent's best-loved spots have strained under visitor numbers in recent years. The list covers 20 destinations, spanning capitals, small towns, and whole regions, and each write-up identifies the kind of traveler a place suits and the season that serves it best. The order follows editorial sequence and implies no ranking, so the 20th name carries the same weight as the first.

Engineers raised the Eiffel Tower as a temporary showpiece for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, and the structure outlived its own deadline to become the shape every visitor pictures when imagining the Paris skyline. Sightseers and photographers crowd its base in every season, and the Louvre pulls nearly as hard. Two landmarks of this stature would anchor an entire itinerary in most cities. Paris treats them as the opening act.

Romance here lives in the hours between the monuments. An unhurried morning at an outdoor cafe table, with strong coffee and a warm pastry while the street supplies the entertainment, delivers as much of the place as any ticketed attraction. Evening walks beside the Seine do similar work. The restaurants, the late-night bars, and the galleries, museums, and flea markets scattered across the city give couples a reason to abandon a plan halfway through and follow whatever turns up.

Twenty arrondissements divide Paris, each with its own temperament, which hands a repeat visitor fresh ground to cover on every trip. Anyone who exhausts the central districts finds the appeal holds further out. The city also sidesteps the seasonal calculation that governs so much of European travel. No month ruins a stay here, so travelers can book around their own schedules instead of chasing a weather window. February delivers a different Paris from the one August offers, and both versions hold up.

Day trips push the itinerary past the city limits. Giverny, where Monet kept his garden, sits close enough for an afternoon among the beds he planted. Versailles, Marie Antoinette's former home, swaps the capital's density for formal grounds on a royal scale. Both fit inside a single day, so one week here can cover a world's fair relic, the Louvre's collections, a painter's garden, and a royal court without a change of hotel. Paris rewards loose planning more than most capitals, since its attractions sit near enough to one another that an unstructured week fills itself.

The Theatre of Dionysos held 17,000 spectators on the slope beneath the Acropolis, a scale that hints at how much public life once gathered around a single hill. The Acropolis rises on a rocky outcrop above the modern streets, and the Parthenon on its summit has become the shorthand image for classical Greece. Ruins surface across the whole country, yet the structures clustered on and below this one promontory carry the heaviest weight.

Two marketplaces sit on the ground beneath the citadel, one Greek and one Roman, and the Temple of Olympian Zeus adds a third ancient complex within walking distance of both. The Roman agora and its Greek counterpart served the same civic purpose centuries apart, so one short walk covers two eras of the city's commercial life. Museums across the city fill the gaps the broken columns leave, holding the sculpture, pottery, and context that open-air excavations cannot supply. A traveler who treats the Acropolis as a single stop and moves on misses the density of the archaeological field spread below it.

Heatwaves have shut major Athenian sights in July and August across recent years, as temperatures climb to levels tied to climate change. Shade runs short on an exposed hilltop, and a midday closure can wipe out the window a short trip set aside for the Parthenon. The same landmarks stay open and draw thinner crowds outside the summer peak, which makes the shoulder months the sturdier bet for anyone who wants an unhurried climb and better odds the gates stay unlocked.

Loukoumades, crisp balls of fried dough, and souvlaki kebabs headline a food culture that earns its own hours in the itinerary. Beaches ring the capital, and day trips reach pine-forested islands, old cities steeped in atmosphere, and trails over rough ground. Athens works as a single base for all of it, so a week of antiquity, swimming, and hill walking never calls for a second hotel.

The Colosseum, the Roman Forum, and the Via Appia Antica survive from the centuries when Rome governed the ancient world's most powerful empire, and 2,000 years separate that era from the crowds walking past today. Gladiators fought before spectators inside the amphitheater while emperors kept households on a scale that defeats modern imagination. The cobbled routes linking those landmarks carry daily foot traffic, and following them shortens the gap between the imperial capital and the metropolis built on top of it. Few ruins of this age sit this close to an ordinary commute.

Independent boutiques sell bags and hand-worked jewelry a short walk from the excavated past. Bars fill in the early evening for aperitivo, the pre-dinner round Romans treat as the hinge between the workday and the night, and the ritual pulls locals into the same piazzas tourists crossed six hours earlier. A morning among the monuments and an evening out cost nothing extra in travel time, since the two Romes overlap street by street. Anyone who spends every hour among arches and pediments misses half of the Rome its residents inhabit.

Street art covers walls in Ostiense and San Lorenzo, two neighborhoods the classical sightseeing circuit skips. Murals give those districts a draw that owes nothing to antiquity, and spray paint changes faster than anything carved in stone, so a second trip turns up work the first one missed. Reaching them pulls travelers out of the tourist core and into streets that belong to the people who live in them. A city layered across 20 centuries keeps adding to the pile.

Summer in Rome punishes sightseers with heat and congestion. Spring and fall thin the lines at the headline attractions and bring temperatures that make a full day on foot bearable. Timing counts for more here than in capitals where the marquee draws sit indoors, since the arena, the old civic center, and the consular road leave visitors under open sky for hours at a stretch. Skipping the peak months restores the one thing Rome's archaeology rewards, which is the patience to stand in front of it unhurried.

Stockholm spreads across 14 islands at the seam where the Baltic meets Lake Mälaren, which puts salt water and fresh water inside one set of city limits. The channels between those islands run clear enough that residents swim in them through the summer, and stands of woodland survive inside the built-up grid. A visitor can leave a cafe table and reach a forest path without boarding anything. Few European capitals hand over that much open ground on foot.

Gamla Stan, the medieval core, carries the historic half of the equation with its tight lanes and steep-gabled facades. The districts that grew up around it trade in design, fashion, and cooking the rest of the continent borrows from, which gives even a three-day stay two moods to move between. The handoff from the old quarter to the newer streets takes minutes, so travelers can take in both before dinner.

Museum collections here cover more ground than the city's size suggests. Viking treasure sits in the same visit as a warship that met a disastrous end, alongside ABBA stage costumes and contemporary work built to provoke whoever walks past it. A rainy afternoon costs a traveler nothing in momentum.

Ferries carry the trip into the Stockholm archipelago, where untouched shorelines back onto unbroken tree cover. Footpaths of the Stockholm Archipelago Trail link stretches of that terrain for anyone who prefers walking to hopping between boats. A day out there reads as a separate vacation, reached on the same transit logic that moves commuters around the center.

January and February pull temperatures down to -5°C (23°F), snow settles over the rooftops, and the bathing spots of July turn into scenery for a bundled walk along the quay. A traveler booking those months needs layers that a summer visitor never unpacks. Stockholm asks a traveler to pick a season before building an itinerary, since one stretch of shoreline delivers two trips that share nothing but an address.

A harbor 1,000 years old sits at the center of the Danish capital, ringed by period architecture that makes the shoreline an attraction in itself. Rosenborg Slot and Marmorkirken stand a short walk inland, the first a royal castle holding centuries of monarchy, the second a domed church that interrupts a low skyline. Three days covers that ground without rushing, which is why Copenhagen fits travelers who can spare a long weekend and nothing longer.

Kitchens with Michelin stars sit at one end of a dining scene that runs down through casual cafes and neighborhood bars, and the gap between those ends narrows in a city where design discipline touches everything. Restrained Danish style shapes the boutiques as much as the restaurants, so browsing and eating blur into a single activity for anyone treating the streetscape as the main event. The creative reputation reaches a guest at the counter, the table, and the shopfront inside one afternoon.

Museums and galleries absorb the hours that cold weather claims from a walking itinerary, a useful reserve in a northern capital. Copenhagen holds its charm outside summer, which widens the booking window well past the peak months and eases pressure on flight and hotel prices. A traveler who picks a November weekend gives up none of the architecture, none of the collections, and none of the waterside views.

Expense shadows Copenhagen's name, and the restaurant bill is where the city earns it. Plenty of what makes the trip worthwhile sits outside that reckoning. Walking the streets and taking in the mood costs nothing, and attractions that charge no admission spread across the city for anyone willing to plan around them. A visitor can assemble a full itinerary from the walkable core, the quays, and the shopfronts that advertise the local aesthetic, then spend real money on one meal worth remembering. The budget question comes down to how often you choose to eat sitting down.

Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain reach full volume on summer weekends, which makes timing the first decision a Berlin nightlife trip demands. The club culture here carries a reputation beyond Germany's borders, and it gathers in those two districts once the warm months arrive. A visitor who lands on a wet Tuesday in February meets a different city from the one every dance-floor dispatch describes. Booking a summer weekend instead puts a traveler at the door while the line is still short.

Decades separate present-day Berlin from the night the Wall came down, and the capital that once sat on one of the Cold War's hardest dividing lines now draws travelers from every direction. Evidence of the division survives in plain sight. The Brandenburg Gate anchors the image most people hold of the split city. The East Side Gallery keeps long stretches of the old barrier standing under layers of spray paint, turning a structure meant to separate people into an open-air canvas anyone can walk the length of. The DDR Museum works at closer range, laying out life under East German rule through its exhibits. Visitors reading those exhibits get the texture of a vanished country, the detail that monuments leave out. The three sites form a daytime route that explains the ground those clubs occupy after dark.

Independent shops across Berlin stock what no chain carries, and each neighborhood holds a character of its own, which gives a visitor reason to cross the city on foot between landmarks instead of hopping from one monument to the next. The modern city rewards wandering as much as the historic one rewards study, and both occupy the same streets. A traveler who treats the 20th century as the whole story misses half of what Berlin now offers.

A capital that answered its own border wall with paint keeps improvising, so a traveler who books the trip for the clubs absorbs the city's history on the walk home.

May and September hand travelers a version of Tallinn that July conceals, with the UNESCO-listed Old Town calm enough to wander without a plan and the weather still agreeable. Estonia's medieval capital packs churches from the Middle Ages, the mansions of wealthy traders, and handsome squares into a quarter small enough to cross on foot, and the pleasure of the place depends on having room to look up. Late spring and early fall supply that room, which makes the month a visitor picks matter more than the itinerary.

Cruise ships set the rhythm of the busy stretch. Each docking releases a wave of passengers into the same few lanes at the same hour, and cobbles that reward an early riser turn into a slow shuffle by midday. The pressure arrives in bursts, not as steady flow, giving the Old Town a split personality inside a single day. Travelers $TRV who arrive by ferry or plane and sleep in town can step around those hours, taking the sights at breakfast or after the last ship pulls out.

Tallinn absorbs the attention better than many small heritage towns, and its own growth explains part of that durability. Restaurants have multiplied into a scene worth an evening of its own, and hotels inside the walls make an overnight stay practical, so the day-tripper has a standing reason to become a guest. Modern Estonian culture shares space with the old scenery instead of competing with it, and the contemporary half of town opens up to anyone who stays past dessert.

Swapping high summer for the quieter months costs a traveler almost nothing. Temperatures hold pleasant on either side of the peak, and the exchange buys a center where photographs come without strangers in the frame and tables open without a wait. Tallinn argues for treating the calendar as the first booking decision of a European trip, since the same spires, stonework, and merchant facades deliver two different cities depending on the month.

Vienna's Habsburg rulers held power for 640 years, and the residences they left behind set the tone of the Austrian capital in winter. Snow settles on the stonework of those palaces while Christmas markets fill the squares below, trading the city's summer composure for the clatter of wooden stalls. Travelers $TRV who arrive in December cover imperial architecture and the holiday trade on one walk, which makes the coldest weeks the strongest argument for the trip.

The Hofburg Palace holds the fullest record of court life in the city. Its treasury displays the imperial crowns, the Spanish Riding School performs the horsemanship the dynasty refined over generations, and the chandelier-lit state apartments once belonged to the ruling pair, Franz Joseph I and Elisabeth. One address delivers regalia, horses, and private quarters, so a visitor assembles a picture of how an empire presented itself without crossing town. The arrangement helps on short winter days, when daylight fails by late afternoon and indoor halls carry the rest of an itinerary.

Schloss Schönbrunn answers the Hofburg with 1,441 rooms and a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Schloss Belvedere supplies a baroque third option, and both estates sit in designed gardens that reward as much walking as their interiors do. Three monumental residences inside one capital hand a visitor several days of Habsburg splendor without a repeated staircase or a familiar garden view. The spread also eases the crush, since sightseers gathered at one address are not standing in front of you at the next.

Schönbrunn's park costs nothing to enter during opening hours, which puts its avenues, lawns, and long sightlines within reach of any budget. The Privy Garden, the maze, and the zoo charge admission, and booking those tickets online spares a wait at the gate. Vienna splits into two itineraries at its palace sites. One runs on ticketed interiors and fills a day. The other stays outdoors and costs the price of a tram fare. Anyone who settles that question before arriving comes out ahead, because the parkland, public squares, and ornate facades that give the city its character stay open to all.

Dubrovnik's defensive walls rose over four centuries, from the 13th to the 16th, and they still close around the Old Town with barely a gap. Few fortifications anywhere match them for scale or survival. Marble paving catches the light inside the circuit, lined by facades carved with detail that repays a slow pace on foot. The ring itself supplies the payoff, a sweep over tile roofs the color of baked clay and the Adriatic opening behind them. Low evening light warms the whole scene, which turns the hour before sunset into the most contested slot on the ramparts.

"Game of Thrones" turned Dubrovnik into a pilgrimage for fantasy fans and drove a steep rise in visitor numbers. Tour companies assembled entire itineraries from the locations the production used, and guides shuttle groups between them through the summer peak. Screen tourism behaves unlike ordinary sightseeing. It compresses a place into a sequence of camera positions, which funnels crowds through a handful of corners on repeat while lanes one block away stay empty. The series stacked a second identity on top of the city's older one, and plenty of people now recognize the stone silhouette from an episode before ever seeing it in daylight.

A Dubrovnik trip changes shape outside the Old Town. The headline sights hold up to a longer look, and the districts past the historic center keep the everyday rhythm the core has surrendered to sightseers. Lokrum lies 15 minutes away by ferry. Cars never reach the island, which holds nature reserve protection and carries botanical gardens across much of its ground. A quarter-hour on the water buys the calm the medieval lanes cannot supply in high season.

The pressure in Dubrovnik concentrates in a few celebrated streets, and they absorb nearly every traveler who comes. Distance does more here than timing. Move a few blocks outward, or a short stretch of water across, and Dubrovnik opens up again.

Thousands of houseboats line Amsterdam's canals, and the households aboard them treat the water as a second set of streets. Tour boats weave between neighborhoods on routes no tram follows, and the shift in vantage point earns its fare. Bridge ornamentation, gables, and brickwork show detail from a deck that the pavement hides, so an hour afloat doubles as an orientation lesson for everything that follows. Mooring a home on a waterway counts as an ordinary housing decision in this city, which explains the local affection for the canals better than any museum placard.

Solo travelers settle into Amsterdam faster than into most European capitals, because the social life of the place happens at shared counters. Brown bars, the dark-paneled pubs that serve as neighborhood living rooms, seat strangers beside one another without ceremony. An afternoon inside one can finish with a handful of new acquaintances, a return no ticket queue delivers. The habit dissolves the usual friction of traveling without company, the hour when a restaurant table starts to feel conspicuous.

Short distances and flat ground let a visitor cross the city on foot or by bike in minutes, which widens the hunt for a good meal or a decent glass of wine to every district at once. Travelers $TRV who skip the marquee attractions give up little. The pleasure here gathers in slow hours, on a bench beside the water, over an unhurried lunch, inside a cozy cafe where nobody rushes the check. Any month supports that itinerary, since none of it waits on summer weather.

Pedestrians and cyclists ride free across the River IJ to Amsterdam Noord, boarding behind Amsterdam Centraal Station. The trip lands them outside the ring of canals that most itineraries circle. A full day assembles itself from that single route, a free passage over the water, a long walk through a district most visitors never reach, then an hour back in a pub on the other side, all for the price of one drink. Amsterdam asks for time instead of money, which suits anyone keeping a schedule of their own and nobody else's.

Steam lifts off bathhouses built in baroque and Turkish-influenced styles, and plenty of visitors treat a long soak as the entire purpose of a Budapest trip. The two architectural traditions sitting a short walk apart tell their own story about who governed Hungary and when, so a bather drifting between pools crosses several centuries without stepping out of the water. Idling through an afternoon in hot water qualifies as a full itinerary here, a claim few European capitals can make with a straight face.

The Danube splits the city into Buda and Pest, two halves that face each other across the current with distinct characters. Hills rise west of the water, and the Great Plain starts its long flat run to the east, so the river marks a real border between upland and lowland Hungary instead of a line drawn for convenience. Cruise boats work the bend the Danube carves north of town, which turns a few hours on deck into a natural counterweight to a morning spent indoors under a tiled dome.

The city's ruin bars and clubs stay open until first light, and festivals fill the calendar from May through September. The pairing suits travelers who want both tempos in one trip, since a 2 a.m. finish and a slow start the next day complement each other better than two nights out in a row. Summer visitors get the fullest version of the city, though the baths hold their appeal in any month.

Green space, museums stocked with serious collections, and architecture that holds up block after block give a visitor reason to cross town on foot instead of taxiing from one bath to the next. Anyone wanting more distance can head out for a lake swim or tour the Gödöllő Royal Palace, built while the Habsburgs ruled, a reminder that imperial Hungary extended well past the capital's bridges. Budapest asks for more nights than a standard city break allows, because its best hours happen at a pace that resists compression.

Antoni Gaudí has been dead for a century, and La Sagrada Família still operates as a construction site, its towers climbing toward a form the architect never saw finished. Gothic convention collides with eccentric invention and angles that defy structural logic, so the building strikes the eye as strange and familiar at once. Gaudí's other Modernista work surfaces across the city in facades and rooflines that bend where stone has no business bending. A single architect accounts for much of what travelers photograph here.

Sand sits inside Barcelona's city limits, which lets a morning in a gallery end with an afternoon in the water and no transfer in between. The geography shapes how Barcelona feels against inland cities of similar size, since a looser pace follows when the sea waits at the end of the street grid. Summer tests the arrangement. The urban beaches fill to capacity through the hot months, and claiming a free patch of sand turns into a logistics exercise.

Trains running out of the center reach calmer shoreline within a short ride, giving back what the city beaches surrender in high season, which is room to spread out. Travelers $TRV who build one or two of these outings into a week also put distance between themselves and the most trafficked streets. Letting the rail timetable set the swimming schedule changes the character of a whole week in Barcelona.

Barri Gòtic and El Born absorb the thickest crowds in Barcelona, and the districts beyond them hold tapas bars, museums, and monuments that draw nowhere near the same attention. Spring and fall thin the queues across the whole city. The city's overtourism problem answers to both choices, since every visitor who skips the peak weeks or walks one neighborhood further out removes a body from the crush. Barcelona's pressure concentrates in a few streets and a few months, so anyone willing to shift either variable gets the rest of the city back.

Alfama, Lisbon's oldest quarter, unspools into a tangle of slender lanes, tucked-away courtyards, and curving streets that hold shadow long past noon. Orientation fails within a few turns, and losing it counts as the point. Grocers trade from rooms the size of a cupboard. Tiled facades bounce light back at odd angles, and gaps between the houses open onto a view of pitched roofs falling away toward the Tagus. Anyone who stops consulting a map covers more of the neighborhood than someone determined to follow one.

Lisbon asks little of a newcomer to Europe, which explains its reputation as an entry point to the continent. The city reveals itself on foot, through slopes and staircases instead of timed-entry queues, so a visitor arrives, wanders, and grasps the place by the second afternoon. Neighborhood bars stay open to anyone who steps in, conversation runs easy, and nobody expects a reservation or a plan. An itinerary that forgives mistakes builds the confidence a first-timer needs for denser, more demanding capitals later.

Charcoal smoke and grilling sardines scent the taverns of Alfama, and the smell marks out the kitchens worth stopping for. Fado fills the same rooms after dark, its singers working a repertoire shaped by sorrow and yearning, and the music reaches listeners who speak no Portuguese. A glass of port closes the evening, an export that made the country's wines famous abroad. Those tables teach more about local temperament than an afternoon in a gallery does.

Tram 28 runs between Martim Moniz, close to the center, and Campo de Ourique, a route that doubles as transport and introduction. The vintage carriages draw travelers who board for the pleasure of the journey itself, so the trip earns a place on a schedule for its own sake. One crossing end to end lays out the shape of the city and leaves a passenger with a rough mental map before the real exploring starts. Lisbon surrenders its geography, its kitchens, and its music to anyone willing to walk, ride, and sit still long enough to listen.

Outdoor music festivals and street parties pack London's summer schedule, from the sound systems of All Points East to the costumes and parades of Notting Hill's August carnival, alongside BST Hyde Park's stadium-sized concerts. The capital draws travelers of every age, and people in their twenties pull the most out of it, since whole districts here run on nightlife and live entertainment. Warm months raise the volume, turning parks into venues and handing entire streets to sound systems. Booking those weeks buys a louder, busier city than the one a spring visitor meets, with social life spilling outdoors.

Speedboat trips along the Thames and West End productions built on scares sell the version of London that sticks in memory. Palaces, cathedrals, and museums of international standing fill out any itinerary and hold their own against anything on the continent. London's open taste for enjoyment does the real work, visible in the pub crowds at six o'clock or the queue outside a theater door. The West End's willingness to stage frights shows how far its programming reaches past the safe tourist matinee.

Shoreditch and Notting Hill repay anyone who abandons the central sights for a day. Shoreditch keeps the late hours with its bars and dance floors, while Notting Hill trades in busy market streets and hands its lanes to the carnival. An afternoon inside one district teaches more about how Londoners live than a forced march between monuments. Both sit a short ride from the center, which makes an evening in either an easy swap for another night beside the big museums.

Bath, Brighton, and Bristol each sit within a day's reach and pitch a different kind of detour. Bath preserves Roman ruins. Brighton puts a party on its seafront. Bristol runs on a creative streak. Each one supplies something London lacks, whether ancient stonework, sea air, or a smaller footprint. Travelers $TRV with a week to spend can base themselves in London, hand two days to one of the three, and still catch a show or a club night by evening.

Six outdoor pursuits ring a single Slovenian shoreline at Lake Bled. Swimmers and cyclists share the valley with anglers, hikers, rafters, and canyoning groups, and the range turns a destination most people know from one postcard image into somewhere capable of absorbing several days. Travelers $TRV who budget an afternoon here often watch the schedule expand, since climbs, descents, and river runs leave from nearly every point around the water.

The setting explains why Slovenia counts this spot as its biggest single draw. A church occupies an island at the center of the lake, a medieval castle commands the ridge overhead, and several of the country's highest summits close off the horizon behind both. Each element sits at a different depth in the frame, which gives the view its layered quality and explains the camera phones pointed at it from every angle.

Bathing facilities matter more here than at most alpine lakes, and the public access points deliver. Anyone can walk in and enter the water without paying, a rare condition at a lake this famous, which keeps Bled usable for budget travelers and families on a long itinerary. Two private beaches sit alongside the open ones, and the Grand Hotel Toplice keeps the most polished of them. The split lets visitors choose between crowded free access and a quieter paid alternative without going anywhere else.

Summer brings a cultural season to match the physical one, with the Bled Festival staging classical music performances. The pairing suits the rhythm of a trip built around exertion. Days go to the trails, the paddle lines, and the open water, and evenings go to a concert. Peak weeks crowd the footpaths and fill the auditorium at once, so the busiest span of the calendar offers the widest menu. A destination this photogenic could coast on its reflection alone, and the roster of things to do is why it holds attention after the first picture.

Dublin strips out the language barrier for travelers from the U.S., Canada, Australia, and the UK, and many of them arrive carrying a second purpose. They come to trace a family line back to Ireland, a country whose emigrants settled across the English-speaking world. Talk costs nothing here. Asking directions, ordering a meal, or falling into a long exchange with a stranger demands no phrasebook and no mental translation, which shapes the texture of a trip more than any single monument manages.

The historic sights sit close enough together to cover on foot. Georgian terraces edge the lawns of St Stephen's Green, Trinity College keeps centuries of scholarship behind its gates, and Kilmainham Gaol puts the country's political past in front of anyone who steps inside. Literary landmarks thread through the same streets. Walkers pass buildings attached to a book, a rebellion, or both every few blocks, which makes unplanned roaming as rewarding as a fixed itinerary.

Good pubs sit well outside Temple Bar, the district that soaks up most of the tourist traffic. Drinkers who wander past that cluster find rooms where regulars outnumber visitors and a bar stool comes with company. The original Guinness brewery pulls its own crowd, and a pint on site closes out a plan many arrivals make before they land. Shared language turns a quick round into a long evening. A Dublin night leaves behind strangers' life stories more often than photographs.

Fall thins the summer crowds that press on Ireland as a whole, and Dublin shifts character as they go. Streets loosen, color spreads through the trees around the squares and parks, and the pubs gain the warmth that cold evenings create indoors. Anyone chasing the sociable version of the capital should aim for those months, when the person on the next seat has time to listen. Travelers $TRV who measure a trip by the people they meet need little beyond free evenings, and the quiet season hands out those evenings in quantity.

Venice saves its sharpest light for winter, when low sun falls across lanes that summer packs solid. The hush runs deep enough to make a map useless. Dorsoduro suits that kind of aimless walking, its passages narrowing between shuttered facades and water-stained brick until each corner seems to hold the memory of some private bargain. The city astonishes in any month. Winter changes how much of it one person gets to keep.

Two galleries anchor an off-season itinerary. Gallerie dell'Accademia and the Peggy Guggenheim Collection hold canvases and sculptures spanning centuries of painters and sculptors from across the continent, and a cold, empty week lets a visitor linger in front of them without a crowd pushing past. Standing before a canvas with no tour group pressing in from behind changes what a visitor carries home from a museum. The same pictures hang through August, when throngs leave no room to linger.

Three habits ease the strain the city's popularity creates. Arrive in a quiet month, book more than two nights, and give part of the trip to the outer islands of the lagoon. A daily vaporetto pass cuts the fare for anyone making more than a couple of hops, and the boat routes reach piers well beyond the historic center.

A longer stay rearranges the whole trip from the start. Three or four nights leave room to wait out a gray morning, return to a gallery, or spend an entire day on the water without giving up the central sights. People who come for a few hours compress an itinerary into the streets around the busiest landmarks, piling the heaviest load onto the ground least able to bear it.

Every one of those choices moves money and foot traffic off the small core that takes the worst of the crush. A traveler who books five nights in February and spends two of them out among the islands sees more of Venice than a weekend allows, and leaves the crowded quarter room to breathe.

The Transfăgărășan road tops out at 2,034 meters as it carves across Romania's Făgăraș Mountains in the southern reach of Transylvania. Engineers cut the route through the range during the 1970s under the Ceaușescu regime, and critics of the era dismissed it as a monument to one man's ambition. Decades later, motorists count its switchbacks among the most thrilling stretches of asphalt on the planet. The scorn and the acclaim attach to the same ribbon of tarmac, a lesson in Romanian politics delivered at altitude.

Lake Bâlea sits at the summit, a glacial pool ringed by bare rock that throws the sky back like polished glass. Cloud swallows the water on some days and leaves visitors staring into gray. Travelers $TRV who build a whole itinerary around one photograph of the lake risk arriving to a whiteout, so a spare day in the plan protects the trip. The peaks surrender the view on their own terms.

Snow shuts the Transfăgărășan from October through May and compresses the open season into June, July, August, and September. Four months of access squeeze the planning calendar tighter than most European destinations demand. Visitors who dodge crowds elsewhere on the continent by booking spring or fall cannot repeat the tactic here, since the quiet months are the closed ones. Anyone eyeing dates outside the summer window should confirm the opening before paying for flights or a rental car.

The journey itself supplies the attraction, which separates this corner of Romania from places built around a single gallery or cathedral. Tight bends and steep gradients ask for concentration, and the payoff arrives in pieces across the ascent instead of behind one ticket barrier. Passengers absorb the scenery while the person at the wheel shoulders the work, and both come away with something no museum queue can match. The Transfăgărășan favors drivers who book a car and keep the schedule loose, since the weather settles what any given day delivers.

Florence carries an assessment from UNESCO that few cities anywhere can claim, a judgment that the Tuscan capital holds one of the densest concentrations of world-famous art on earth. Major collections sit a short walk from grand churches and Renaissance street plans that have held their proportions for centuries. Visitors who allot a single afternoon to Florence will leave having seen a sliver of it. The art spreads across many addresses, so crossing town between collections becomes part of the experience itself.

Siena, Pisa, Montepulciano, and Livorno give the region a second register beyond its capital. Siena's main square rewards an hour of sitting still, and Pisa holds more architectural riches than the throngs at its leaning tower suggest. Montepulciano and Livorno anchor the eating and drinking at opposite ends of the map, one a hilltop wine town, the other a coastal city whose market deli counters make their own case for lunch. A traveler who treats Florence as the whole of Tuscany misses the half that sits in towns of a few thousand people.

Chianti supplies the vintages that carried Tuscany's name abroad, and its vineyards cover the rolling hills between the larger towns. The countryside works as a destination on its own terms, with warm light falling across ridges of vines. Food and wine travel together here, which means the drive between two galleries can produce the day's best meal. Hilltop settlements stack up along those routes, each with a square, a church, and a kitchen worth the stop.

Spring delivers the version of Tuscany most people picture, with thinner queues at the headline sights and weather mild enough for long walks through the farmland. Summer brings the heat and the volume that attach to any destination with this much pull. The season also suits the pace a Tuscan trip demands, since moving from a Florentine gallery to a Chianti vineyard to a Sienese piazza eats hours on the road and on foot. Tuscany repays a looping itinerary spread across several bases far more than one hotel and a string of day trips.

Belgian beer arrives strong, and the bars of Bruges serve it on squares framed by high towers and centuries-old churches. Brewing here carries the weight of a craft refined over generations, and a barroom is where a drinker meets that inheritance face to face. One glass invites slow sipping, which reshapes the arithmetic of a night out. Two or three in a single bar can fill the hours that a lighter drink would spread across five.

Cobbled streets and canals knit those squares together, so moving from one bar to the next doubles as a walk through a medieval street plan that survived intact. Low white almshouses line parts of the route, their plain fronts no match for the spires overhead. Bruges packs its attractions into a core small enough to cross on foot, which erases the transit time that fragments a stay in a larger city. The beer and the architecture occupy the same few blocks.

Summer turns that compactness into a liability, as travelers pack every lane, square, and taproom through the peak months. The fix demands a tolerance for the cold. Weekday visits at the coldest point of winter thin the crowds until the city reads the way its builders intended, with the Christmas stretch standing as the one exception to the calm. Anyone chasing that version of Bruges trades mild weather for elbow room.

Floodlights remake the streets after dark, washing towers and canal-side facades in a glow that the afternoon never produces. Booking a bed changes the entire trip, since the day-trippers clear out well before those lights come up. An overnight stay also buys the early morning, when the lanes belong to residents again. A weekday winter date, a room inside the old center, and a glass of something potent add up to one strategy instead of three separate decisions. Bruges rewards the traveler willing to be inconvenienced by its calendar and its thermometer.

#5452. Intel stock's record October plunge puts its foundry ambitions to the test

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Intel stock fell 29% on Friday after the company issued a fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $15 billion to $16 billion

Intel $INTC is under mounting pressure to make its foundry business work after its stock lost 45% of its value in October, the largest one-month decline ever recorded, according to CNBC.

Intel stock shed 29% on Friday, a one-day loss it had not seen since the 1970s, according to CNBC. The drop followed the company's Thursday release, in which it reported third-quarter results and forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and non-GAAP earnings of 25 cents a share. The stock slid a further 8% during Monday's session. The revenue forecast fell $1 billion to $2 billion short of analyst estimates, according to CNBC.

Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion. Data center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 billion, while client computing revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion. CFO David Zinsner said the company expects the PC downturn to persist for at least the first six months of next year.

Intel Foundry revenue rose 58% to $6.7 billion. The unit posted an operating loss of $1.85 billion, compared with a loss of $2.32 billion a year earlier. Intel said it released the Intel 14A 0.9 process design kit in October.

The foundry business has yet to sign a flagship client for Intel's leading-edge chips, and most of what it produces goes into Intel's own products, according to CNBC. The company has put roughly five years of effort, and much of the $108 billion it invested in capital projects over that time, into taking on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

Intel said it is redirecting part of its Oregon factory output away from 18A wafers and toward wafers built on the older Intel 3 process that go into its data center products, according to CNBC. Intel is banking on 18A to win over external customers, which means the reallocation could make that push harder.

David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who sat on Intel's board for nearly 30 years, said prospective customers worry about capacity, according to CNBC. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. He said the pressure on Intel's finances will intensify if it fails to sign a major foundry client in the next 12 months, and that spinning off the foundry business is "maybe the only solution."

CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on the earnings call that "a couple of customers" would be ready to announce over the next two quarters, according to CNBC. Tan has held back on spending until customers have firmly committed to buying.

Intel in July announced a collaboration with Fortinet $FTNT to make Fortinet's next-generation SP6 security processor, the first publicly named cybersecurity chip customer for its foundry business. The chip will be built on Intel 4, a more mature process node than 14A and 18A.

An April regulatory filing showed Intel had yet to land a significant customer for its most advanced manufacturing processes.

#5450. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5449. Martha Stewart's ventures, from Entertaining to Martha Stewart Living Radio

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 Martha Stewart business ventures, from a Connecticut catering company to a Macy's home line, trace how she turned entertaining know-how into a media and retail brand

Martha Stewart built a business in which her own name served as the product, the label and the editorial voice at once. Over the decades, that name has appeared on cookbooks, magazine covers, television programs, store shelves and a satellite radio channel.

Her path did not begin in media. Stewart worked as a stockbroker before she turned to food. In the 1970s, she started a catering business from her home in Westport, Connecticut. That business became the base for the entertaining advice she would later package for a national audience.

The next ventures moved that home expertise into books, retail and media. Her catering experience shaped her first book, Entertaining, which Clarkson Potter published in 1982. In 1987, she began consulting for Kmart. A magazine, Martha Stewart Living, launched in the early 1990s with Time Publishing Ventures, a Time Warner unit. A syndicated television show of the same name began in 1993.

The ventures share a common structure. Stewart took one subject, such as cooking, gardening, crafting or decorating, and offered it through several channels. A reader could find a project in the magazine, watch it on TV and then look for related products in a store or catalog. The approach turned household know-how into publishing, broadcasting and retail businesses.

Ownership became part of the story as well. Stewart bought back her brand rights from Time Warner and formed Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia in 1997. The company went public on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1999 under the ticker MSO. Sequential Brands acquired it in 2015.

This list covers a selection of 10 Martha Stewart business ventures, arranged roughly in the order they began. It is not a complete account of everything she has launched, and it is not a ranking. Each entry explains what the venture was, when it started and how it connected to the wider Martha Stewart brand. The list runs from a Connecticut catering kitchen to the Martha Stewart Collection at Macy's $M.

Martha Stewart started a catering business from her home in Westport, Connecticut, in the 1970s. That business became the base for the entertaining expertise later attached to her name.

Stewart came to catering from finance. She worked as a stockbroker before she started the business. She then left that career to cook for paying clients.

The two jobs had little in common. A stockbroker buys and sells securities on behalf of clients. A caterer plans and prepares food for events that clients host.

Catering differs from running a restaurant. A restaurant serves guests at its own premises. A caterer brings food to the client's event, whether that is a dinner party, a cocktail reception or a wedding.

Each job is planned around a single occasion. The caterer settles a menu with the client, cooks in advance and delivers the food ready to serve. Many caterers also supply serving staff and handle cleanup after guests leave. The work combines cooking with logistics, such as timing courses and arranging food for presentation.

Westport sits in Fairfield County, in the southwestern corner of Connecticut, on Long Island Sound. Stewart ran the operation from her own house there rather than from a separate commercial site.

The catering company is where her interest in food for gatherings became a business. Cooking for other people's parties became the subject that later ventures built on.

The link shows up directly in her publishing career. Her first book drew on the catering work. It moved her from serving clients one event at a time to selling her approach to a wider audience.

The later ventures carried the same theme into other formats. Magazines, television programs and home goods lines all returned to entertaining at home. Each of those formats traced its subject back to the Westport catering business.

Entertaining, Martha Stewart's first book, was published in 1982 by Clarkson Potter. It drew on her catering work and began her publishing career.

The book turned a service into a product. A catering job feeds the guests at one event. A book about hosting can reach any reader who buys a copy, wherever that reader lives.

Catering had given Stewart working knowledge of planning food for gatherings. Entertaining put that knowledge into print under her name. Its one-word title stated the subject plainly.

The move also changed how her expertise could earn money. A caterer is paid job by job. A book can keep selling after it is written, with no new event to staff or cook for.

A book also reaches people its author never meets. A caterer's clients deal directly with the person running the kitchen. A reader deals only with the advice on the page and the name on the cover.

Publishing put a partner between Stewart and her audience. A publisher such as Clarkson Potter produces and distributes the books it releases. The author supplies the content.

Entertaining is the earliest entry in her publishing record, and more books under her name followed it. It was the first time she offered her approach to hosting through print rather than through paid client work.

Martha Stewart began working with Kmart as a consultant in 1987. A decade later, in 1997, the retailer launched Martha Stewart Everyday, a home line sold under her name.

The two dates mark separate stages of one relationship. The first was an advisory role. The second put her name directly on merchandise in Kmart stores. Each stage asked something different of her name.

The difference matters for how a personal brand works. A consultant shapes decisions out of public view, and customers may never know who advised the store. A named product line ties a public figure's reputation to each item on the shelf. If a product disappoints a shopper, the name on the label absorbs some of that reaction.

With Everyday, shoppers could buy goods carrying the Martha Stewart name without picking up a book or a magazine. That gave the brand a physical presence with shoppers who might not read her magazine or watch her show. It also turned her advice into something a customer could hold, use and replace.

Kmart was a discount chain. The Everyday line placed her name in front of a mass-market retail audience shopping for ordinary household goods. Her media work had built a reputation around careful, detailed homemaking. The Kmart line carried that reputation into lower-priced goods sold to a broad customer base.

The decade between the consulting deal and the Everyday launch shows a retail business built in steps. Stewart spent years advising the chain before her name went on its products. The Kmart work ran alongside her publishing and television projects rather than replacing them.

The Kmart relationship eventually ended. Her retail partnerships did not end with it. The Martha Stewart Collection at Macy's $M, launched in 2007, later filled the role the Kmart-era arrangement had played. That move shifted the name from a discount chain to a department store.

Martha Stewart Living magazine launched in the early 1990s through Time Publishing Ventures, a unit of Time Warner. The title gave Stewart a regular publication of her own, backed by a large media company.

Before the magazine, her audience reached her through catering clients and books. A periodical works differently. A book reaches a reader once. A magazine comes back with each new issue. That lets a publisher keep returning to the same readers over time.

The recurring format suited the subjects she was already known for. Cooking, gardening, crafting and decorating all shift with the seasons. A periodical can follow those cycles from one issue to the next. A single book is fixed once it goes to print.

The partnership paired a personal brand with a corporate publisher. Time Publishing Ventures operated inside Time Warner, which put the new title within an established publishing business. A large publisher already has the printing, distribution and newsstand reach that a new title would otherwise have to assemble on its own.

The magazine put Stewart's own name at the front of its title. That tied the publication directly to her public identity rather than to a standalone masthead. It also made Martha Stewart Living a label that could extend beyond print.

Consumer magazines typically earn revenue from two groups at once. Readers pay for subscriptions and single copies. Advertisers pay to reach those readers. Under that model, the audience Stewart drew became something a publisher could sell to brands.

Martha Stewart moved her brand onto television in 1993 with a syndicated show called Martha Stewart Living. A second program, the daytime show The Martha Stewart Show, followed in 2005 and stayed on air into the early 2010s.

Syndication shaped how the first show reached viewers. A syndicated program is sold to individual stations rather than produced for one national network's schedule. Each station decides whether to carry the show and where to place it in its lineup. That model let a series appear in markets across the U.S. without a single network's commitment. It also meant airtimes could differ from one city to the next. Stations that carried it could also drop it, so the show had to hold its audience market by market.

Television suited the kind of material Stewart was known for. Cooking, crafts and home projects are hard to learn from text alone. A camera can show the order of steps, the texture of a dough or the way a fold is made. On the page, the same details need photographs and careful written instructions. On screen, a viewer can watch each technique being done.

Demonstration suits a how-to subject. A single segment can take one project, such as a recipe or a craft, and walk through it from start to finish. That mirrors the step-by-step structure of a recipe, where the result depends on doing things in order.

The Martha Stewart Show arrived 12 years after the first series. Daytime programs typically air on weekdays, so a daytime show reaches its audience several times a week rather than once. That pace calls for a steady supply of new segments.

For the business, the shows worked alongside print rather than replacing it. They put her name in front of viewers who might never pick up a magazine. A television slot also returns on a fixed schedule. That gives a brand regular contact with its audience between magazine issues.

Martha by Mail was a catalog of home and craft products that Martha Stewart launched in 1995. It sold goods straight to customers. That made it an early direct-to-consumer business under her name.

In a typical catalog business, a shopper browses printed pages at home, places an order and waits for delivery. The seller handles that customer relationship itself instead of passing it through a retailer. The name Martha by Mail spelled out that model in three words.

The arrangement also shifts work onto the seller. A catalog company has to source and stock its own merchandise, print and mail its pages, take orders and ship each package. In return, it keeps control over the product range, the presentation and the prices.

Direct selling also produces a customer list. Every order records a buyer's name and address. The seller can use that list to mail the next catalog without relying on a retailer to bring shoppers in.

That model set Martha by Mail apart from Stewart's work with Kmart. There, a national discount chain controlled the stores and the shelves. With the catalog, her own operation decided what to offer and how to show it.

The catalog had a ready audience in people who already followed Stewart's home and craft projects in print and on television. It gave them a way to buy goods from a business carrying her name.

Home and craft goods suit the mail-order format. Craft projects often call for specific materials and tools. A catalog can gather those items in one place. A shopper then does not have to search several stores to find them.

Martha by Mail arrived two years before Stewart formed Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia. It also predated widespread online shopping. Many later direct-to-consumer brands sell mainly through websites. The basic idea of a brand selling straight to its own audience was already at work in this catalog.

Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia went public on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1999, trading under the ticker MSO. The listing turned a company built around one person's name and know-how into a publicly traded business.

The company was only two years old at the time. In 1997, Stewart bought back the rights to her brand from Time Warner, whose publishing unit had backed the launch of Martha Stewart Living magazine. She then formed Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia to own and run that brand directly.

The buyback shifted control of the name. Under the earlier arrangement, a large media corporation held the rights to a brand that carried her name. Owning those rights gave Stewart's own company the say over how the Martha Stewart name was used.

The word Omnimedia described the company's intended scope. It was set up to house her work across several formats, including magazines, television, books and merchandise, under one corporate roof.

Going public changed how the business worked. An initial public offering lets outside investors buy shares that then trade on an exchange. After the October 1999 listing, any investor could own a stake in MSO. The company also took on the public financial reporting required of U.S.-listed firms.

The listing had a personal link to her past. Before she began catering from her home in Westport, Connecticut, in the 1970s, Stewart worked as a stockbroker. Her own company now had shares trading in the kind of market she once worked in.

MSO did not stay independent. Sequential Brands acquired Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia in 2015. The deal ended the company's run as a standalone public company trading as MSO.

That timeline gave the company about 18 years as an independent business, roughly 16 of them as a listed stock. The sale placed the company Stewart had founded under a new corporate owner. The name she had bought back from Time Warner in 1997 passed to Sequential Brands in 2015.

Martha Stewart Weddings launched in 1999 as a bridal magazine spun off from Martha Stewart Living. It took the Living brand's attention to food, flowers and hosting and applied it to one occasion: the wedding.

A spin-off let the company build on a name readers already knew. A new wedding title could start with the recognition of the Living brand rather than building an audience from nothing.

The subject also fit the hosting focus behind the brand. A wedding gathers many of those tasks into one event. Those include planning menus, arranging flowers, setting tables and timing a meal for a large group of guests.

The magazine format also suits the subject. A wedding is planned largely around how it will look, from the cake to the centerpieces. A print title can show those details in photographs that readers can keep and return to while they plan.

A bridal magazine serves a different reader than a general home title does. Someone interested in cooking or decorating may keep reading a home magazine for years. Someone planning a wedding has a fixed deadline. That need usually ends once the event is over.

That difference shapes how a bridal title works. Its audience turns over as each group of couples marries and a new group begins planning. A separate magazine can serve those readers without reshaping the main title around a single event.

Bridal publishing also connects readers with a specific set of businesses. Wedding planning involves decisions about dresses, rings, venues, invitations, flowers and gift registries. A magazine built around the wedding put the Martha Stewart brand in front of readers making those choices.

That concentration of purchases is what makes a bridal audience valuable to advertisers. A dressmaker, jeweler or stationer can reach readers at the moment they are deciding what to buy.

The title extended the Living brand into a new category of publishing while keeping its subject matter close to the brand's roots in entertaining.

Martha Stewart Living Radio was a satellite radio channel that launched on Sirius in the mid-2000s. It carried the Martha Stewart Living name into audio.

The channel arrived while Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia controlled the brand. For the company, radio became one more outlet for a name it already used across print, television and retail.

Sirius sold its service by subscription. Listeners paid for access to its full lineup of channels. They did not tune in free over the air, as they would with a local AM or FM station. A Martha Stewart channel on Sirius therefore reached people who had already chosen to pay for satellite programming.

Sirius built its lineup from many dedicated channels, each devoted to a single genre, topic or personality. That format gave a lifestyle brand room for a full channel of its own, rather than a short segment inside someone else's programming.

Satellite delivery also shaped where that audience could listen. Sirius programming reached listeners through dedicated receivers, many of them installed in cars. A satellite signal does not fade at the edge of a city's broadcast range, as a terrestrial station's signal does. That gave one channel national reach across the U.S.

Audio changed how the brand's material reached people. The magazine relied on photography. The television shows relied on on-screen demonstration. A radio channel had neither. Its content had to work through the spoken word alone.

That limit tested how much of the brand depended on visuals. A recipe or a cleaning method can be explained aloud, step by step. A table setting or a finished craft project is harder to convey without pictures.

The channel kept the Living title rather than introducing a new label. That choice tied the radio channel to the magazine and the syndicated show that shared the name. A listener who already knew one of them could recognize the others.

The Martha Stewart Collection is a home goods line that launched at Macy's $M in 2007. It followed her Kmart-era retail partnership and gave the Martha Stewart brand a new home in a U.S. department store chain.

The switch changed the kind of store carrying her name. Kmart was a discount chain built around low prices. Macy's is a department store, where home goods sit alongside clothing, beauty and other categories under one roof. That put the brand in front of a different set of shoppers.

The move also changed how the products were presented. In a discount store, a product competes mostly on price. In a department store, it sits in a setting built around browsing, displays and named labels. A line carrying her name fit that setting. Her name worked as the label.

The underlying model stayed the same. A national retailer sold a home goods range under her name through its own stores and staff. Her business did not need to open or run shops of its own to reach customers. The retailer handled store space, stock and checkout. Her side supplied the name and the brand identity behind it.

The Macy's line also connected to her media work. The Martha Stewart Show was on daytime television when the collection arrived. Her satellite radio channel was on the air in the same period. A viewer or listener who knew her name could then find it on department store goods.

The collection launched while Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia, the publicly traded company built around her brand, oversaw her media and merchandising businesses. That arrangement placed a department store line alongside the company's magazines, television programs and radio channel.

In that sense, the collection carried the brand's household subject matter from the page and the screen onto store shelves. The same name now covered what a reader learned and what a shopper bought.
