#5448. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5447. Tornado damage and insurance: what homeowners, renters and car policies cover

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Insurance usually covers tornado damage, and these 10 coverage areas explain what homeowners, renters and car policies pay for, from roofs and belongings to hotel bills

Insurers do not treat a tornado as a special event. On a standard policy, a tornado counts as windstorm damage. That single classification settles most coverage questions before a claim is ever filed.

Does insurance cover tornado damage? In most cases, yes. Standard homeowners forms such as the HO-3 include wind among the perils they cover, and tornadoes are not a standard exclusion. The harder questions sit in the details: which policy pays, how much it pays and what the policyholder pays first.

Three types of policy usually come into play after a tornado. A homeowners policy can pay to repair the house, replace belongings and cover the cost of living elsewhere during repairs. A renters policy protects a tenant's possessions and temporary housing costs. It leaves the building itself to the landlord's insurer. An auto policy pays for a damaged car only if it includes the right optional coverage.

Each of those policies is built from separate parts with separate limits. Damage to a roof, a detached garage, a sofa and a parked sedan can fall under four different coverages. Each coverage has its own limit. The home and auto policies each carry their own deductible. Some homeowners policies also apply a distinct deductible to wind and hail losses. That deductible changes how much the policyholder pays before coverage begins.

Coverage also depends on the specific policy form, any endorsements added to it and the state where the property sits. Two neighbors on the same street can hold policies that respond differently to the same storm. The declarations page — the summary at the front of a policy — lists the coverages, limits and deductibles that apply. An insurance agent or the insurer can explain any terms that remain unclear.

The 10 slides that follow walk through a selection of coverage areas that matter after a tornado. They cover the structure of a home, outbuildings, personal property, temporary living costs and wind deductibles. They also cover renters policies, comprehensive and liability-only car insurance, emergency repairs and the claims process. Each slide explains what a policy typically pays for, where coverage stops and what to check before a storm arrives.

A standard homeowners policy generally pays to repair or rebuild a house damaged by a tornado. On the ISO HO-3, a widely used homeowners form, that payment comes from dwelling coverage, also known as Coverage A.

This part of the policy applies to the home and to structures attached to it, such as an attached garage, porch or deck. It also extends to the parts built into the house. Those include the roof, walls, windows, flooring, plumbing, electrical wiring and heating and cooling systems.

Tornado damage to a house can take many forms. Wind can strip shingles, collapse a wall or blow out windows. Flying debris can punch through siding, and a falling tree can crush part of a roof. When wind caused the damage, each of these losses falls under the dwelling portion of the policy.

The HO-3 covers the dwelling on an open-perils basis. Under that approach, the policy pays for any cause of physical loss unless the form specifically excludes it. Wind, including a tornado, is not on that list of exclusions.

The exclusions that do exist still matter after a severe storm. Flood is excluded from standard homeowners policies. Water that rises from the ground, overflows a river or arrives as storm surge counts as flood damage, not tornado damage. That holds even when the same weather system produced both. Flood protection requires a separate policy, either through the National Flood Insurance Program, which FEMA manages, or from a private flood insurer.

Earthquake damage falls under a separate exclusion. Homeowners who want that protection need a dedicated earthquake policy or an endorsement added to their existing coverage.

Wear and tear and poor maintenance are also excluded under the HO-3. An insurer may decline to pay for roof deterioration that existed before the storm while still paying for the damage the tornado itself caused.

Coverage A pays only up to the dwelling limit listed on the policy's declarations page. That limit is meant to reflect the cost of rebuilding the house, not its market value or the value of the land beneath it.

A standard homeowners policy pays for tornado damage to a detached garage, shed or fence through other structures coverage, known as Coverage B. This coverage has its own limit, separate from the limit on the house itself.

The dividing line is physical. The ISO HO-3 form defines other structures as those on the residence premises that are set apart from the dwelling by clear space. A structure connected to the house only by a fence, a utility line or a similar connection still counts as an other structure. A garage that shares a wall with the house does not. That garage falls under dwelling coverage instead.

The definition reaches well beyond a backyard shed. A detached garage, a fence along the property line, a gazebo, a pergola, a freestanding carport and a guest cottage can all qualify, depending on how the policy is written. On the HO-3 form, these structures are covered on the same open-perils basis as the house. Wind from a tornado is a covered cause of loss.

Windstorms can push trees onto garages, sheds and fences. When a tree lands on a covered structure, the damage to that structure is part of the claim. Replacing the tree itself is a different matter. The ISO HO-3 form covers trees, shrubs and plants only for a short list of perils, and windstorm is not on that list.

Some structures are carved out. The HO-3 form does not cover an other structure rented to someone who is not a tenant of the dwelling, unless it is used only as a private garage. The form also excludes structures used for business or from which a business is conducted. A detached workshop where a homeowner runs a business may need an endorsement or a commercial policy.

The contents of a shed or garage raise a separate question. Lawn mowers, tools and bicycles stored there are belongings, not structures. They fall under the policy's personal property coverage.

The Coverage B limit is set when the policy is written and appears on the declarations page. In the ISO form, using it does not reduce the dwelling limit. A homeowner with a large detached garage, a barn or a long run of fencing can compare that limit with the cost of rebuilding those structures. An insurer or agent can raise the limit if it falls short.

Personal property coverage, listed as Coverage C on a standard homeowners policy, pays for belongings a tornado damages or destroys. The size of the check depends on whether the policy settles claims at replacement cost or at actual cash value.

Coverage C applies to the things inside a home rather than the building itself. Furniture, clothing, electronics, kitchen appliances, bedding, books and tools all fall under it. On the ISO HO-3 form, this coverage works on a named-perils basis. Belongings are protected only against the specific causes of loss the policy lists. Windstorm or hail is one of those listed perils, and tornado damage falls under it.

That windstorm peril carries a condition that matters after a tornado. Rain, snow, sleet, sand or dust that damages belongings inside the house is covered only if the force of wind or hail first made an opening in the roof or a wall. Rain that blows in through a window left open does not meet that test. Contents soaked through a hole the storm tore in the roof generally do.

Coverage C also follows belongings away from the home. Under the HO-3 form, personal property is covered anywhere in the world. Luggage on a trip or a laptop at a relative's house can qualify if a tornado damages it there. The form sets a lower limit for belongings normally kept at a second residence.

The settlement method shapes the payout. Actual cash value pays what an item was worth at the moment of loss. The insurer starts with the cost to replace it and subtracts depreciation for age and wear. Replacement cost pays the price of a comparable new item, with no deduction for depreciation.

The gap shows up most with older belongings. A sofa bought years before a tornado has lost much of its value on paper. Under actual cash value, the payment reflects that worn value. Under replacement cost, it covers a similar new sofa.

The standard HO-3 form settles personal property at actual cash value. Replacement cost for contents usually requires an endorsement added to the policy. Many replacement cost endorsements pay in two stages. The insurer first pays actual cash value, then releases the withheld depreciation once the item is actually replaced.

Each policy also sets a Coverage C limit, and some categories, such as cash, carry lower sub-limits. The declarations page shows that limit and whether replacement cost applies to belongings.

Loss of use coverage, listed as Coverage D on a standard homeowners policy, pays the extra cost of living elsewhere when tornado damage makes a house unfit to live in. It covers the gap between temporary living costs and a household's normal spending, not the full bill.

That gap is called additional living expenses, often shortened to ALE. The coverage is meant to let a household keep its usual standard of living while the home is repaired. A family that normally cooks at home but must eat in restaurants can claim the added food cost. Groceries the family would have bought anyway are not part of the payment.

Typical additional living expenses include a hotel room, a short-term rental or a furnished apartment. They can also include extra mileage from a longer commute, laundromat costs and pet boarding. Each item must be an increase caused by the displacement.

Costs that continue as usual are generally not covered. A monthly mortgage payment, for example, remains the homeowner's responsibility. That bill would have come due whether or not the tornado struck. Bills that stop during the displacement, such as a canceled utility service, can reduce the amount the insurer owes.

On the standard ISO HO-3 form, payment lasts for the shortest time needed to repair or replace the damage. If the household instead moves permanently, payment runs for the shortest time needed to settle elsewhere. Coverage D also carries its own dollar limit, shown on the declarations page. Some policies cap the time period as well.

Loss of use has a second part that matters for owners who rent out part of their property. Fair rental value covers rent lost from a tenant's unit made unlivable by covered damage. Expenses that stop while the unit sits empty are subtracted.

A related provision applies even when the house itself is intact. If a civil authority bars residents from a neighborhood because a covered peril damaged nearby property, the policy can pay additional living expenses for a limited period.

Receipts are the evidence behind a loss of use claim. Hotel folios, restaurant checks, fuel receipts and rental agreements should be kept from the first night away. A record of normal monthly spending before the tornado helps show which costs are additional.

A tornado claim on a homeowners policy may carry a separate wind and hail deductible instead of the policy's standard deductible. Some insurers in some states use this structure. On a policy that includes one, it sets the homeowner's share of a tornado repair bill.

A deductible is the share of a covered loss that the policyholder absorbs. The insurer subtracts it from the claim payment rather than collecting it as a separate bill. If the cost of the damage comes in below the deductible, the insurer pays nothing on that claim.

Many homeowners policies list one deductible that applies to most covered perils. It is usually written as a flat dollar amount. That amount stays the same no matter how large the house's coverage limit is.

A wind and hail deductible works differently on policies that include one. It applies only to losses caused by windstorm or hail. Tornado damage falls into that category. Other covered losses, such as a kitchen fire, still go through the standard deductible.

Wind and hail deductibles are often expressed as a percentage of the dwelling coverage limit. The percentage is calculated against the insured value of the house, not against the size of the claim. A home insured for a higher amount therefore carries a larger dollar deductible at the same percentage. Identical roof damage on two houses can leave their owners with different out-of-pocket costs if the houses are insured for different amounts.

Whether a policy uses a percentage, a flat amount or no separate wind deductible at all varies by insurer and by state. Some policies also carry a separate hurricane or named-storm deductible. The policy language defines when each one applies.

The declarations page lists every deductible on the policy and how each is calculated. Homeowners who cannot find a wind or hail deductible there, or who are unsure which one governs a tornado loss, can ask their insurer or agent before a storm hits. Deductible choices usually affect the premium. A higher deductible generally lowers the cost of the policy, while a lower one raises it.

Renters insurance pays for a tenant's own belongings and extra living costs after a tornado, but not for the building itself. The standard renters form, known as HO-4, lists windstorm as a covered peril. That brings tornado damage within its scope.

The policy splits its protection into separate parts. Personal property coverage applies to furniture, clothing, electronics, kitchenware and other possessions a tornado destroys or damages. Loss of use coverage helps pay for somewhere else to stay when the rental unit cannot be lived in after the storm.

The walls, roof, windows and floors belong to the landlord, and so does the job of insuring them. Repairs to the structure fall under the landlord's property policy. That policy does not pay to replace a tenant's sofa or laptop. A renter without their own coverage generally absorbs the cost of lost possessions.

HO-4 covers belongings on a named-perils basis. That makes the exact wording of each peril important. The windstorm peril on standard forms does not pay for rain or dust that blows inside unless wind first breaks through the roof or a wall. A tornado that tears off part of a roof and lets rain soak belongings in a bedroom fits that description. Water seeping under a door during a storm does not.

The standard form also includes a limited amount of coverage for building additions and alterations. This applies to improvements a tenant paid for inside the unit, such as built-in shelving or upgraded fixtures. The amount is tied to the personal property limit and varies by policy.

Belongings do not have to be inside the apartment to be covered. Personal property coverage on the standard form extends to possessions away from the residence, such as items in a storage unit. Some policies set lower limits for property kept elsewhere.

A renters policy typically protects the named policyholder and relatives who live in the same household. An unrelated roommate usually needs a separate policy or must be added to the existing one.

Coverage amounts and endorsements differ by insurer and state. The declarations page shows the personal property and loss of use limits. An insurer or agent can confirm how a specific policy treats wind damage.

Comprehensive coverage is the part of a car insurance policy that pays for tornado damage to the policyholder's own vehicle. It handles losses that don't come from a crash, including wind, hail, falling trees and debris thrown by a storm.

Comprehensive is optional coverage. A driver has to add it to a policy, and it is not included automatically. Anyone unsure whether it is on their policy can check the declarations page. That page lists each coverage the driver carries and the deductible attached to it.

A tornado can damage a car in several ways, and comprehensive covers each of them. A falling tree limb can crush a car's roof. Wind can shove a vehicle into a wall or tip it over in a parking lot. Gravel, shingles and sheet metal carried by the wind can shatter windows and dent body panels. Hail from the same storm is covered the same way.

Every comprehensive claim is subject to the deductible the policyholder chose when buying the coverage. The insurer subtracts that amount from the payout. If the repair bill comes in below the deductible, a claim produces no payment. A higher deductible generally lowers the premium. It also leaves the driver paying more out of pocket after a storm.

When repairs would cost more than the car is worth, the insurer may declare it a total loss. In that case the insurer pays the vehicle's actual cash value, minus the deductible, instead of paying for repairs. A driver who owes more on a car loan than the car is worth can be left with a remaining balance. Gap $GPS insurance is the optional coverage designed to pay that difference.

Lenders and leasing companies commonly require comprehensive coverage on financed or leased vehicles. Drivers who own their cars outright decide for themselves whether to carry it.

Comprehensive has to be on the policy before the storm arrives. Adding it afterward does not cover damage that has already happened.

A car insured only for liability has no coverage for tornado damage. Liability insurance pays for injuries and property damage a driver causes to other people. It does not pay to repair or replace the driver's own vehicle.

Most states require drivers to carry liability coverage, and it comes in two parts. Bodily injury liability covers other people's medical costs and related losses after a crash the policyholder causes. Property damage liability covers things such as another driver's car, a fence or a storefront. Neither part responds when a storm damages the insured car itself.

A tornado also leaves no at-fault driver to pursue. If a falling tree limb crushes a parked car during a storm, there is generally no other driver's liability policy to claim against. Uninsured motorist property damage coverage, where a policy includes it, is built for losses caused by an uninsured driver. It does not apply to a weather event.

Collision coverage is the other part of a car policy that might seem relevant. It pays when a car hits another vehicle or an object, or when it rolls over. Damage from wind, hail and flying debris generally falls outside it. Insurers classify those losses as comprehensive claims. Comprehensive is the coverage that applies to a tornado.

"Full coverage" is an informal term rather than a type of policy. It usually describes a policy that combines liability with both comprehensive and collision. A driver who uses the phrase should still check the declarations page to see which coverages are actually listed.

Lenders and leasing companies commonly require comprehensive and collision on a financed or leased car. A driver who owns a car outright can drop those coverages and keep only liability. In that case, the cost of tornado damage to the car falls on the owner.

A homeowners or renters policy will not fill the gap. Standard home insurance forms exclude motor vehicles from personal property coverage. Comprehensive has to be on the auto policy before a storm hits. Insurers can temporarily stop writing new coverage in an area when severe weather is approaching. This practice is known as a binding moratorium.

Debris removal coverage on a standard homeowners policy generally pays to clear away wreckage left when a tornado damages covered property. The same policy also pays for reasonable emergency repairs, such as tarping a roof, that protect the home from further damage.

On the ISO HO-3 form, both appear as additional coverages. Debris removal pays to clear the wreckage of a damaged roof, wall or other insured structure. That cost is usually counted inside the limit for the damaged property rather than paid on top of it. The form does allow some extra room when the property's limit has been used up. The declarations page and the policy wording show how a specific policy handles it.

Fallen trees follow narrower rules. Many policies pay to remove a tree knocked down by wind only when it strikes a covered structure or blocks a driveway. They often cap the amount per tree and per loss. A tree that lands in an open yard may not qualify for removal at all. When a neighbor's tree falls onto a house, the homeowner's own policy generally handles the claim.

Emergency repairs connect to a duty the policy places on the policyholder. After a loss, the homeowner is expected to protect the property from further damage. Typical steps include stretching a tarp over a torn roof, boarding up broken windows and covering holes in exterior walls. The reasonable repairs coverage pays for necessary measures of this kind. It does not increase the limit that applies to the property being repaired.

The duty carries consequences. The HO-3 form excludes loss caused by neglect, meaning a failure to use reasonable means to save and preserve property after a loss. Rain that pours through an uncovered opening for days can become a separate loss the policy does not pay for.

The policy also asks for an accurate record of repair expenses. That means contractor invoices, receipts for tarps, plywood and fasteners, and notes on what work was done and when.

Temporary fixes are not the same as permanent repairs. A tarp or sheet of plywood is meant to hold until an adjuster inspects the damage and the permanent work is settled through the claim. The insurer or agent can confirm which costs count as emergency measures under a given policy.

A tornado insurance claim starts with two steps: documenting the damage thoroughly and notifying the insurer or agent promptly. If the home has a mortgage, the payment for structural repairs will often be made out to both the homeowner and the lender.

Photos and video taken before cleanup begins show the damage as the storm left it. Wide shots record the overall condition of the house and the lot. Close-ups capture specific problems, such as missing shingles, broken windows, cracked siding or a tree resting on the roof. Footage of each room, including ceilings and floors, records interior damage that can be hard to describe later.

A home inventory covers the belongings side of the claim. It lists each damaged or destroyed item with a description and its approximate age. Where known, it also records the brand, model and purchase price. An inventory made before the storm makes this step faster. One assembled afterward still gives the insurer a structured record to review.

Damaged items should generally be kept until the insurer has seen them. Standard homeowners forms ask the policyholder to show the damaged property to the insurer as often as reasonably required. Throwing out a ruined sofa or appliance before an adjuster sees it can complicate that part of the claim.

The insurer can be reached by phone, through its app or website, or through the agent who sold the policy. The policy number and declarations page are useful to have on hand for the first call. The insurer typically assigns a claim number and sends an adjuster to inspect the property. A written log of each conversation, with the date, the representative's name and what was agreed, creates a paper trail.

The insurer may also ask for a signed, sworn proof of loss. This document states the amount being claimed and the circumstances of the damage.

Mortgage lenders appear on claim checks because of the mortgage clause in the homeowners policy. That clause recognizes the lender's financial interest in the house. A check for dwelling repairs often lists both the homeowner and the lender as payees. Both parties must endorse it before the money can be used. The lender may hold the funds and release them in stages as repairs progress, sometimes after an inspection. Contacting the lender's insurance claims or loss draft department early clarifies what paperwork it requires.

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5445. Tornadoes by state: 10 U.S. states ranked by yearly average, Texas to Minnesota

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tornadoes by state, from Texas's yearly average of 124 to Minnesota's 46: 10 U.S. states ranked by Storm Prediction Center data for 2003 to 2022, with notable storms

Texas averaged 124 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, the highest figure among the 48 states in a ranking built on Storm Prediction Center data. Kansas placed second at 87. That puts Texas 37 tornadoes a year ahead of its nearest rival.

Tornadoes by state vary widely, and the yearly averages for that 20-year window show where the storms touch down most often. Several states share a rank because of ties. This piece covers 10 of them, running from Texas down to Florida and Minnesota, which tie for ninth at 46 tornadoes a year. Louisiana and Nebraska come next in the full table at 45.

A yearly average measures how often tornadoes strike, not how strong they are. Strength is rated on the Enhanced Fujita scale, or EF scale, which sorts tornadoes by wind speed. EF0 covers winds of 65 to 85 mph, and EF1 runs from 86 to 110 mph. EF2 spans 111 to 135 mph, and EF3 covers 136 to 165 mph. EF4 storms reach 166 to 200 mph. Anything above 200 mph is an EF5.

Tornado activity peaks in May and June. Individual states run on their own calendars. In Missouri, the peak stretches from April through June, though a tornado can strike there in any month. Iowa's activity peaks from May through July.

Terrain and air masses shape each state's count. Kansas sits in the middle of Tornado Alley, where flat land offers few natural features to slow a storm. The pattern shifts farther east. In Alabama, the Tennessee Valley and the Appalachian foothills tend to funnel storms. Flat, open farmland in northern and central Mississippi favors long-lived tornadoes. In Missouri, warm, humid Gulf air collides with cooler air from the Rockies and the upper Midwest.

Each slide gives a state's rank and yearly average, then the conditions behind its count. It also covers storms that shaped each state's history, from the 1925 Tri-State Tornado in Illinois, the deadliest in U.S. history, to the 2011 Joplin EF5 in Missouri.

Texas records more tornadoes than any other state, averaging 124 a year from 2003 to 2022. That figure comes from Storm Prediction Center data compiled in a state ranking by WorldAtlas.

Spread across a calendar, an average of 124 works out to more than two tornadoes a week.

WorldAtlas links much of the Texas total to the state's size. Its territory covers very different environments. Flat plains dominate the west, while the east is humid and forested.

Tornadoes do not fall evenly across that territory. WorldAtlas places most of the activity in two regions. One is the Panhandle, the northernmost part of the state. The other is northeastern Texas.

Large cities sit within reach of these storms. Dallas, Fort Worth and Houston have each experienced damaging tornadoes. Dallas and Fort Worth are in north Texas.

Houston sits on the upper Texas coast, outside both of the regions WorldAtlas names. Its record shows that damaging tornadoes in Texas are not limited to the areas where they are most common.

WorldAtlas highlights the 1953 Waco tornado. It killed 114 people and injured about 600 more.

The storm also damaged around 1,600 buildings and an estimated 2,000 vehicles.

Kansas averages 87 tornadoes a year, the second-highest count of any state in Storm Prediction Center data for 2003 to 2022. Only Texas records more.

Kansas logs about 70% as many tornadoes a year as Texas. Texas also spans several times as much land. The Kansas total is packed into a far smaller area.

Kansas runs 21 tornadoes a year ahead of Oklahoma, which ranks third at 66. Missouri, its neighbor to the east, averages 53 a year, or 34 fewer than Kansas.

The 87 figure is an average. It describes a typical year across two decades of data rather than any single season. Individual years can land above or below it.

WorldAtlas places Kansas in the middle of Tornado Alley. Within the state, tornado activity concentrates in the central and western regions.

The land across those regions is flat. Few natural features stand in a storm's path to slow it down, WorldAtlas notes.

Kansans prepare for that exposure. Warning systems are common across the state, and so are storm shelters. Home safe rooms are common as well. A safe room is a reinforced room in a home, built to shield the people in it from a tornado's winds.

In 2007, a tornado struck the city of Greensburg, Kansas. It destroyed 95% of the city. Destruction on that scale left little of Greensburg standing.

This Kansas slide runs about 226 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source supports only the state's rank and yearly average, its Tornado Alley location, its flat central and western terrain, common warning systems, shelters and safe rooms, and the 95% destruction of Greensburg in 2007. No approved web detail covers Kansas.

Oklahoma ranks third among U.S. states for tornadoes, with an average of 66 a year from 2003 to 2022. Most of them touch down in the central and northern parts of the state, with the heaviest concentration along the Interstate 35 corridor.

Interstate 35 crosses Oklahoma from the Texas line to the Kansas line. It passes through Oklahoma City, the state capital and largest city, along the way. The state's busiest tornado zone therefore follows one of its main north-south routes.

The only two states with higher yearly averages border Oklahoma: Texas to the south and Kansas to the north. Mississippi follows in fourth place at 64 a year, two fewer than Oklahoma.

Tornadoes in Oklahoma usually arrive in clusters during spring outbreaks rather than one at a time.

WorldAtlas notes that Oklahoma sees many EF4 and EF5 tornadoes, the two most violent ratings on the Enhanced Fujita scale.

Oklahoma City and Tulsa are both growing urban centers. Tulsa, the state's second-largest city, sits in the northeast, away from Interstate 35.

The Woodward $WWD tornado of April 9, 1947, remains one of the deadliest in Oklahoma's history. It struck the town of Woodward in the northwestern part of the state. The storm killed 116 people and injured 782.

Woodward lies well west of Interstate 35. Deadly tornadoes in Oklahoma have struck outside the corridor as well.

WorldAtlas credits the Bridge Creek-Moore tornado with winds of 321 mph. It describes that figure as the highest wind speed ever recorded on Earth. The storm struck on May 3, 1999. Its reported speed sits more than 100 mph above the threshold for an EF5 rating.

Bridge Creek, the community named first, lies southwest of Oklahoma City in Grady County. Moore is a suburb just south of Oklahoma City on Interstate 35. The storm's path ran through the same central corridor where the state's tornado activity is most concentrated.

Mississippi averages 64 tornadoes a year, the fourth-highest count among U.S. states in Storm Prediction Center data for 2003 to 2022. Its most severe tornadoes tend to strike the northern and central parts of the state.

A narrow margin separates Mississippi from the states ranked on either side of it. Oklahoma, in third place, averages two more tornadoes a year. Alabama, Mississippi's eastern neighbor, averages one fewer and ranks fifth.

Terrain helps explain where the worst storms occur. Much of northern and central Mississippi is flat, open farmland. WorldAtlas notes that this kind of landscape makes long-lived tornadoes likely.

A long-lived tornado stays on the ground for longer. That gives a single storm more distance over which to cause damage before it dissipates.

The state's settlement pattern shapes who takes the damage. Mississippi has few major metropolitan areas. Tornado impacts therefore often land on small towns rather than big cities.

Larger communities have not been spared. Jackson, the state capital, has had significant tornado events. So have Tupelo and Corinth, two cities in northeastern Mississippi. Both sit in the northern part of the state, where the most severe storms tend to occur.

WorldAtlas singles out a 1971 EF4 tornado around the Issaquena-Grenada area. That storm killed 58 people and injured almost 800.

An EF4 rating sits second from the top of the Enhanced Fujita scale. Only EF5 tornadoes rank higher.

The yearly average of 64 counts how often tornadoes touch down in Mississippi. It does not measure how strong they are. The 1971 storm shows what a single high-end tornado can do in a state where most storms fall on small communities.

Alabama averaged 63 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, placing fifth in the WorldAtlas ranking of Storm Prediction Center data. Its 2011 tornado outbreak hit Tuscaloosa, northern Birmingham and two small towns farther north.

That count sits one tornado a year behind Mississippi, at 64, and three behind Oklahoma, at 66. Illinois ranks sixth with 57, six fewer than Alabama. Alabama's yearly total is a little more than half the 124 that Texas averages.

Those gaps are narrow. Alabama and Mississippi, two Southeast states, each sit within three tornadoes a year of Oklahoma, a Plains state.

WorldAtlas ties much of the state's tornado activity to its landscape. It reports that the Tennessee Valley across northern Alabama and the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains tend to funnel storms.

Those storms have reached the state's cities. Birmingham and Huntsville have both taken significant tornado hits.

In 2011, an EF4 tornado struck Tuscaloosa and the northern part of Birmingham. EF4 is the second-highest rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale.

The same year, an EF5 tornado hit the towns of Phil Campbell and Hackleburg. EF5 is the scale's top category, covering the strongest winds.

The two storms show the outbreak's range. The EF4 cut through urban areas, while the EF5 struck small communities. Both city and countryside took direct hits from the two strongest tornado ratings.

WorldAtlas estimates the 2011 damage at about $4.3 billion. It puts the death toll at about 240 people in Alabama, with about 110 more in nearby states.

Those estimates add up to roughly 350 deaths, more than two-thirds of them in Alabama. The toll beyond its borders shows the outbreak was a regional event, not a single-state one.

The 2003 to 2022 window behind Alabama's average includes the 2011 outbreak year. Over those 20 years, an average of 63 a year works out to roughly 1,260 tornadoes.

Illinois averaged 57 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, the sixth-highest yearly count in a ranking of states built on Storm Prediction Center data. The state's history also includes the Tri-State Tornado of 1925.

That average puts Illinois six tornadoes a year behind Alabama, which averaged 63. It sits four a year ahead of Missouri and Iowa, which tie for seventh at 53. Illinois holds sixth place on its own, with no other state sharing its count.

Illinois lies where warm and cool air masses converge. That collision builds severe thunderstorms, which are most frequent in early summer. Most of the tornadoes these storms produce in Illinois are moderate in strength rather than violent.

The Illinois season starts well before summer. Roughly four of every five Illinois tornadoes form between the start of April and the end of June, according to the National Weather Service. They usually strike in the late afternoon or early evening.

Stronger tornadoes keep a similar calendar. The National Weather Service reports that April is the peak month for strong-to-violent tornado activity in its Chicago forecast area. May and June follow closely, and August rounds out the top four months. Those rankings come from one forecast office's territory around Chicago, not from statewide records.

Late-season storms are part of the record, too. Significant tornadoes in the eight-county Chicago metro area have occurred as often in November as in July, according to a separate National Weather Service analysis. For the Chicago region, the threat of a significant tornado does not end when summer does.

The Tri-State Tornado killed nearly 700 people, most of them in southern Illinois. No tornado in U.S. history has killed more. Its toll fell at the far end of the state from the Chicago area covered by the forecast-office figures. It stands apart in a state where most tornadoes stay moderate.

Missouri averaged 53 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, tying Iowa for seventh place in the national ranking. That period includes the 2011 Joplin tornado, which earned EF5, the top rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale.

Missouri sits where the Great Plains meet the Mississippi Valley. That position puts it in the path of two contrasting air masses. Warm, humid air flows north from the Gulf. Cooler air arrives from the Rockies and the upper Midwest. Severe storms develop along the boundary where the two collide.

Tornado activity in Missouri peaks from April through June. The risk does not end with spring. Tornadoes can form in the state in any month of the year. A quiet stretch in late summer or winter does not rule out a storm.

In the ranking, Missouri trails sixth-place Illinois by four tornadoes a year. It sits seven a year ahead of Florida and Minnesota, which share ninth place. Texas, in first, averages more than twice Missouri's count.

Those numbers place Missouri in a tight middle band of the table. A handful of tornadoes a year separates it from the states just above and below it. The gap to the top is far wider. Missouri's tie with Iowa, its neighbor to the north, adds to that clustering.

Both of Missouri's largest metro areas have been affected. St. Louis sits on the state's eastern border along the Mississippi River. Kansas City sits on its western border. Each has been in the path of tornadoes. With major cities at both edges of the state, tornado risk in Missouri reaches well beyond farmland and small towns.

The Joplin tornado struck southwestern Missouri in 2011. It killed 158 people and injured well over 1,100 others. Its death toll is higher than those of Oklahoma's 1947 Woodward $WWD tornado and the 1953 Waco tornado in Texas. That toll came from a single tornado in a state that ranks seventh, not first, for how often tornadoes strike.

Iowa's tornado season peaks from May through July. The state averaged 53 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, tying Missouri for seventh in the WorldAtlas ranking of Storm Prediction Center data.

Iowa's peak runs a month later than Missouri's, which stretches from April through June. It also carries past the broader May and June peak into midsummer.

WorldAtlas reports that wind shear and unstable air feed Iowa's storms during those months.

Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction with height. It can set air spinning horizontally in the lower atmosphere. A thunderstorm's updraft can then tilt that spin upright.

Unstable air lets warm, moist air near the ground rise quickly. That rising air builds the tall storm clouds that can produce tornadoes.

Iowa has seen notable outbreaks in recent years, according to WorldAtlas. Some produced long-track tornadoes with paths of more than 25 miles. Others brought high-intensity storms. One outbreak in 2024 struck near Minden, Iowa.

Most of Iowa is rural, and much of its land is farmed. That landscape means tornadoes in the state more often damage fields than towns or cities.

Iowa's yearly count matches that of Missouri, its neighbor to the south. Illinois, across the Mississippi River to the east, averaged 57 a year, four more than Iowa.

Florida averaged 46 tornadoes a year from 2003 to 2022, based on Storm Prediction Center data compiled by WorldAtlas. That count ties Florida with Minnesota for ninth place in the ranking.

The tie links two states at opposite ends of the country. Florida is a southeastern peninsula. Minnesota sits on the Canadian border. Over the same period, both reached the same yearly average.

Missouri and Iowa share seventh place at 53 tornadoes a year. That leaves Florida seven a year behind them.

Florida tornadoes have caused severe damage. In one outbreak, the deadliest tornado passed through Kissimmee, a city in central Florida. The Morningside Acres Mobile Home Park and the Ponderosa Recreational Vehicle Park took the most severe damage from that storm.

Minnesota averages 46 tornadoes a year, tying Florida for ninth place in the WorldAtlas ranking built on Storm Prediction Center data for 2003 to 2022. It is the northernmost of the 10 states covered here.

The tie pairs Minnesota with Florida, the southernmost state on this list. The two share an identical yearly average from opposite ends of the country.

Minnesota's count sits well below the top of the ranking. Texas, in first place, averages 78 more tornadoes a year. Kansas, in second, averages 41 more.

Tornado season in Minnesota falls in June or July, according to NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory. The agency groups the state with the northern Plains and upper Midwest when it describes when tornado season arrives in different parts of the country.

#5444. Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 9:51 amOctober 28, 2026 at 10:17 am

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan.

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”

T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

#5443. Tornado preparation for pet owners: kits, shelter rooms and carriers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tornado safety for pets starts before the sirens: 10 steps covering emergency kits, ID, shelter rooms, carriers, anxious dogs and finding a lost pet after the storm

A tornado warning can leave a household very little time to act. That window rarely allows for a search under the bed for a hiding cat or a hunt through the yard for a dog. The choices that keep animals safe during a tornado are made weeks or months earlier. They come down to three things: where the pets will shelter, which supplies sit ready and how fast every animal in the home can be found and contained.

Fear changes how animals behave. A dog that comes when called on an ordinary afternoon may bolt at the sound of a storm. A cat may wedge itself into the smallest gap it can find. Birds, rabbits and reptiles cannot reach safety on their own. They depend on an owner to carry them there.

The safest place for a pet is the same as the safest place for a person. That means a basement, a storm cellar or an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Mobile homes are not safe shelter for people or animals. Households that live in one need a sturdier location planned well before storm season.

Tornado safety for pets also depends on reading the alerts correctly. The National Weather Service issues a tornado watch when conditions could produce a tornado. A tornado warning means a tornado has been spotted or indicated by radar. A warning is the signal to take shelter immediately. A watch is the time to bring animals indoors and keep them within reach.

The 10 steps that follow move through three phases. Before the storm, they cover a pet emergency kit, microchip and ID tag details, and a prepared shelter spot. During the storm, they cover acting the moment a warning is issued, keeping pets in carriers, crates or on leashes, and handling a dog that panics. After the storm, they cover checking pets and property for debris, broken glass and downed power lines, and searching for an animal that got away.

The guide also reaches past dogs and cats. Birds, small mammals and reptiles need secure, covered enclosures that can be moved into the shelter room quickly. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can go straight to the stage or species that matters most to their household.

A pet emergency kit should hold food, water, medications, veterinary records and a recent photo of each animal, packed before tornado season begins. Disaster guidance from the Humane Society of the United States and the American Red Cross lists these items as the core of a pet kit.

The reason to pack early is time. Once a tornado warning is issued, there is rarely a chance to search cabinets for a pill bottle or a bag of kibble. A kit assembled well in advance turns a scramble into a single grab.

Food and water come first. Pack the food your pet already eats. A sudden change in diet can upset an animal's digestion during an event that is already stressful. Sealed, shelf-stable containers resist moisture and pests. Add bowls and a manual can opener if the food is canned. Set aside drinking water for the animals rather than counting on the household's own reserve.

Medications deserve their own waterproof bag. Include written dosing instructions. Those notes let a neighbor, relative or shelter worker give the right dose if the owner is injured or separated from the animal. A copy of each prescription helps with refills if the usual veterinary clinic is closed or damaged.

Records serve a different purpose. Boarding facilities and emergency animal shelters commonly ask for proof of rabies vaccination before accepting an animal. Store copies of vaccination history in a sealed plastic bag. Keep a digital version on a phone or cloud account as a backup. Add the name and phone number of the regular veterinarian.

The recent photo is easy to overlook. A clear, current image that shows markings and coloring makes it easier to describe an animal to others. A photo of the owner together with the pet also helps establish ownership.

Sanitation and comfort round out the kit. Waste bags, cat litter with a disposable tray, paper towels and disinfectant keep a small shelter room livable for hours. A familiar blanket or toy can help a frightened animal settle.

Store the kit in the spot where the household plans to shelter. That way it is already in place when the sirens sound. Review it before each storm season, and replace food, water and medications before they expire.

A microchip can only reunite a lost pet with its owner if the registry linked to that chip holds current contact details. Pair the chip with a collar ID tag, and check both before tornado season begins.

A microchip is a small passive transponder, roughly the size of a grain of rice. A veterinarian implants it under the skin, usually between the shoulder blades in dogs and cats. It has no battery and does not track location the way a GPS device does. It stores a unique identification number that a handheld scanner reads.

That number means nothing on its own. When a shelter or veterinary clinic scans a found animal, staff look up the number in a registry database to find the owner. If the phone number or address on file is out of date, the search stops there.

Registration is a separate step from implantation. Some chips are implanted at a shelter or by a breeder and never registered to the new owner. Others remain registered to a previous owner. A veterinarian can scan a pet to confirm the chip still reads and to retrieve its number. The owner can then contact the registry to check whose details are listed.

Contact details go stale after ordinary life changes. A move, a new phone number or a new email address all call for an update to the registry. Adding a second contact, such as a relative or friend who lives outside the area, gives a finder another person to reach. A tornado can damage a home or cut phone service across a neighborhood. A backup contact means the search does not depend on a single phone line.

A collar tag does a job a chip cannot. Anyone who finds the pet can read it on the spot, without a scanner or a trip to a clinic. A tag should show the owner's phone number at minimum. Collars and tags can slip off in debris or during a struggle. A chip stays in place when a tag is lost, so the two forms of ID cover for each other.

Keep a copy of the registry paperwork, including the chip number and the registry's name, with the pet's other records in the emergency kit. A paper copy means an owner can still reach the registry if a phone or computer is lost in the storm.

Pets should shelter in the same place as people during a tornado: a basement, a storm cellar or an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Choose that spot in advance and confirm it has room for every person and animal in the household.

Most tornado injuries come from flying debris and collapsing structures. Each wall between the shelter and the outdoors adds a layer of protection. Windows are among the first things to break. A small windowless space near the center of the house, such as a closet, bathroom or inner hallway, puts the most building between a pet and the storm.

Position matters in a basement too. The National Weather Service advises against sheltering directly beneath heavy objects resting on the floor above, such as a refrigerator, piano or waterbed. A spot under a sturdy workbench or heavy table offers better cover for people and smaller animals alike.

Mobile and manufactured homes are not safe shelter, even when tied down. Households living in one need a sturdier destination arranged before storm season, such as a friend's basement, a community storm shelter or a permanent building nearby. Pet policies differ from one location to the next. Confirm early that the chosen place will accept animals.

The room also needs to hold a frightened animal securely. A scared cat can squeeze behind a washer, under a cabinet or into an opening in a wall or ceiling, where it is hard to reach. Block $SQ those gaps before storms arrive. Bathrooms and laundry rooms often store cleaning products and medications. Move them out of a pet's reach.

Familiarity helps a pet settle when a storm arrives. Spend calm time in the shelter room with each animal, offer treats or a meal there and let pets explore it with the door closed. An animal that already knows the space is easier to bring in and keep there when the house is loud and tense.

Households with several pets should also plan how animals that do not get along will share the space. A dog and a cat that tolerate each other in a large house may not do so when confined together in a cramped closet. Decide beforehand which corner or section of the room each animal will occupy.

Bring pets into your shelter room the moment a tornado warning is issued for your area. The National Weather Service issues a warning when a tornado has been reported by spotters or indicated by weather radar. That is the signal to take shelter right away.

A tornado watch is a different alert. The National Weather Service issues a watch when weather conditions could produce a tornado. No tornado has been confirmed at that stage. For pet owners, a watch is the window to get organized while there is still time to do it calmly.

Use that window to account for every animal in the household. Bring outdoor pets inside. Close any pet doors so a dog or cat cannot slip back out into the yard. Keep each animal in a room where you can see it, rather than letting it roam the house.

Once a warning arrives, the priority shifts from preparation to speed. Move people and pets to the basement, storm cellar or interior room chosen ahead of time. Carry small animals or lead dogs straight there, and close the door behind you. Do not wait to see or hear the storm before acting. A warning means a tornado has already been detected.

A warning is not the time for a long search through the house. If one pet cannot be found quickly, the people in the household still need to reach shelter. That is the reason the watch period matters. Pets that are already gathered in one place can be moved in seconds instead of minutes.

Night storms add another complication. A warning issued while a household is asleep leaves little time to find pets in the dark. When a watch is in effect overnight, bring pets into the bedroom or the shelter room before going to sleep. That shortens the time needed to reach shelter if a warning wakes the household.

Stay in the shelter with your pets until the warning expires or local officials say the threat has passed. Animals may pace, whine or scratch at the door. Keep the door closed until the danger is over, then let them out one at a time.

Frightened pets can bolt, hide or slip through a gap in seconds. A carrier, crate or leash keeps each animal in one place inside the shelter room while a tornado passes.

Containment solves a timing problem. Once a warning sounds, there is no time to coax an animal out from behind an appliance or chase it from room to room. A pet that is already secured can be carried or walked to shelter in one trip.

Choose a carrier or crate large enough for the animal to stand up, turn around and lie down. Hard-sided carriers hold their shape if something falls against them. Soft-sided bags are lighter to carry down stairs. Either works if the door latches securely. Each pet should have its own carrier. Animals packed together under stress can fight or injure one another.

Store carriers where they can be grabbed quickly, in or beside the shelter room. An attic, a detached garage or the back of a crowded closet is a poor choice. A carrier buried under storage boxes is of little use once a warning has been issued.

Label each carrier with the pet's name and the owner's name and phone number. A luggage tag or a strip of tape works. If the home is damaged and a pet ends up with a neighbor or at an emergency shelter, that label helps responders match the animal to its owner.

For dogs, a sturdy leash clipped to a well-fitted collar or harness is the minimum. Many dogs find it harder to back out of a harness than a flat collar. Keep the leash attached inside the shelter room. A door may need to be opened during the storm. A loose dog can be through it before anyone reacts.

A crate inside the shelter room also stops pets from squeezing under shelving or into corners where they are hard to reach. A towel or familiar blanket inside makes the space more comfortable. A light cover draped over the crate can reduce visual stimulation for some animals.

Practice makes containment faster. Leave carriers open around the house in the weeks before storm season. Pets then treat them as ordinary furniture rather than a signal of a vet visit. An animal that walks into its crate willingly can be secured far more quickly than one that has to be chased.

A dog that fears storms needs a plan made well before the weather turns. Secure the dog early, keep it within arm's reach in the shelter and talk to a veterinarian ahead of storm season about ways to manage the fear.

Storm anxiety in dogs shows up in recognizable ways. A frightened dog may pant, pace, tremble, drool, whine or bark. Some dogs try to hide under furniture or in a closet. Others chew doors, scratch at walls or dig at floors in an attempt to get away from the noise.

That urge to flee is the main danger during a tornado. A panicked dog can slip through a door that is open for only a moment. It can also squeeze through a gap in a fence or back out of a loose collar. A dog that runs during severe weather faces flying debris and traffic. It may also end up far from home.

Many storm-anxious dogs start showing stress before the bad weather reaches the house. Each dog tends to have its own early signals, such as pacing, clinging to a person or refusing food. Learning those patterns gives an owner extra time to act.

Bring an anxious dog inside at the first of those signs. Close exterior doors and keep the dog in the same room as a family member. A snug harness is harder to back out of than a loose flat collar. That matters if the dog has to be moved in a hurry.

Familiar objects give a nervous dog something to settle into. Its own bed, a worn blanket or a favorite chew toy carries recognizable scents. Placing those items in the shelter area ahead of time means the dog arrives somewhere that already smells like home.

The owner's behavior matters too. A calm, steady voice and gentle contact give the dog a point of reference. Punishing a dog for fearful behavior can deepen the fear rather than reduce it.

For dogs with severe storm phobia, the first step is a visit to a veterinarian. A vet can rule out medical problems that make anxiety worse. The vet can also discuss whether anti-anxiety medication is appropriate and suggest a behavior plan. Owners can work with a veterinary behaviorist or a certified trainer on desensitization. That process pairs recorded storm sounds, played at low volume, with treats and play. The volume rises gradually over weeks. The training is meant to start during calm months, not the week a storm is forecast.

Cats, birds, reptiles and small mammals each need a secure, covered enclosure that can be carried into the shelter room in seconds. A plan built around a dog on a leash will not protect them. Each group reacts to danger in its own way and needs its own preparation.

Cats are often the hardest pets to gather in a hurry. A frightened cat tends to retreat into tight, hidden spaces. Common hiding spots include the back of a closet, the inside of a box spring and the gap behind a washing machine. Searching for a cat after a warning is issued uses up time meant for sheltering. Finding the cat while the weather is still calm, and closing it into one room, removes that search.

Birds startle easily. A panicked bird can injure itself by flapping against the bars of a large cage. A smaller travel cage is easier to carry and leaves less room for that kind of injury. Draping a light sheet or towel over the cage darkens the space. Darkness tends to settle a bird. Birds also have sensitive respiratory systems. Dust, insulation fibers and smoke from storm damage can harm them. Keeping the cage covered and away from damaged parts of the home limits that exposure.

Reptiles cannot generate their own body heat. Snakes, lizards and turtles rely on outside sources such as heat lamps and heating pads. A tornado can cut power for an extended period, and those heat sources go with it. An insulated container helps a reptile hold warmth through an outage. Large glass terrariums are heavy and can break. A sturdy plastic tub with air holes and a locking lid is easier to move. Snakes can slip through small gaps. A secure latch keeps them inside.

Rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils and ferrets fit in compact carriers. Rodents can chew through cardboard. Hard plastic or wire is the safer material. Rabbits have powerful hind legs and fragile spines. A rabbit that kicks while being lifted can injure its own back. Supporting its hindquarters during handling reduces that risk. Rabbits and guinea pigs are prey animals. A towel or small hide inside the carrier gives them somewhere to retreat.

Predators and prey should stay apart in the shelter room. A rabbit or hamster carrier placed beside a cat or ferret adds stress to an animal that is already frightened.

A pet left in the yard, tied to a post or shut inside a house the family has left has no way to reach safety when a tornado arrives. Every animal in the household belongs in the same shelter as its people.

Wind is only part of the danger. The National Weather Service identifies flying debris as the cause of most tornado deaths and injuries. An animal outdoors faces that debris with nothing solid overhead. A dog on a chain or a tie-out line is in a worse position. It cannot run, hide or crawl under anything sturdy.

Outdoor structures do not offer real protection. A doghouse, a backyard shed, a kennel run or a detached garage is not built to withstand tornado winds. None of them should count as shelter for an animal any more than they would for a person.

Dogs and cats that spend most of their time outdoors need a standing plan for getting them in. Some will not come when called once the sky darkens and the wind rises. A pet that already eats indoors, or that stays inside on days when severe weather is in the forecast, is easier to gather when the moment comes.

Leaving pets behind in the house carries a separate risk. A family that goes elsewhere to shelter may not be able to return for hours or days. The home may be damaged, without power or cut off by debris. An animal shut inside cannot get out, and it cannot find food or water on its own.

Families who live in mobile homes have to leave for sturdier shelter, and their pets need to leave with them. The destination might be a solid building nearby, a friend's or relative's home or a community storm shelter. Whichever it is, confirm in advance that animals are allowed. Some public shelters do not accept pets. Knowing the policy ahead of time means no one has to choose between staying in an unsafe structure and leaving an animal behind.

An animal that stays with its family can be watched, kept contained and protected by the same walls that protect the people around it.

Once a tornado has passed, check each pet for injuries and keep every animal leashed or contained until the area around the home has been inspected. Debris, broken glass and downed power lines can turn a familiar yard into a dangerous place.

Start with the animal itself. Look over the paws, legs and coat for cuts, limping or embedded fragments of glass or wood. A frightened or hurt animal may bite or scratch even a trusted owner. Handle it slowly and calmly. Contact a veterinarian about any wound, breathing difficulty or sign of pain, even one that looks minor.

Walk the property before a pet goes outside. Look for nails, splintered lumber, sheet metal and shattered glass in the grass and along paths. Check fences and gates for gaps. A storm can loosen a panel or flatten a section. That damage can open an exit that did not exist before.

Treat every downed power line as live. Keep pets well clear of fallen wires. Keep them away from puddles and wet ground near those wires as well, because water can conduct electricity. Report downed lines to the local utility instead of trying to move them.

Indoors, watch for hazards that are easy to miss. Spilled cleaning products, fuel, insulation and broken household items can all end up on the floor within reach of a curious nose. If you smell gas, take people and pets out of the building. Call the gas company or emergency services from a safe distance.

Standing water after a storm can carry sewage, chemicals or sharp debris. Keep pets from drinking from it or wading through it. Offer clean, stored water instead.

Expect changes in behavior as well. Pets often become disoriented after a tornado because familiar landmarks and scents have shifted or disappeared. An animal that knows its neighborhood well can lose its bearings quickly in altered surroundings. Keep walks short and close to home. Keep cats indoors until the area is cleared. Some animals may seem withdrawn, restless or unusually clingy for a while after the storm.

Start searching for a missing pet right away, close to home. Contact local animal shelters, animal control and the pet's microchip registry the same day, with a recent photo ready to share.

Many frightened animals hide near home instead of traveling far. A cat may crawl under a porch, into a damaged shed or beneath debris and stay silent for hours. A dog may run several blocks before stopping in an unfamiliar yard. Walk the immediate area first. Call the pet's name in a calm voice and check any gap an animal could squeeze into.

Quiet hours make searching easier. Early morning and late evening bring less traffic, fewer work crews and less noise. Those calmer conditions can draw a hiding animal out. A flashlight helps with crawl spaces and dark pockets in wreckage. Search only where it is safe, and stay out of areas closed by emergency crews.

Shelters and animal control agencies are the next calls. Ask how they log incoming animals, and visit in person when possible. A description given over the phone can miss a pet that a shelter worker has recorded differently. After a large storm, strays may also go to temporary shelters set up by local or disaster response groups. Ask staff where else found animals are being taken.

The microchip registry should hear from the owner directly. Report the animal as lost so its record shows it is missing. A scan at a shelter or clinic can then lead back to the family. Nearby veterinary clinics are worth calling too. People who find an injured stray may bring it to a vet first.

Notices extend the search beyond what one household can cover. Paper flyers with a clear photo, the pet's name, a short description and a phone number belong at intersections, stores and shelter bulletin boards. Neighborhood social media groups and community lost-pet pages reach residents who are outside clearing debris and may spot an animal.

Keep checking. Visit shelters again every few days. New animals keep arriving as people across the area recover strays. Bring vaccination records, adoption papers or photos that show the pet with its owner. These documents help prove ownership when a match turns up.

Be cautious with anyone who claims to have the pet but asks for money before showing it. Ask the caller to describe a marking that was left off the flyer.
