#5442. Space heater safety: 10 tips for using a portable heater at home

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These space heater safety tips cover clearance, outlets, certification marks and shutoff features that help keep portable heaters from starting fires or causing burns at home

A space heater does something unusual for a household appliance: it puts a concentrated source of heat in the middle of rooms full of things that burn. Curtains, bedding, sofa cushions, stacks of mail and laundry baskets all sit within reach of a device whose job is to get hot and stay hot. That basic tension underlies most of the rules for using one safely.

An electric resistance heater converts nearly all the electricity it draws into heat. It delivers that warmth to a small area close to the unit. That makes it a way to take the chill off a home office, a drafty bedroom or a basement workspace without raising the thermostat for the house.

A plug-in heater is built for supplemental, spot heating. It is not designed to replace a home's main heating system or to run all day in a space it was never sized for. Several of the tips below address that gap between how portable heaters are made and how people use them.

The 10 space heater safety tips in this guide fall into three broad areas. The first is placement: where the heater sits, what surrounds it and what surface holds it up. The second is power: how the unit connects to the wall and what condition its cord and plug are in. The third is protection: the certification marks and automatic shutoff features built into the heater itself.

A few tips cover habits rather than hardware. Those include when to switch a heater off and how to keep children and pets clear of hot surfaces. Another explains why fuel-burning heaters bring a separate danger: carbon monoxide.

None of these steps requires special tools or technical knowledge. Some take seconds, such as checking a label before buying or moving a chair farther back. Others are a matter of routine, like inspecting a cord at the start of each cold season.

Each slide that follows covers one practice on its own terms. Readers can start with the slide that matches their question. That might be how far to keep a heater from furniture, or whether it is safe to leave one on overnight.

Keep anything that can burn at least three feet away from a space heater on all sides. That buffer covers curtains, bedding, sofas, armchairs, clothing, paper and cardboard. It applies to the back and sides of the unit as well as the front.

A heater does not need to touch a material to set it alight. Radiant models send heat outward in a straight line. They warm the objects in their path more than the surrounding air. Fabric, paper and wood can absorb that energy until they scorch or catch fire.

Fan-forced heaters create a different risk. They push a stream of hot air across the room. Lightweight items in that stream can heat up quickly. The airflow, or a draft from a window or door, can also pull a loose curtain toward the grille.

Clearance has to hold up over time, not just at the moment the heater is switched on. A throw blanket can slide off the arm of a sofa. A desk chair rolls back toward the unit. A shopping bag or a stack of newspapers lands on the floor beside it. Each of those changes can close a three-foot gap without anyone noticing.

One way to keep the zone clear is to mark it. A strip of tape on the floor about three feet out from the heater makes the boundary visible to everyone in the household. It also gives a quick reference point when the heater moves to another room.

Aim the heater toward open floor space rather than at a bed, a couch or a wall of curtains. Avoid tucking it under a desk, where papers, bags and cables tend to collect within reach of the heat.

Flammable liquids and their vapors need distance too. Keep gasoline, paint thinner, solvents and aerosol cans out of any room where a heater is running.

Never cover a space heater, even partially. Draping a towel or blanket over it traps heat inside the housing and blocks the vents that let it cool. That can push temperatures high enough to ignite the covering or damage the heater itself.

Drying clothes on a heater carries the same danger. Socks, gloves and wet jackets laid across the top or front restrict airflow. The fabric also sits directly against a hot surface. As the garment dries, it becomes easier to ignite. A drying rack placed outside the three-foot zone uses the warmth without that risk.

A space heater should plug straight into a wall outlet. Heaters pull far more current than most household devices. Extension cords and power strips are often not built to carry that load for hours without overheating.

The problem comes down to how much power a heater uses. Most plug-in electric heaters sold in the U.S. draw up to 1,500 watts on their highest setting. A lamp, phone charger or laptop uses a small fraction of that. A heater also tends to run for long stretches. Its wiring carries a heavy load with few breaks.

Light-duty extension cords use thinner wire than a heater's own cord. Thinner wire has more electrical resistance. When high current flows through it, that resistance turns into heat inside the cord itself. Over time, the insulation can soften, melt or ignite. That can happen in a spot hidden behind a couch or a bookcase, where no one sees it.

Power strips carry the same risk. Many are designed for clusters of low-draw electronics such as televisions and computers, not a single high-wattage appliance. A built-in surge protector guards against voltage spikes. It does not let the strip carry more current.

If no wall outlet is within reach, an extension cord should be a last resort. It needs to be heavy-duty, with a rating at or above the heater's wattage. It should also be as short as possible. The cord's rating is printed on the cord or its packaging. The heater's wattage appears on its label. The cord should run fully uncoiled. A coiled cord traps heat. It should also stay out from under rugs and away from foot traffic.

The outlet's circuit matters too. A heater should not share a circuit with other high-draw appliances such as a microwave, hair dryer, toaster or coffee maker. Several outlets in a room, and sometimes in neighboring rooms, can sit on the same circuit. A breaker that trips when the heater switches on is a sign the circuit is already carrying too much.

The simplest setup is a heater with nothing else plugged into the same wall outlet. That keeps the heater's load on the building's permanent wiring rather than on a temporary cord or strip.

A space heater should carry a safety certification mark from a recognized testing laboratory, such as UL or ETL, before it comes home. The mark shows that a sample of that model was tested against a published safety standard for electric room heaters.

UL stands for Underwriters Laboratories, a U.S. safety organization founded in 1894. The ETL mark is issued by Intertek, a testing and certification company. Both appear on the list of Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories maintained by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. A CSA mark from CSA Group is another listing shoppers may see on heaters sold in North America.

For portable electric heaters, the relevant U.S. safety standard is UL 1278. It covers movable and wall- or ceiling-hung electric room heaters. A laboratory other than UL can certify a heater to that standard. An ETL-listed heater and a UL-listed heater can therefore be evaluated against the same set of requirements.

Certification is not a one-time event. Listing programs include follow-up inspections at the factory. Those visits check that production units still match the sample that passed testing.

The mark belongs on the heater itself, not only on the box. It usually appears on a rating label on the back or underside of the unit. That label also lists the model number, voltage and wattage. Shoppers can look for the mark on the packaging before purchase, then confirm the same mark appears on the heater after unboxing.

The type of mark also matters. A listing mark applies to the finished product. A UL Recognized Component mark is a different symbol. It applies only to a part used inside a product. It does not mean the whole heater was certified.

Certification marks can be copied or misused. UL and Intertek each publish online directories where buyers can search by manufacturer or model number to confirm a listing. That check can help with heaters sold by third-party sellers on large online marketplaces, where a product's origin can be harder to trace.

A tip-over switch cuts power to a space heater the moment it falls or tilts too far. Look for this feature, usually listed as tip-over protection, on the box, label or product description before buying any portable electric heater.

The mechanism is simple. On many models, a small spring-loaded button or plunger sits on the underside of the base. The heater's own weight keeps that button pressed down while the unit stands upright. If the heater is lifted, tilted or knocked onto its side, the button pops out and breaks the circuit. Other designs use an internal tilt sensor that does the same job without a visible button.

The reason this matters is where a toppled heater ends up. A heater lying on its face can press its hot grille or heating element against carpet, a rug, a dropped blanket or the floor itself. Heat meant to flow into open air instead builds up against whatever the heater landed on. Cutting power right away stops the element from producing more heat before that contact can start a fire.

A heater can be knocked over in ordinary ways. A foot catches the cord, a vacuum bumps the base, a door swings into it or someone shoves a chair aside. Tall, narrow tower heaters have a small footprint relative to their height. That shape makes them easier to topple than low, wide units.

Behavior after a shutoff varies by model. Some heaters resume heating as soon as they are set upright again. Others stay off until the power button is pressed. Check the owner's manual to learn which approach a given heater uses before relying on it.

Never tape down, wedge or otherwise disable the switch, even if it trips more often than seems necessary. A switch that clicks off repeatedly signals that the heater is being bumped or sits in a spot where people pass by often.

Older and secondhand heaters may not have this protection at all. If neither the label nor the manual mentions a tip-over switch, treat the heater as though it lacks one.

Overheat protection is a built-in safety switch that cuts power when a space heater's internal parts get too hot. Look for it on the box, label or product listing before you buy. Treat it as a backstop, not a reason to relax other precautions.

The feature relies on a temperature-sensitive component inside the housing. Depending on the design, that part may be a bimetallic switch that resets after cooling or a thermal fuse that works only once. When the heating element or nearby components pass a preset temperature, the circuit opens and the heater stops producing heat.

A thermostat does a different job. It reads the room and cycles the heater on and off to hold a chosen setting. An overheat cutoff does not respond to room temperature. It reacts only to unsafe temperatures inside the unit itself.

Overheat protection also differs from tip-over protection, which reacts to the heater's position. A heater can stand upright on a level floor and still overheat. That can happen when air cannot move freely through the intake and outlet grilles.

Dust built up on the element or fan is a common trigger. In a fan-forced model, a fan motor that has slowed or stopped can cause the same problem. Objects pressed against the vents can also trap heat inside the casing.

Models handle a shutdown in different ways. Some reset on their own once they cool. Others require you to switch the heater off, unplug it, wait and then restart it. A heater built with a one-time thermal fuse may not work again until the fuse is replaced. That repair is usually a job for the manufacturer or a qualified repair service.

The owner's manual explains which type a specific heater uses and how to reset it. It also lists cleaning steps. Regular cleaning removes dust, one of the overheating triggers that owners can most easily control.

A heater that keeps shutting itself off has a problem that needs attention. Unplug it, check the vents and clean it according to the manual. If the shutdowns continue after that, stop using the unit and have it repaired or replaced.

Switch a space heater off whenever you go to bed or walk out of the room. A heater running unattended has no one nearby to notice a problem early. That gap is when a small hazard can grow into a fire.

People often ask whether a space heater can stay on overnight. The answer is no. Bedding shifts during sleep. A comforter can slide off the mattress, a pillow can fall to the floor, and a loose blanket can land against a hot grille. A sleeping person may not notice scorching fabric or see a curtain drift toward the heating element.

The same reasoning applies to stepping out of a room. A pet can nudge a chair closer to the heater. A child can drop a stuffed animal beside it. Someone who doesn't realize the unit is on can drape a coat over a nearby chair. A short trip to the kitchen leaves the heater just as unwatched as a trip out of the house.

One routine is to run the heater while getting ready for bed, then turn it off before lying down. Heavier blankets, flannel sheets or warm sleepwear can keep a person comfortable through the night. None of them needs a powered heat source running beside the bed.

Some portable heaters include a built-in timer or an automatic shutoff that ends heating after a set period. That feature helps if someone forgets, but it does not replace switching the unit off by hand. Unplugging the heater when it is not in use adds another layer of protection. A unit that is switched off but still plugged in can be bumped back on.

Smoke alarms serve as the backup for any heat source in the home. Test each alarm at least once a month with its test button. Install alarms inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level of the home. Replace any smoke alarm once it reaches 10 years old. Its sensor loses reliability over time.

Sleeping with the bedroom door closed adds one more safeguard. A closed door slows the spread of smoke, heat and flames from elsewhere in the house. That buys extra time to get out after an alarm sounds.

A portable heater belongs on a hard, flat, level floor, such as tile, wood, vinyl or concrete. Keep it off carpet, rugs, tables, shelves, chairs, couches and beds. On those surfaces, a heater can tip, choke its own airflow or rest against material that burns.

Floor placement comes down to two things: stability and airflow. A heater on a firm surface stays upright and keeps a steady footprint. On a soft or uneven surface, it can lean, rock or slide when someone walks past or brushes the cord.

Carpet creates a specific problem. Some fan-forced heaters draw air through vents near the base. Thick pile or a shaggy rug can press against those openings and restrict the flow of air. With less airflow, the unit runs hotter. The fibers underneath also sit in direct contact with a warm housing.

Raised surfaces carry a different risk. A heater on a desk, nightstand, dresser or bookshelf has farther to fall. A drop from that height can crack the casing or expose the heating element. The unit can also land on bedding, papers or a rug. Keeping it on the floor removes that fall entirely.

Upholstered furniture and beds combine both hazards. Cushions and mattresses are soft, so a heater cannot sit level on them. They are also made of fabric and foam that can burn. Never set a heater on a couch, armchair or bed, even briefly while a room warms up.

Position within the room counts too. Keep the heater out of doorways and main walking paths, where people can bump it or catch a foot on it. Do not run the power cord under a rug or carpet. A covered cord can trap heat. People can also step on it without seeing it.

Bathrooms, laundry rooms and other damp spaces need separate treatment. Moisture can reach a heater's internal electrical parts and create a shock or fire hazard. Use a space heater in these rooms only if the manufacturer specifically rates it for bathroom or damp-location use.

Each model's owner's manual lists its own placement requirements. Read it before first use. Some units include added instructions about floor types or minimum distances that apply to that design.

Children and pets should not be able to reach a running space heater. The grille, housing or fins on many models get hot enough to burn skin on contact. Small kids and animals do not recognize that danger the way adults do.

Young children explore by touch. A glowing element or a stream of warm air draws them closer. A toddler can grab a hot grille faster than an adult can react. Children's skin is also thinner than an adult's. A contact burn can develop more quickly as a result.

A safety gate or a fixed barrier keeps small children physically away from the heater. Place the heater behind a gate in a room the child does not use for play. A freestanding guard can also keep hands and faces away from the hot surfaces. A heater should never sit in a nursery corner, beside a crib rail or in the middle of a play mat.

Pets bring their own risks. Cats often seek out warm spots and may curl up against a heater or try to sleep on top of it. Dogs with long tails or thick coats can brush against a hot surface. They may not notice until the fur scorches or the skin burns.

The type of heater affects how hot its exterior gets. Radiant and infrared models can have very hot grilles. Oil-filled radiators heat their metal fins and can stay hot for a while after they are switched off. Some fan-forced ceramic units use housings designed to stay cooler to the touch. Their air outlets still get hot. The same barriers apply to them.

Controls are another point of contact. A child who can reach the dial can turn the heat up or switch the unit on. Keeping the heater out of reach, or choosing a model with a control lock, holds the settings where an adult left them.

Older children can learn a few simple rules. Do not touch the heater. Do not leave toys beside it. Do not play in the space around it. Repeat these rules at the start of each winter, before the heater comes out of storage.

A kerosene or propane heater belongs inside a home only if its label and manual say it is designed and approved for indoor use. Fuel-burning heaters can release carbon monoxide. Any home that runs one needs working carbon monoxide alarms near every sleeping area.

Carbon monoxide forms when a fuel such as kerosene, propane or natural gas burns without enough oxygen to burn completely. The gas has no color, smell or taste. People cannot sense it building up in a closed room. It can reach dangerous levels before anyone notices a problem.

Early symptoms of exposure resemble the flu: headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness and confusion. Higher concentrations can cause loss of consciousness and death. People who are asleep or intoxicated can be overcome before they wake or recognize what is happening.

Many portable kerosene and propane heaters are built for open garages, job sites, patios or camping. Running one of those in a bedroom or living room puts it in conditions it was not designed for. The manufacturer's label is the place to confirm whether a unit can be used indoors at all.

Propane heaters sold for indoor use typically include an oxygen depletion sensor. This device shuts off the gas supply when oxygen in the room drops below a set level. Even with that feature, the manual will usually call for fresh-air ventilation while the heater runs. A partly open window is a common example.

The fuel carries its own set of rules. A kerosene heater should burn only the grade of kerosene its manufacturer specifies, typically clear 1-K kerosene. Gasoline and other substitute fuels must never go into the tank. They can cause a fire or explosion. Refuel outdoors, and only after the heater has been turned off and has cooled.

Carbon monoxide alarms are the backstop. Place one near each sleeping area and test it regularly, following the instructions printed on the unit. Replace the alarm when it reaches the end of the service life its maker lists. If an alarm sounds, everyone should leave for fresh air immediately and call emergency services from outside.

A household that wants to remove carbon monoxide risk from its heating can choose an electric model instead. Electric space heaters burn no fuel and produce no carbon monoxide.

Check a space heater's power cord and plug before the first cold snap each year, and again periodically while the unit is in use. A frayed cord, cracked insulation or a plug that feels hot means the heater should be switched off and unplugged. It should then be repaired by a qualified technician or replaced.

Start the seasonal check with the heater unplugged and cool. Run the full length of the cord through your hand. Look for cuts, kinks, flattened sections or spots where the outer jacket has split. Exposed copper strands are a clear sign the cord is no longer safe to use.

The plug deserves the same attention. Look for bent or loose prongs, cracks in the plastic housing and any brown or black discoloration. Scorch marks on the plug or on the outlet's cover plate point to heat building up at the connection.

A common cause of that heat is a poor fit. A plug that wobbles or slides out of the outlet easily makes weak contact. Weak contact creates electrical resistance, and resistance creates heat. If a heater's plug sits loosely in one outlet, the outlet itself may be worn and should be checked by an electrician.

During use, touch the plug occasionally after the heater has been on for a while. It may feel slightly warm. It should not feel hot. A burning smell or the odor of melting plastic is another signal to shut the heater off at once.

Some cord damage comes from how the cord is routed. Running a heater cord under a rug or carpet hides wear from view and traps heat around the wire. Foot traffic and furniture legs can also crush the insulation over time. Keep the cord in the open and out of walkways.

Electrical tape is not a fix for a damaged heater cord. A taped-over split still carries current through compromised insulation. A plug-in heater also pulls a heavy load through that wire for hours at a time.

Storage at the end of winter shapes what next season's inspection will find. Let the heater cool fully before putting it away. Coil the cord loosely rather than wrapping it tightly around the heater's body. Tight wrapping bends and strains the cord where it enters the housing. Over repeated seasons, that stress can break the wires inside.

#5441. Hackers pushed freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to 122 degrees. Now the Pentagon is asking whether the same thing hit U.S. military bases

The Pentagon’s criminal investigators are leading a joint probe into freezer failures at U.S. military commissaries in August, and four officials told Reuters this week that the Pentagon is treating them as a possible cyberattack. It comes weeks after hackers took over the refrigeration controls at hundreds of French supermarkets overnight.

There’s no proof yet that the two are connected, or that the commissary failures were a hack at all. But the same kind of target experienced the same type of outage within about two months of each other, which is enough to raise the eyebrows of Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University.

“You’d be silly not to be suspicious,” he told Fortune.

For the stores, the damage can’t be undone: Two supermarkets, Intermarché and E.Leclerc, reported an estimated €270,000, about $300,000, in combined stock damages, according to local news outlet Sud Ouest.

“Refrigerators give an attacker a weirdly direct route…to financial loss that’s, with cyber, unusually irreversible,” Whyte said. “You can’t unspoil food or other products from these freezers. It’s just euros and dollars down the drain.”

Napoleon Bonaparte, the French military general who met an infamous defeat in Russia after overextending his supplies, is credited as saying, “An army marches on its stomach.”

The aphorism, also attributed to Prussian King Frederick the Great, refers to the necessity of food and basic logistics for a military campaign’s success. It’s not surprising, then, that refrigeration may be the next frontier of widespread cybersecurity attacks.

Earlier this month, hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets, raising the temperature of their refrigeration and freezer systems overnight to more than 122 degrees Fahrenheit, spoiling food and causing fires. The affected grocery stores included 80 Carrefour locations, about two dozen Monoprix stores, and 150 Intermarché stores. The Paris prosecutor’s office called the outages a “large-scale” attack. Similar outages were reported across Europe.

The Pentagon’s investigation—and a partnership with French authorities to probe the French supermarket outages—followed a series of refrigerator outages across several U.S. military commissaries in August. More than a half-dozen commissaries were impacted by the disruption, including in Fort Irwin, California; Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico; Naval Station Newport, Rhode Island; Little Rock Air Force Base, Arkansas; F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming; Robins Air Force Base, Georgia; and Fort Huachuca, Arizona, the Military Times reported at the time. Commissaries typically offer subsidized goods to those living on military bases, costing about 25% less than civilian grocery stores.

The Substack Signal and Silence was first to report the possibility that outages were a result of a hack.

The Pentagon confirmed the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the criminal investigative arm of the agency’s Office of Inspector General, is leading a joint investigation into the outages, but said in a statement to Fortune, “For security reasons, we do not comment on ongoing law-enforcement investigations.”

Cyber incidents, particularly targeting corporations and government agencies, have been on the rise over the last two decades, including more than a dozen major attacks this September alone, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Cybercrime is projected to cost the global economy $10.8 trillion this year, according to Cybersecurity Ventures, more than triple the $3 trillion it cost in 2015. Rapidly developing AI capabilities have made hacking more sophisticated, while the number of appliances attached to the internet have created more targets.

Cybersecurity experts believe it was only a matter of time before practical appliances like refrigerators became the target of cyberattacks. Nadiya Kostyuk, an assistant professor at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology, told Fortune it was an ongoing joke among her cohort to discuss when their home fridges would be hacked.

“I’m surprised that it took so long,” she said.

“A lot of these devices have a lot of really cool features, but the security is not the first priority for them,” Kostyuk added. “Hopefully future inventions will come with more security in mind when it comes to the design, and the existing ones also will be revisited to incorporate all the potential vectors of the cyberattacks.”

In the case of the outages in France, the vulnerabilities originated from access to the Danish-made Danfoss AK-SM, AK-SC series remote controllers for refrigeration systems, as well as Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, according to an alert bulletin published by French authorities, and affected units were running outdated firmware hackers could exploit by accessing the devices through the internet.

More broadly, refrigeration systems present vulnerabilities because many of the devices are similar across commercial chains, and identifying an exposure in one means hackers can generalize that exposure to other systems, according to Whyte.

Beyond the accessibility of refrigeration systems, the consequences of outages yield practical consequences, which can make them appealing targets for hackers who want to make a statement or take a financial jab at a victim.

The U.S. military theater is vulnerable to emblematic attacks on supply stores as well. The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, which had a record deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea before it docked in San Diego earlier this month, became a symbol of weaknesses in U.S. military amenities. During its Iran war mission, the crew faced poor morale and mental health, including as a result of food and hygiene supply shortage.

Gregory Winger, an assistant professor of international relations and cybersecurity at University of Maryland, Baltimore County, told Fortune that actors from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea typically rely on cyber incidents that appear random but are actually connected.

Allied countries have built partnerships for the express reason of identifying and sharing the techniques of hackers, particularly NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in Mons, Belgium, which is the body’s cybersecurity headquarters. Significant attacks can trigger NATO’s invocation of Article 5, a collective defense that defines a threat against one country as an effective threat against the body’s 32 members. Regardless if the outages in the U.S. military commissaries were from the same actor as the French supermarket outages, the U.S. was strategic to launch a joint investigation with France purely from an information-sharing standpoint, Winger argued.

“Right now,” he said, “every future military operation is going to have a cyber component to it.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5440. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5439. The $13 billion startup racing to close America’s hypersonic gap

The first thing to know about hypersonic missiles is that they’re air-rippingly fast.

A hypersonic missile, definitionally, moves at least at Mach 5, or five times the speed of sound; one could cross the U.S. coast to coast in under 45 minutes. Unlike ballistic missiles, hypersonics are maneuverable and unpredictable to watchers, with an uncanny ability to fly low, change course, and skirt radar.

The second thing to know about hypersonics is that China and Russia have them, and the U.S. doesn’t—not really. It’s not for lack of trying: Despite years of research costing billions and some successful tests, the U.S. has yet to fully field a hypersonic missile of its own due to testing complications and production issues. The tech’s been around, but it’s been expensive and difficult to produce at scale.

That’s the chasm that startup Castelion, valued at $13 billion, is betting it can close, even if the defense giants have so far fallen short. “Humans have done it, just not Americans,” says Castelion CEO and cofounder Bryon Hargis. “I firmly believe it’s doable.”

The Torrance, Calif.-based startup has become a darling of the defense tech boom, in part because it encapsulates the movement’s raison d’être: The U.S. must rebuild its industrial base faster, cheaper, and with an eye to scale. The war in Iran has crystallized that bleak reality: The U.S. is firing missiles faster than it can replace them, by an order of years.

Castelion was founded in 2022 by three former SpaceX executives: Hargis, Andrew Kreitz, and Sean Pitt. (Hargis started the military-grade satellite network Starshield; Kreitz ran classified finance; and Pitt led sales of Falcon 9s in Europe.)

The enterprise got off to an almost comically inauspicious start: In an early Zoom pitch to the Pentagon’s innovation outfit, the founders said they planned to compete with Lockheed Martin at building affordable hypersonics. The room laughed, Pitt recalls.

But the tables have turned: Castelion, in less than two-and-a-half years, took its low-cost hypersonic missile Blackbeard from a drawing to progressing reality—and it’s designated as a “program of record,” the elusive and coveted government budget line that makes (and often breaks) defense sector entrants.

This places Castelion in direct competition with Lockheed, the maker of hypersonic race favorite Dark Eagle, a program that’s been in process since 2017—and is reportedly three years behind schedule. (“Dark Eagle has successfully deployed in support of Indo-Pacific exercises and completed multiple successful flight-test events,” an Army spokesperson said via email. “The Army continues planned operational assessment activities.”)

In September, the U.S. Navy awarded Castelion a contract worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard, which documents say can be made for less than $500,000 each. (In comparison, Tomahawk missiles can cost millions each.) Blackbeards have had successful test flights on fighter jets like the F/A-18 Super Hornet, and the company is currently racing to open its 1,000-acre New Mexico site, which could eventually turn out thousands of Blackbeards each year.

“This capability is needed now, and you have to sprint directly at what the country needs,” says Kreitz, Castelion’s CFO. Hypersonics are effective not just as weapons but, even more essentially, as deterrents, Kreitz argues. “It’s really important we have a credible deterrent that we pass down for generations to come,” adds Hargis. Pitt gestures at a Mad Men-esque poster in Castelion’s mid-century office. “Cheesy as it is, this was the first poster we ever made for the company,” he explains. “You can see the tagline was: ‘Win before it begins.’”

Of course, deterrence only has a chance if the weapons exist. And recent conflicts have created an unmissable urgency, Kreitz says. “This is the capability that will define warfare in the 2030s and beyond,” he said. “The campaign was basically large, sustained volleys of back-and-forth long-range fires. That’s what the future of warfare will look like.”

In 2022, as Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt were just getting started, they presented to the Defense Innovation Unit, the Pentagon’s tech acceleration division. It didn’t go well. “It was the tailish end of COVID,” said Pitt. “So, it was a video presentation, and we explained ‘we’re here to make low-cost missiles.’ They asked: ‘Are you going to compete with Lockheed?’ We said yes, and it was not a little laugh. There were a good number of people laughing.”

In venture capital, 2022 was the bizarre era of peak metaverse. Defense tech was a novelty and largely seen as controversial or ignored. (Anduril, defense tech’s greatest hardware success, had a skyrocketing 2022, but there was no sense that breakthrough was imitable.) The three founders are all candid about the impasse of the very beginning.

Hargis, who has a forceful warmth and natural deadpan—his father, he says, worked at a nuclear power plant “like Homer Simpson”—doesn’t hold back.

“I was using my retirement to fund my living,” he said. “I was messaging these guys: ‘At what point would they have to call it quits if we didn’t make anything?’”

In their first investment contracts, Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt promised to return the money if they couldn’t raise $1 million. In the end, they cleared that bar through a SpaceX tender offer, in which Hargis and another employee sold shares and invested in the company. Then, in April 2023, Lavrock, a Washington, D.C.-based VC firm, led a seed round of $5.6 million, a shoestring sum for an aspiring missile-maker. But it was enough: The founders went off into the Mojave Desert, near Edwards Air Force Base, to build their first rocket motor.

“The early, early days in the desert were threadbare,” remembers Kreitz, a history buff keenly aware of the lines between past and present. “We all wore Tyvek suits and respirators, helped make propellant and assembled parts, and we were getting hardware built alongside the engineers and techs.”

It took months, funds dwindled, and it was soon time for a Hail Mary: They found a high-speed cameraman to film a static-fire test. The resulting video, of a rumbling firing motor, drew the attention of the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which quickly led an $8.6 million seed extension in Castelion.

The race then really began. Building a defense company is an amalgamation of tiny precisions, from the rigamarole of clearances to establishing processes for classified information. The endgame, for Castelion and any defense startup, is selling to the Department of War, a bureaucratic behemoth with labyrinthine fiefdoms. Normal startup challenges—from office setup to engineering game plans—are all magnified by the specifics of hardware and defense.

“What mattered most for us then was finding a customer who was willing to try something new and was willing to be different in how they approach the acquisition cycle,” said Pitt, who’s wryly persuasive and was a SpaceX spokesperson in his 20s. “[The Navy] gave us that initial contract, $3 million. We did what we said we would for $3 million. That led to a $15 million contract, and it all went from there.”

Now, Castelion has a program of record with the U.S. Navy. To Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt, there’s a sense this has all happened dizzyingly fast. Castelion has gone from 159 employees at the end of 2025 to over 400 employees. And the tougher truth is that, from here, the company needs to keep it up or go even faster. “Can you make enough? Are they cheap enough that the country can buy that many? And can you do that in a time frame of relevance?” said Pitt. “That’s the bar.”

Much of that scaling will happen at Castelion’s Project Ranger site in Rio Rancho, N.M., where some residents have reportedly balked at a missile factory moving in. The company’s held regular community meetings, worked extensively with local authorities, and its chief engineer has moved to town.

“This is going to be the defining production site for Castelion,” said Kreitz. “We, the three of us, will be here all the time. All our senior leadership is going to be there all the time. These are going to be our friends and colleagues. They’re going to be working there. They’re going to be living there. We want this to be safe. We want this to be done correctly.”

Ultimately, there’s a back-to-the-future quality to Castelion’s efforts. They’re careful not to blast the modern defense primes—after all, the Pentagon’s expressed a great need for both high and low-cost hypersonics. But it’s telling that Castelion’s reference points are further in the past, like the Apollo era, which produced humanity’s first moon landings in about a decade.

“In the Apollo era, the country used to build hardware like there was no tomorrow, test it, fly it, iterate and do it all again,” said Hargis.

That’s partly how other nations have moved ahead of the U.S. in the hypersonic race, in Hargis’s telling: “The way it was done was with an iterative approach and a lot of testing. America has moved away from that iterative approach over the past decades, and we’re now reaping the expected benefits from that.”

Castelion could still fall short, it should be said. The company currently has over $500 million in U.S. government contracts, yes, but ultimately they’re in big-swing-or-bust territory. The company, in some sense, is doing a reverse Anduril: The $61 billion defense tech giant started with sentry towers and built out a massive suite of products over time and deals, while Castelion barreled straight into one massive, intractable problem. If they’re right, they’re very right. And if they’re wrong, they’re very wrong. To Pitt, the gamble’s worth it.

“The pure existence of Castelion as a credible threat to the primes significantly benefits the country, because behavior has to change to deal with a competitive entrant that’s offering services at a significantly lower cost,” he said.

Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt are all acutely aware of the harshest underlying reality of what they do: They are building lethal weapons capable of destroying military targets and infrastructure, and of killing. “You have to think about it and confront the fact that one day it can be used for its intended purpose,” said Kreitz. But, he added, “When we say ‘peace through deterrence,’ when we say ‘deterrence works,’ we really do mean that.”

Hargis pushed back when I raised a common criticism: that building weapons inherently facilitates war. “If you want to deter someone’s actions, they have to feel there’s a consequence to those actions,” he said. “Hypersonics give the country that ability and a level between economic sanctions and nuclear war, which no one wants to happen, ever.”

As an uneasy post-Cold War equilibrium morphs into a more geopolitically volatile world, the question hanging over Castelion—and the entire U.S. defense industry—is utterly urgent: What will the next major conflict look like, and will we be ready?

“We’re in a sprint,” Kreitz said. “We’re going as fast as humanly possible. I want to know how much time we have… We have to act as if it’s tomorrow.”

Correction, Nov. 2, 2026: A previous version of this article misstated the speaker of a quote about a poster at Castelion’s office. The speaker was Sean Pitt.

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5438. Why your plane waits on the tarmac in winter: de-icing, explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Why planes wait on the tarmac in winter comes down to a clean wing: 10 parts of airplane de-icing, from glycol fluids to holdover time and remote pads

A winter delay at the de-icing pad looks like idle time from a passenger window, but it is a safety procedure running against a clock. The trucks, the colored spray and the slow line of jets all serve one goal. The aircraft has to be free of frost, ice and snow at the moment it begins its takeoff roll.

That requirement is the short answer to why planes wait on the tarmac in winter. A wing generates lift because air flows smoothly over its shaped surface. Contamination roughens that surface and changes how the air behaves. Aviation rules treat a contaminated wing as unfit for takeoff. Airlines build their cold-weather operations around that principle.

De-icing does two separate jobs. The first is removal: heated fluid sprayed under pressure clears what has already built up on the airframe. The second is prevention: a protective coating keeps new snow or freezing rain from sticking before the plane leaves the ground. Those jobs can happen in a single application or in two distinct steps.

Prevention is where the clock comes in. Protective fluids do not last indefinitely. Once they stop working, contamination can start to cling again. That limit shapes nearly every part of the process — where airports set up their de-icing operations, when crews request treatment and what happens if a departure slips.

The result is a sequence passengers see only in part. A plane may push back from the gate, taxi to a remote area, wait its turn at the de-icing trucks and then head directly for the runway. If a delay stretches too long after treatment, the aircraft may need to be inspected or sprayed again.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of topics, not a complete guide to the subject. They cover the physics of why ice matters on a wing and the U.S. rule that defines a clean aircraft. They also explain the chemistry of glycol-based fluids and the differences between fluid types. Later slides walk through holdover time, one-step and two-step procedures and the logistics of de-icing pads. Others address post-treatment inspections and a form of frost that can appear even when the air is above freezing. The final slide looks back at two crashes, in 1982 and 1989, that are widely cited in discussions of why de-icing procedures tightened.

Frost, ice or snow on a wing breaks up the smooth airflow over its surface. That cuts the lift the wing can produce and adds drag. Even a thin, rough layer can change how the wing performs.

A wing makes lift by shaping the air that moves across it. The curved upper surface and the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air turn that airflow downward. The wing is pushed up in return. The process depends on air staying close to the surface and following its contour from the front edge to the back.

Contamination interferes with that process. Ice and frost add roughness, and snow can build up into uneven lumps. A rough surface disturbs the thin layer of air moving right next to the wing, known as the boundary layer. Once that layer is disturbed, the airflow can separate from the upper surface earlier than it would on a clean wing.

Separated airflow produces less lift. The wing can stall — losing much of its lift abruptly — at a lower angle of attack than a clean wing would. The speed at which it stalls rises as well. A pilot flying the normal takeoff speeds for a clean wing may have a smaller safety margin than expected, or none.

Drag rises at the same time. Rough surfaces create more friction and turbulence. That makes the airplane harder to accelerate and slower to climb. Accumulated snow and ice also add weight.

Thickness is a poor guide to the risk. A layer of frost that looks harmless can have a texture rough enough to disturb the airflow. Contamination on the leading edge and the upper surface of the wing matters most. Those are the areas where the airflow is most sensitive.

The effects can also be uneven. If one wing carries more contamination than the other, the two sides may lose lift differently. That can make the airplane roll unexpectedly just after liftoff.

Takeoff is the phase where these effects carry the most risk. The aircraft is low, slow and pitched up for its initial climb, with little room to recover from a stall. Stall-warning systems are typically designed around a clean wing. A contaminated wing can stall before the warning activates.

U.S. airline rules forbid a takeoff when frost, ice or snow is adhering to a plane's critical surfaces. The aircraft must be free of that contamination when its takeoff roll begins, not only when it leaves the gate.

Aviation calls this principle the clean aircraft concept. For U.S. airlines, it is written into federal regulation at 14 CFR 121.629. That section sits in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, within Part 121, the set of operating rules for U.S. air carriers.

The rule names the surfaces that count: the wings, control surfaces, propellers and engine inlets. Its wording also extends to other critical surfaces. The named parts are examples, not a complete list. Control surfaces are the movable panels a crew uses to steer and balance the aircraft. They include the ailerons on the wings and the elevators and rudder on the tail.

Each of those parts does a separate job in getting a plane airborne. Wings generate lift. Control surfaces let the crew change the aircraft's attitude and direction. Propellers and engine inlets handle the airflow that produces thrust. The rule groups them together instead of singling out the wings.

The timing requirement is the part that shapes winter operations. A plane that is clean at the gate can collect fresh snow or frost while it taxis or waits in line for the runway. Under the clean aircraft concept, the gate condition does not settle the question. What matters is the state of the surfaces when the takeoff begins.

The regulation also requires airlines to plan ahead. A carrier operating when frost, ice or snow may reasonably be expected to adhere must have an approved ground de-icing and anti-icing program. That program sets out the procedures, training and responsibilities the airline uses to meet the clean aircraft standard.

The same section reaches beyond the ground. A flight may not be dispatched, continue en route or land if the pilot in command or the aircraft dispatcher believes icing conditions might adversely affect its safety. Together, these provisions turn a clean aircraft into a legal requirement for winter departures.

Aircraft de-icing fluid is a glycol-based liquid. It is made from either propylene glycol or ethylene glycol, blended with water and a set of additives. The glycol does the core work: it lowers the freezing point of the water on the aircraft's surfaces.

Both glycols are alcohols that mix completely with water. That property matters on a wing. When the fluid meets snow, frost or ice, the glycol blends into the melted water instead of sitting on top of it. The resulting mixture stays liquid at temperatures where plain water would freeze solid.

Ethylene glycol is the same compound used in most automotive antifreeze. Propylene glycol is its less toxic relative. It also appears in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals. Ethylene glycol is poisonous to people and animals if swallowed. That difference in toxicity is one reason many operators choose propylene glycol formulations.

The water in the blend is part of the design. Ground crews mix fluid to a strength matched to the weather and the outside air temperature. A diluted mixture can still hold down the freezing point enough for the conditions at hand.

Heat and glycol play different roles during removal. The fluid is warmed before it leaves the spray nozzle, and that heat melts contamination quickly. Spraying under pressure then knocks loosened snow and ice off the surface. The glycol keeps the leftover slush from refreezing in place.

Additives complete the formula. Surfactants, or wetting agents, help the fluid spread in an even film instead of beading up. Corrosion inhibitors protect the metal structure and components the fluid touches. Exact recipes are proprietary and vary by manufacturer.

The chemistry also explains why a treated surface can eventually refreeze. Falling snow or freezing rain keeps adding water to the film on the wing. Each addition dilutes the glycol, and the mixture's freezing point rises. Once enough water has mixed in, the film can turn to ice.

Glycol fluids for aircraft are separate from the chemicals spread on runways and taxiways. Airport pavement de-icers are typically based on compounds such as potassium acetate or sodium formate. Aircraft fluids are made to their own specifications for use on airframes.

Type I is the thin, unthickened de-icing fluid that ground crews spray hot to strip snow, ice and frost from an aircraft. It is usually dyed orange. It offers only brief protection against new ice forming afterward.

The orange spray is the most visible part of a winter departure. Passengers often see it sheeting down cabin windows and dripping off the back edge of the wing. That color is deliberate. A dye helps ground crews see where fluid has landed and where coverage is missing. It also sets Type I apart from the thickened fluids, which carry their own colors.

Heat does much of the work. Warm fluid melts frozen contamination where it lands. The force of the spray then pushes loosened snow and slush off the aircraft's skin.

Low viscosity explains both the fluid's strength and its limit. Type I contains no thickening agents. It flows easily into seams, hinges and the gaps around control surfaces. The same thinness means it drains off quickly. Once most of it has run away, little is left on the wing to absorb fresh precipitation.

That is why Type I is treated as a cleaning fluid first. It removes contamination well, but its window of protection is short. In steady snow or freezing drizzle, a coat of Type I on its own may not keep a wing clean through a long taxi to the runway.

Crews typically blend Type I with water before it goes on the aircraft. The mix is adjusted to the weather. Milder conditions call for a weaker blend, while colder ones need more glycol. The concentration has to stay within the limits set for that specific fluid.

Type I is built to a published industry standard. SAE International, the engineering standards body, covers it under Aerospace Material Specification AMS 1424. That document sets the requirements manufacturers must meet. As a result, airlines can expect fluid from different suppliers to behave consistently on the wing.

Type II and Type IV anti-icing fluids are thickened with polymers. They stay on an aircraft's surfaces far longer than thin de-icing fluid and stop new snow, sleet or freezing rain from bonding to a wing that has already been cleaned.

The thickening agents give these fluids a gel-like consistency at rest. Once sprayed onto a wing, the coat stays in place instead of running off the trailing edge within moments. That standing layer acts as a buffer. Falling precipitation lands in the fluid rather than on the bare skin of the wing.

The fluid absorbs that moisture and becomes more diluted as it does. While the mixture stays above its freezing point, contamination cannot stick to the surface underneath. Once enough water has soaked in, the layer stops protecting the wing.

Color helps ground crews tell the products apart. Type IV fluid is usually dyed green. Type II fluid is typically pale straw-colored. The tint also lets crews see whether a wing carries an even, complete coat or whether a patch has been missed.

A thick coat left on a wing during takeoff would disturb the airflow that produces lift. These fluids avoid that through a property called shear thinning. They are formulated to stay viscous while the aircraft sits still or taxis slowly.

During the takeoff run, the rush of air across the wing changes that. The fluid thins under the airflow, shears off and flows away as the aircraft accelerates. Most of the coat leaves the wing before the aircraft lifts off. That restores the clean airflow the wing depends on.

That design ties these fluids to aircraft that reach high speeds on the runway. A slow aircraft may not produce enough airflow to clear the coat before it lifts off. SAE standard AMS 1428 covers Type II and Type IV fluids. The same standard also covers Type III, a formulation intended for slower aircraft.

Thickened fluids can leave residue behind. Repeated applications can leave dried gel in gaps around flight control surfaces. Moisture can rehydrate that residue into a swollen gel, which can then freeze at altitude. Frozen residue in those gaps can restrict the movement of the controls. Maintenance programs for aircraft that are treated often with thickened fluids include checks of those areas.

Holdover time is the window during which de-icing or anti-icing fluid keeps frost, ice and snow from sticking to an aircraft. The clock starts when the final fluid application begins. It stops when the fluid fails.

That starting point matters. Protection is measured from the beginning of the last spray. It is not measured from the moment the truck finishes or the plane leaves the treatment area. Time spent completing the application, taxiing and waiting in line all comes out of the same window.

The fluid fails because of the precipitation it is designed to absorb. Glycol keeps water from freezing only while there is enough of it in the mix. Each snowflake or drizzle droplet that lands dilutes the fluid a little more. At some point the mixture can no longer stay liquid, and contamination starts to stick to the surface.

Four main variables decide how quickly that happens. The first is the fluid type. Type I, Type II and Type IV fluids each have separate holdover guidance. The second is concentration. A fluid mixed with more water has less glycol to spare and gives a shorter window than the same fluid applied undiluted.

The third variable is outside air temperature. The fourth is the kind of precipitation falling and how hard it is falling. Freezing rain, freezing drizzle, light snow and heavy snow each load water onto the wing at different rates. A heavier rate uses up the fluid's capacity faster.

Those factors interact, so no single number describes holdover time. Regulators instead publish holdover tables that cross-reference fluid type and concentration against temperature and weather conditions. In the U.S., the Federal Aviation Administration issues these guidelines, and Transport Canada publishes its own. Both are revised periodically as fluids and test data change.

Flight crews consult the table that matches the fluid applied and the conditions at the time. Many entries give a range rather than a single figure. The window is an estimate, not a guarantee. A shift in the weather after treatment can cut real protection below what the table shows.

One-step de-icing uses a single application of heated, diluted fluid to remove frost, ice or snow and leave behind temporary protection. Two-step de-icing splits those jobs. Crews clean the aircraft first and then apply a separate anti-icing fluid.

The split exists because removing contamination and keeping it off are two different tasks. A fluid that strips ice well is not necessarily the one that holds up best against fresh snow. Separating the steps lets ground crews match each fluid to its job.

In the one-step method, a single spray handles both. The heated spray loosens frost, ice and snow on the wings and tail and washes it away. The fluid left on the surface then resists refreezing for a limited period. The aircraft is sprayed only once, which keeps the procedure short.

In the two-step method, the first application only has to clean. Crews spray heated fluid until the critical surfaces are clear. They then follow with a second coat of anti-icing fluid, usually Type II or Type IV. That thickened coat holds up longer against falling snow than the cleaning fluid would.

The second coat has to go on before the cleaning fluid can refreeze. If the first layer froze, the anti-icing fluid would sit on top of fresh contamination. That would defeat the purpose of the treatment.

The protection clock also runs differently between the two methods. In a two-step treatment, the window is measured from the start of the second step, not the first. Time spent on the cleaning pass does not count toward the aircraft's protection. In a one-step treatment, the window starts with the single application itself.

Which method a crew uses depends on conditions at the airport. Light frost on a clear morning is a different problem from steady snowfall that keeps landing on the wings during taxi. U.S. airlines that may face ground icing conditions must follow an approved ground de-icing and anti-icing program. That program spells out the procedures their ground crews and pilots use.

Many airports carry out winter de-icing at remote pads or dedicated areas rather than at the gate. Aircraft line up there for the de-icing trucks, then taxi straight to the runway.

Those pads are often placed near the ends of departure runways. A plane that leaves the gate in snow may stop again within minutes. It can end up sitting behind other jets that are waiting for the same trucks.

The queue is driven by timing. Anti-icing fluid protects a wing only for a limited period, known as holdover time. A plane that is sprayed and then held too long can lose that protection before it reaches the runway.

For that reason, flight crews and air traffic controllers try to schedule treatment close to each departure. A jet treated too early may use up its protection while still waiting. A flight can therefore wait before it reaches the pad as well as once it is there.

On the pad, pilots and the de-icing crew coordinate by radio. The crew confirms when spraying starts and when it ends, and the pilots note the time. Many crews also shut off the air conditioning packs during spraying to keep glycol fumes out of the cabin.

After treatment, the aircraft taxis from the pad toward the runway instead of returning to the terminal. That one-way flow also keeps gates free for arriving flights.

The pads have a second job: capturing runoff. De-icing fluid is made from glycol, and much of it drips off the aircraft during spraying. A dedicated pad concentrates that runoff in one place instead of spreading it across gates and aprons.

Glycol that reaches streams and rivers uses up oxygen in the water as it breaks down. Low oxygen levels can harm fish and other aquatic life. Pads with drainage systems let airports collect the fluid before it reaches storm drains. Some airports send the collected fluid to treatment plants, and some recycle the glycol for reuse.

Not every airport works this way. Some treat aircraft at or near the gate instead. Wherever the spraying happens, the timing problem is the same. It is why a winter departure can involve a wait between pushback and takeoff.

After de-icing, the flight crew and the ground crew inspect the aircraft to confirm that its critical surfaces are clean. If the holdover time runs out before the plane starts its takeoff roll, it needs another inspection or a repeat treatment.

The ground crew's check comes first. Once the trucks finish spraying, the de-icing team looks over the wings, tail and other treated surfaces. The goal is to confirm that no frost, ice or snow is still stuck to them. The team then passes the result to the flight crew before the aircraft leaves the treatment area.

The pilots carry that responsibility into the taxi. As the plane moves toward the runway, they track the time left in the protection window. They also watch the weather. Heavier snow or a switch to freezing rain can make the protective fluid fail sooner.

Clear ice adds a complication. It can be hard to see on a wet, fluid-coated wing. For that reason, some inspections include a physical touch check of the wing surface rather than a visual look alone.

When the holdover window closes before departure, the plane cannot continue to the runway as planned. The surfaces must be checked again, or the aircraft must go back for another round of fluid. At a busy airport during a snowstorm, that can mean rejoining the line of planes waiting for treatment.

Frost does not need freezing air to form. Cold-soaked fuel frost appears when the fuel inside the wing tanks is very cold, even if the surrounding air is above freezing. It typically follows a long flight at high altitude, where the fuel chills to very low temperatures. If the plane then lands somewhere humid, moisture in the air can freeze onto the wing skin above the tanks.

As a result, a plane parked on a mild, damp morning may still need attention before its next flight. The frost sits on the wing itself. The crew has to deal with it under the aircraft's approved procedures before departure.

On-board wing heating systems do not replace this ground process. Those systems are designed to manage ice in flight. On the ground, the aircraft still has to begin its takeoff roll with clean surfaces.

Air Florida Flight 90 crashed after taking off in snow from Washington National Airport on January 13, 1982, and ice contamination was a factor. Air Ontario Flight 1363 went down at Dryden, Ontario, on March 10, 1989, after departing with contaminated wings.

The accidents involved different countries, different aircraft types and different circumstances. Each showed what happens when a jet leaves the ground with frozen deposits on surfaces that must be clean. Both are widely cited in explanations of why winter procedures tightened.

Flight 90 was a Boeing $BA 737-200 departing during a heavy snowstorm. Shortly after liftoff, it struck the 14th Street Bridge and fell into the ice-covered Potomac River. Rescue efforts in the river were broadcast live on television.

The National Transportation Safety Board investigated the crash. It cited the crew's decision to take off with snow or ice on the wing surfaces. It also cited the crew's failure to switch on engine anti-ice during ground operation and takeoff.

Without anti-ice, an engine sensor iced over. The cockpit gauges then showed more thrust than the engines were actually producing. The board also faulted the captain for not rejecting the takeoff after the first officer pointed out abnormal engine readings. The jet had been de-iced at the gate but then waited in a long departure line as snow kept falling.

Air Ontario Flight 1363 was a Fokker F28 jet on a scheduled flight that stopped at Dryden to refuel. Snow was falling during the stop. The aircraft took off without being de-iced, failed to climb properly and crashed into woods beyond the end of the runway.

Canada responded with a federal Commission of Inquiry led by Justice Virgil Moshansky. His final report, published in 1992, looked well beyond the cockpit. It examined the airline's operating practices, crew training and oversight by Transport Canada. It also produced a long list of safety recommendations.

The inquiry examined why the crew did not de-ice. The aircraft's auxiliary power unit was unserviceable, and Dryden had no ground equipment to restart the engines. The crew kept one engine running during the stop. Guidance at the time discouraged de-icing the F28 with an engine running.

The case later became a standard example in aviation human-factors training. The Moshansky report traced how scheduling pressure, equipment faults and company practices combined to shape the crew's decision to depart.

#5437. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
