#5436. How to spot carbon monoxide poisoning and keep your home safe this winter

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms and prevention steps explained, from flu-like warning signs to alarm placement, generator safety and what to do if an alarm sounds this winter

Carbon monoxide is a poison the human body has no way to sense. A person cannot see it, smell it or taste it. It gives no warning before it starts to cause harm. That makes protection a matter of equipment and habits rather than instinct.

The gas forms whenever a fuel burns without enough oxygen to burn completely. Natural gas, propane, oil, wood, charcoal and gasoline can all produce it. A furnace, a water heater, a fireplace, a portable generator and a car engine are all possible sources inside or next to a home.

Winter concentrates those sources. Furnaces, boilers and fireplaces run for hours at a time when temperatures drop. Windows stay shut and doors stay closed to hold in heat. Less fresh air moves through the house as a result. Snow can pile up against exterior vents and cover tailpipes. Storms that knock out power push households toward portable generators, camp stoves and grills — equipment built to run outdoors, not in a garage or living room.

The early effects are easy to misread. A dull headache, dizziness or nausea on a cold evening can look like a seasonal bug. People who assume they are coming down with something often stay home to rest. That keeps them in the same air that is making them sick.

A working grasp of carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms and prevention comes down to a few practical habits. One is knowing how the warning signs differ from an ordinary illness. Another is putting working CO alarms in the right places and checking them on a schedule. The rest involves keeping fuel-burning equipment maintained, properly vented and used only where it was designed to operate.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of key points for the cold months. They begin with how poisoning shows up in the body and why the gas is so hard to notice. They then move through detector placement and testing, generator safety, grills and stoves, annual appliance servicing, blocked vents and chimneys, and car exhaust in garages. The final slide explains what to do if an alarm goes off or someone in the home starts to feel unwell.

Headache, dizziness, weakness and an upset stomach are the most common early signs of carbon monoxide poisoning. As exposure continues, vomiting, chest pain and confusion can follow.

These complaints overlap heavily with a winter cold or flu. Temperature is one useful difference. The flu usually brings a fever, while carbon monoxide poisoning typically does not. A household full of flu-like symptoms with normal thermometer readings deserves a second look.

Mistaking these signs for an ordinary illness is what makes the early stage risky. A person who blames a headache on a virus has no reason to leave the building. Every extra hour in contaminated air prolongs the exposure.

Confusion adds another layer of risk. Someone who is thinking less clearly may not connect the symptoms to their surroundings. They may also find it harder to decide to leave. That makes the earliest signs the best moment to act.

The most useful clue is a pattern rather than any single symptom. A virus tends to pass from one person to the next over a period of days. Carbon monoxide affects everyone breathing the same air at roughly the same time. Several people in one home feeling unwell at once points toward a shared environmental cause.

Pets offer a similar signal. A dog or cat that appears sick alongside its owners is breathing the same indoor air. Illness that shows up in people and animals in one home at the same moment is a reason for suspicion.

Location and timing provide the second clue. Symptoms from carbon monoxide often ease after a person leaves the building. They can return once that person comes back inside. Someone who feels fine at work or school but gets a headache each evening at home has a pattern worth noting.

The onset of symptoms can also point to a source. Symptoms that begin soon after the furnace starts up for the season, or that feel worst near a fireplace or other fuel-burning appliance, suggest a household cause rather than an infection.

Treating a sudden, shared, fever-free illness as a possible exposure rather than a bug gives a household the chance to get out while symptoms are still mild.

Carbon monoxide has no color, no odor and no taste, so a person cannot sense it building up in a room. It is a product of incomplete combustion.

Complete combustion turns the carbon in fuel into carbon dioxide. That process needs a steady supply of oxygen. A flame may be starved of air, poorly adjusted or burning in a cramped space. In those conditions, some carbon bonds with only one oxygen atom instead of two. The result is carbon monoxide, often shortened to CO.

Nothing about the gas gives it away. It does not sting the eyes or irritate the throat the way smoke does. It produces no haze. The rotten-egg smell many people associate with a gas problem comes from an odorant that utilities add to natural gas. Carbon monoxide carries no such warning. A home can smell normal while CO levels climb.

Once inhaled, the gas passes from the lungs into the bloodstream. There it binds to hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Hemoglobin takes up carbon monoxide more readily than it takes up oxygen. Each binding site occupied by CO is one that cannot deliver oxygen to the body's tissues.

The heart and brain are especially sensitive to this shortage. Both organs need a constant oxygen supply to function. As exposure continues, less oxygen reaches them. That oxygen deprivation is what makes carbon monoxide poisoning dangerous and, in serious cases, fatal.

With no sensory cue to wake them, people who are asleep may have no chance to react. The same is true for anyone intoxicated by alcohol or drugs. Both groups can lose consciousness or die before they recognize that anything is wrong. Exposure during the night, when a household is asleep, carries particular danger for this reason.

Some people face higher risk from the same exposure. Infants and older adults are more vulnerable. So are people with chronic heart disease, anemia or breathing problems. Each of those conditions already limits how much oxygen the body can take in or deliver. That leaves less margin when carbon monoxide displaces oxygen in the blood.

Carbon monoxide alarms belong on every level of a home and outside each separate sleeping area. A home with bedrooms on two floors, or a bedroom wing set apart from the main living space, needs coverage in each of those places.

The sleeping-area rule exists because people are most vulnerable at night, when symptoms go unnoticed. An alarm in the hallway just outside the bedrooms sits where it can wake the people sleeping there. Where bedrooms sit at opposite ends of a house, one hallway alarm may not cover both. A closed bedroom door can also muffle an alarm mounted farther away.

The every-level rule covers the places where fuel-burning equipment tends to sit. Furnaces, boilers and water heaters are often in basements or utility rooms, out of sight and far from bedrooms. A basement counts as a level and needs its own alarm, as does a finished attic or upper floor.

Smoke alarms do not detect carbon monoxide. A house fitted with smoke alarms in every room can still have no protection against CO. Combination smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are available and can handle both jobs from one mounting point. The label or packaging states which hazards a device senses. Check it rather than assume.

Mounting height and exact position vary by model. The manufacturer's instructions set those details, which may include how far the unit should sit from appliances. Those instructions are the rule to follow. Do not place an alarm directly next to a furnace, water heater, stove or other fuel-burning appliance.

An attached garage creates a separate concern. Car exhaust can seep from the garage through the shared wall or the connecting door into the house. Placing an alarm in the living space next to an attached garage gives warning if that happens. That room is often a kitchen, mudroom or hallway. Plan coverage there even if another alarm already sits elsewhere on the same floor.

Press the test button on every carbon monoxide alarm regularly, change its batteries as the manufacturer directs and replace the whole unit by the date printed on it. A CO alarm that is dead, expired or untested offers no protection.

The test button is the quickest check. Holding it down should set off the alarm's horn. That confirms the device has power and can make a sound loud enough to hear. On many models, the button checks the battery, circuitry and sounder rather than exposing the sensor to carbon monoxide gas. That is one reason the expiration date matters as much as a passing test.

Never try to test a detector with car exhaust, a lit grill or any other real source of carbon monoxide. Doing so puts the person holding the alarm at risk. The test button and the steps in the manufacturer's manual are the methods a homeowner should use.

Carbon monoxide alarms wear out. The sensor inside degrades over time, and an aging unit may stop responding reliably even if its lights still come on. Manufacturers set a service life for each model and print the replacement date on the unit itself. That date often appears on a label on the back or side. Lifespans differ between brands and models, so the label is the figure to trust, not a general rule of thumb. When a combination smoke and carbon monoxide alarm reaches its date, the entire unit needs replacing.

Batteries need their own attention. Some alarms run on standard replaceable batteries. Others plug into an outlet or are hardwired, with a battery as backup during a power cut. Some models have a sealed battery meant to last the life of the unit, and those are replaced whole. The manual explains which type a home has and how often to change the battery.

The sound an alarm makes also carries information. An intermittent chirp usually signals a low battery or an alarm that has reached the end of its life. A full, continuous alarm is different. It means the device has detected carbon monoxide at a dangerous level. Treat that sound as an emergency, not a malfunction. Exact sound patterns vary by manufacturer, and many units print a guide on the label.

Linking checks to a fixed point on the calendar makes them easier to remember. One option is the start of the heating season. Another is the weekend the clocks change in places that observe daylight saving time. Checking the printed replacement date at the same time catches an expired unit before winter sets in.

A portable generator must never run inside a home, garage, basement or crawlspace. Opening doors or windows does not make indoor use safe. The machine belongs outdoors every time it runs.

A portable generator is driven by a small fuel-burning engine. Like a car engine, it burns fuel and pushes out exhaust as it runs. That exhaust contains carbon monoxide. In an enclosed or partly enclosed space, the gas builds up faster than outside air can replace it.

An open door or window changes little. Air does not move through a building in a steady stream that carries exhaust away. The gas collects in rooms and corners instead. A garage with its door raised still has three walls and a ceiling to hold it in. Fans do not prevent the buildup either.

The CDC advises setting a generator up outdoors, well away from windows, doors and vents. That distance keeps exhaust from drifting back into the house. A unit parked just outside a kitchen window or beside an air intake can still send carbon monoxide indoors. Wind can also push exhaust toward an opening the operator did not consider. The owner's manual for each model gives the manufacturer's own placement guidance.

Winter storms are a common time for generator-related poisonings. Ice and heavy snow bring down power lines, and some outages last for days. Households turn to a generator to keep a furnace, refrigerator or lights running. Cold, wind and snow make working outdoors harder. That pressure leads some people to run the unit in a garage, a shed or an enclosed porch.

Planning before a storm removes the need to improvise during one. Choose an outdoor spot ahead of the season, on level ground and clear of the home's doors, windows and vents. Keep a path to it shoveled when snow falls. Some manufacturers make covers or tents that shield a generator from rain and snow. Use only one the manufacturer approves for that model, and never one that encloses the engine.

Outages also affect the alarms meant to catch a problem. A carbon monoxide alarm that plugs into a wall outlet with no battery backup stops working when the power fails. A battery-powered or battery-backup unit keeps working during the hours a generator is most likely to be running.

Charcoal grills, gas grills, camp stoves and propane heaters built for outdoor use should never run inside a house, tent, garage or camper. Each one releases carbon monoxide as it burns, and an enclosed space traps that gas.

A grill on the patio or a camp stove in the hall closet can look like a quick fix for a cold house or a meal without electricity. Bringing that equipment inside turns it into a CO source with nowhere for its exhaust to go.

Outdoor cooking gear is designed on the assumption that open air will carry combustion gases away. Indoors, the exhaust stays in the room. Burning fuel also draws down the oxygen in a closed space. As oxygen falls, the flame burns less cleanly and gives off more carbon monoxide.

Charcoal carries its own hazard. Briquettes keep giving off carbon monoxide after the flames die down and the coals are only glowing. A grill that looks finished can still be releasing gas. That rules out moving a cooling grill into a garage, an enclosed porch or a tent to use its leftover warmth. The safer step is to let it burn out and cool completely outside, well away from the house.

Tents, campers and small cabins hold far less air than a house. Carbon monoxide can reach harmful levels in them faster as a result. Camp stoves and grills belong outside the shelter, including on cold nights at a campsite or during a winter cabin trip.

Portable propane heaters differ by design. Some models are labeled for indoor use, and others are made for outdoor use only. The product label and the manufacturer's instructions set where a heater can operate. A unit marked for outdoor use stays outdoors, whatever the temperature.

The kitchen stove is the household version of the same mistake. Gas ovens and stovetops are built for cooking, not for heating a home. Leaving the oven door open or running burners for warmth keeps a combustion appliance going far longer than intended. Its exhaust then spreads through the living space.

During an outage, warmer clothing, extra blankets and closing off unused rooms help hold heat without adding a new fuel source. A public warming center or the home of a friend with power is another option.

The CDC recommends having a qualified technician inspect the furnace, boiler, water heater, gas dryer, fireplace and any other fuel-burning appliance in the home every year. That visit is best scheduled before the heating season begins.

A yearly check matters because carbon monoxide output depends on how well an appliance burns its fuel. Gas, oil and wood need the right balance of fuel and air to burn cleanly. When that balance slips, combustion becomes incomplete. The appliance then produces more CO than it was designed to.

A poorly adjusted burner is one common cause. If a burner receives too little air, the flame cannot convert all of the fuel into carbon dioxide and water vapor. Some of the carbon leaves as carbon monoxide instead. The problem can develop slowly as parts wear or shift. It may bring no obvious change in how the furnace sounds or heats.

A cracked heat exchanger is another fault a technician looks for. In a forced-air furnace, the heat exchanger keeps the burning fuel and its exhaust separate from the air the blower pushes through the ducts. A crack can let combustion gases mix with that household air. The metal heats and cools through many cycles each winter. That repeated stress can open cracks over time.

A faulty connection is the third common problem. Vent pipes, joints and fittings carry exhaust from the appliance to the outdoors. A loose, corroded or separated connection can release exhaust into a basement, utility room or closet before it reaches the flue.

During a typical service call, a technician examines the burners and flame and inspects the heat exchanger. The technician also checks the venting and its connections for leaks or damage. The visit may include a check of how the appliance drafts. That test shows whether exhaust is moving up and out as intended.

Scheduling the inspection in late summer or early fall leaves time for repairs before cold weather arrives. A furnace or boiler that sat idle for months will soon run for long stretches in a closed-up house. Water heaters and gas dryers operate all year, and they belong on the same annual schedule.

A blocked chimney, flue or appliance vent can push exhaust, including carbon monoxide, back into the home. Keep every vent open, and check the exterior ones after each heavy snowfall.

Fuel-burning appliances depend on a clear path to the outdoors. A furnace, boiler or water heater sends its combustion gases out through a flue or vent pipe. A fireplace relies on the chimney. When that path narrows or closes, the gases have nowhere to go. They spill back through the appliance and into the rooms where people breathe.

Three kinds of blockage are common. Snow and ice can bury vent openings on the outside of a house. Leaves, twigs and other debris can collect in chimneys and vent caps. Birds, squirrels and other animals can build nests inside chimneys and flues. A chimney that sat unused through the warmer months is especially likely to hold one.

Snow is a particular risk for high-efficiency furnaces and water heaters. Many of these appliances vent through plastic pipes that exit a side wall rather than the roof. Those openings often sit low on the house, where drifting or plowed snow can cover them. After a storm, walk around the house and find the exhaust and intake pipes for the furnace and water heater. Clear the snow around them by hand or with a brush. A shovel blade could crack the pipe.

The dryer vent needs the same check. A gas dryer burns fuel, and its exhaust leaves through the same duct that carries lint outside. Lint, snow or a stuck exterior flap can all restrict that flow. Make sure the outdoor flap opens freely when the dryer runs.

Openings at roof level matter as well. A chimney cap with mesh sides helps keep animals and debris out of the flue. Before the first fire of the season, have the chimney inspected and cleaned as needed. A chimney sweep can spot nests, soot buildup and liner damage that cannot be seen from the hearth.

Heavy snow on a roof can also cover short vent stacks. If a roof vent is buried, do not climb onto an icy roof to reach it. Call a roofing contractor or the appliance's service company instead.

Never leave a car running inside a garage, even with the garage door wide open. Carbon monoxide from the exhaust can build up in the enclosed space and seep into an attached home.

A gasoline engine produces carbon monoxide whenever it runs. Combustion inside the engine is never complete. Some of the fuel's carbon leaves the tailpipe as CO rather than carbon dioxide. Outdoors, that exhaust disperses into open air. Inside a garage, the walls and ceiling hold it close to the car.

An open garage door does not solve the problem. A single opening gives exhaust no reliable path out, and still air does little to carry it away. Garages attached to a house share walls and doors with the living space, and sometimes ductwork. Gaps around an interior door and openings around pipes or wiring give the gas a route indoors. People inside the home may not realize a car is idling on the other side of the wall.

The safer habit on a cold morning is to back the car out of the garage first. Then let it warm up in the driveway. Close the garage door behind it so exhaust does not drift back in. The same logic applies to a remote starter, which should never be triggered while the car is parked inside.

Snow creates a second hazard outside the garage. A tailpipe packed with snow can push exhaust back under the car and into the cabin, where the driver and passengers breathe it. Before starting the engine after a storm, clear the tailpipe and the area around it. This check matters when a plow leaves a ridge of snow behind a parked car. It also matters when a car is stuck in a drift.

Keyless-ignition vehicles add a quieter risk. Without a physical key to pull out, a driver can walk away from a car that is still running. A modern engine can idle quietly enough to go unnoticed in a closed garage. Before leaving the vehicle, check the dashboard to confirm the engine is off.

If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds or anyone suspects poisoning, get every person and pet out of the building and into fresh air right away. Then call 911 or the local emergency number from outside.

Speed matters more than diagnosis. There is no way to confirm or rule out a problem by walking through the house and checking rooms. Treat every full alarm as real until trained responders say otherwise.

Leave without stopping to hunt for the source, switch off appliances room by room or gather belongings. Each extra minute indoors means more exposure. Help anyone who cannot move on their own, such as small children, if it can be done quickly. Bring pets out as well. They breathe the same air as everyone else in the home.

Opening windows and staying inside is not a substitute for leaving. A few open windows do not reliably clear the gas from the whole house. Whatever is producing it may also still be running.

Make the emergency call from the yard, a neighbor's home or a spot well outside the building, not from a hallway or doorway. Tell the dispatcher that a carbon monoxide alarm went off and how many people were inside. Mention whether anyone feels unwell. If someone is still in the building, say so immediately. That lets crews reach them first.

Do not go back inside until emergency responders say it is safe. Fire crews can measure carbon monoxide levels in the air and look for the source. Going back in early to grab a phone or check on an appliance only adds to the exposure.

Anyone with symptoms needs a medical evaluation, even if they start to feel better outside. Feeling better in fresh air does not mean the gas has cleared from the body. Tell the paramedic or doctor that carbon monoxide exposure is suspected. Its warning signs can resemble other common illnesses.

The standard treatment is oxygen, usually given through a mask. Breathing concentrated oxygen helps clear carbon monoxide from the blood faster than ordinary air does. In severe cases, doctors may use hyperbaric oxygen therapy. In that treatment, the patient breathes oxygen inside a pressurized chamber.

After responders clear the home, do not restart the furnace, generator, vehicle or other equipment suspected of causing the problem. Have a qualified technician inspect it first. A repair at that stage keeps the same fault from causing a second emergency.

#5435. The Pentagon is investigating if rogue freezers are tied to cyberattacks in France. Another wave of hacks is hitting supermarkets across Europe

Lightning may not strike the same place twice, but hackers appear to be targeting the same systems, as refrigeration becomes the next frontier for cyberattacks.

About 20 refrigerator systems in supermarkets Delhaize, Carrefour and Spar experienced outages late Sunday night into Monday morning, Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration installer Sabcobel, told Belgium’s Belga News Agency on Monday. Swedish daily newspaper Aftonbladet reported similar outages in Swedish chains ICA and Coop, with outages also reported in Luxembourg and Estonia.

“We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control,” Moelans said. “We’ve been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network.”

He noted this wave of suspected cyberattacks mirrored the hacking of hundreds of French supermarkets last month, when the temperature of grocery stores’ refrigerators and freezers was raised, spoiling food and causing small fires. Those supermarkets included 80 Carrefour locations, about 24 Monoprix locations, and 150 Intermarche locations.

Hackers left the same calling card in the latest attacks. One location of a Swedish grocery store, ICA Kvantum Sjöbo, said in a Facebook post that its refrigerators and freezers were hacked overnight, and the temperature of the devices were set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit. As a result of the rising temperatures, the location has to throw away the stored food.

“We are extremely sorry to have to throw out all this food, but we see no other way,” the store wrote. “Now we are focusing on getting everything back on track.”

ICA told Fortune the outages were in a limited number of stores using an external supplier with networks outside of ICA’s main network, but the company’s central systems were unaffected.

The European Commission did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment but said in a statement that the incident shows how much cyberattacks can “disrupt services, affect businesses and directly affect citizens’ daily lives.”

In August, half a dozen U.S. military commissaries experienced a similar refrigeration system outage, and the Pentagon is now investigating both the French supermarket outages as well as the commissary outages as a potential cyberattack.

Cybersecurity experts said it was only a matter of time before refrigerators and freezers became the target of hackers. As more appliances become internet-connected, they become more accessible to outside agents, and therefore more susceptible to potential network breaches, Nadiya Kostyuk, an assistant professor at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology, told Fortune.

“A lot of these devices have a lot of really cool features, but the security is not the first priority for them,” Kostyuk said. “Hopefully future inventions will come with more security in mind when it comes to the design, and the existing ones also will be revisited to incorporate all the potential vectors of the cyberattacks.”

Refrigerators in particular tend to use the same devices across commercial chains, meaning finding a weak point in one can expose vulnerabilities across other systems, according to Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University.

The practical features of refrigerators and freezers also make them a target because outages can result in direct and immediate financial consequences, Whyte said. After the cyberattacks in France, two supermarkets, Intermarché and E.Leclerc, reported about €270,000, or $300,000, in combined damages, according to local news outlet Sud Ouest.

“You can’t unspoil food or other products from these freezers. It’s just euros and dollars down the drain,” Whyte told Fortune.

While there’s no official proof these outages are connected, Whyte noted the proximity of the French and U.S. outages to one another as well as the similarities in the systems impacted.

“You’d be silly not to be suspicious,” he said.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5434. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5433. 10 ways to prevent frozen pipes and thaw them safely

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How to prevent frozen pipes with 10 practical steps, from insulating exposed lines and dripping faucets to thawing a frozen pipe safely without an open flame

A frozen pipe usually bursts because of pressure, not because water expands as it turns to ice. When ice blocks a pipe, water gets trapped between the blockage and a closed faucet. Pressure builds in that short section until the pipe gives way. That mechanism shapes the approach to winter plumbing. The goal is to keep water moving, keep cold air away from vulnerable lines and keep pressure from building up.

The risk is not spread evenly through a house. It concentrates in a handful of predictable places. These include pipes in attics, crawl spaces and garages, lines along exterior walls and the plumbing that feeds outdoor faucets. In these spots, pipes sit closest to outside air and farthest from the home's heat. A house can feel warm in every bedroom while a supply line behind a kitchen cabinet stays much colder.

Learning how to prevent frozen pipes is mostly a matter of preparation, and much of it costs little. Some steps take a few minutes before a cold snap, such as opening cabinet doors or disconnecting a garden hose. Others are small one-time projects. Fitting foam sleeves on exposed lines and sealing gaps where cables and vents enter the house both fall into that group. Electric heat cable adds active warmth for pipes that insulation alone cannot protect.

Prevention does not always work. The later slides in this list cover what to do when it fails. That starts with knowing where the main water shutoff valve is before anything goes wrong. Closing that valve quickly is the first step to limit damage when a pipe bursts.

Thawing a frozen pipe carries its own risks. The wrong heat source can start a fire or damage the pipe it is meant to save. The safe methods are slow and simple. They rely on household tools rather than flame. The final slide explains the signs that a frozen or damaged pipe has become a job for a plumber.

Each of the 10 slides below covers one step. Each can be read on its own, whether you are preparing for winter weeks in advance or dealing with a faucet that stopped running on a cold morning.

Letting a faucet drip during a hard freeze is one of the simplest ways to protect a plumbing line. A slow, steady trickle keeps water moving. It also gives the pressure inside the pipe a way out if ice starts to form.

The first benefit is movement. Still water sitting in a cold pipe gives ice time to build up along the walls and close off the line. Water that keeps flowing, even slowly, is harder to freeze. A drip does not make a pipe immune to extreme cold, but it buys time on the coldest nights.

The second benefit matters more for avoiding a burst pipe. A pipe rarely splits from the push of expanding ice alone. The usual culprit is water pressure. Once a plug of ice seals the line, water downstream of it is caught between the ice and the closed tap. Each bit of new ice squeezes that trapped water harder. In time the pipe wall fails under the strain.

This is why a pipe can rupture some distance from the frozen spot itself. The weak section is the length of line between the ice and the shut faucet, where the pressure builds. An open faucet breaks that trap. Even if a blockage develops, the water and pressure in that stretch can bleed off through the tap.

The faucets worth dripping are the ones fed by vulnerable lines. That usually means fixtures on exterior walls and any faucet served by pipes that run through unheated or exposed spaces. Fixtures on warm interior walls rarely need the same treatment.

A drip protects only the supply line it draws from. On a faucet with separate hot and cold handles, water left trickling from one handle does nothing for the line behind the other.

The drip does not need to be heavy. A thin, continuous stream is enough to keep water moving. A larger flow mostly adds to the water bill without adding much protection. The habit matters most overnight and during stretches when temperatures stay well below freezing. Exposed plumbing runs coldest at those times.

A dripping faucet also works as an early warning. If the trickle slows or stops on a cold night, ice may be forming somewhere along that line. That line needs attention before the problem gets worse.

Pipes in attics, crawl spaces, garages and exterior walls are the ones most likely to freeze, and insulation is a direct way to protect them. Foam pipe sleeves and fiberglass wrap both slow the loss of heat from the water inside.

These spaces share one weakness. They sit outside the heated part of a home, or right at its edge. On a cold night, the air around the pipes there can fall close to the outdoor temperature. A supply line in a vented crawl space or along the rafters of an unheated attic has little shielding from that cold. A pipe inside an exterior wall faces a similar problem, with only a thin layer of building material between it and the outside.

Foam sleeves are the usual choice for straight, reachable runs of pipe. Each sleeve is a foam tube slit along one side, which lets it be pressed over a pipe that is already installed. Sleeves come in different inside diameters. The right one fits snugly. A loose sleeve leaves an air gap around the pipe. Many sleeves have a self-sealing adhesive strip along the slit. Others need to be closed with tape. The joints where two sleeves meet should be taped as well, so no bare pipe shows at the seam.

Fiberglass wrap handles bends, valves and fittings, where a straight tube is hard to fit. It is wound around the pipe in overlapping layers. Many fiberglass wraps come with a foil or plastic facing, or are finished with tape, to keep moisture out. Wet fiberglass loses much of its insulating value. The fibers also irritate skin, eyes and lungs. Gloves, long sleeves, eye protection and a dust mask are standard gear when handling it.

Coverage matters as much as the material. Elbows, tees and short exposed stretches near the point where a pipe enters a wall are easy to skip. A gap of bare pipe is where freezing tends to start. Both hot and cold supply lines in an unheated space need covering. A hot water line holds standing water whenever no tap is running. Once that water cools, it can freeze too.

Insulation has a clear limit. It slows heat loss, but it does not generate heat. A wrapped pipe holds its warmth longer than a bare one, which buys time during a cold night. If the surrounding space stays below freezing long enough, the water inside will still cool and freeze. For that reason, insulation works best as one layer of protection rather than a complete fix on its own.

Inspect pipe insulation each fall before the first hard freeze. Rodents, moisture and repair work in an attic or crawl space can tear or dislodge sleeves and wrap. Any damaged section leaves that stretch of pipe exposed and should be replaced or retaped.

Closing the gaps where cables, dryer vents and pipes pass through exterior walls keeps freezing air away from nearby plumbing. Caulk or expanding foam seals most of these openings.

A pipe does not need to sit outdoors to freeze. A steady draft through a small opening can chill one section of a water line far below the temperature of the room around it. That cold spot is often where ice forms first, even in a home that feels warm.

The openings to check are the ones made when a house was wired, plumbed and vented. Cable and phone lines, outdoor faucet supply lines, dryer ducts and plumbing vents all pass through the building shell. Builders cut holes to fit them, and the space left around each one is rarely sealed perfectly. Over time, old caulk can dry out and crack, and gaps can widen.

Basements and crawl spaces deserve a close look. Water lines often run along the rim joist, the framing that rests on top of the foundation wall. Gaps there sit right next to the pipes. On a cold, windy day, holding a hand near a suspected gap or watching a thin strip of tissue for movement can show where air is getting in.

The right material depends on the size of the gap. Caulk suits narrow cracks and small seams. Expanding spray foam fills larger, irregular openings around pipes and cables. Low-expansion foam is sold for window and door frames, where heavy expansion can push framing out of shape.

Some openings need extra care. Seal only the space around a dryer duct, never the duct itself. The dryer has to vent its exhaust outside. Standard foam and caulk should not be used against chimneys or furnace flues. Those openings call for fire-rated sealants made for high heat.

An attached garage is another common source of cold air. Keeping the garage door closed during freezing weather limits the cold that reaches water lines running through the garage or along a shared wall.

Leaving the heat on at a consistent setting is a basic defense against frozen pipes. A thermostat held at the same temperature day and night keeps warmth moving into the walls, floors and cabinets where water lines run.

The reading on a thermostat reflects the air around the device itself. That device usually sits on an interior wall in a lived-in room. Pipes sit somewhere else. They run through exterior walls, under floors and along the edges of a house, where temperatures are lower than the number on the display. The setting on the wall is a starting point, not a measure of how cold the plumbing gets.

That gap matters most at night. Outdoor temperatures typically bottom out in the hours before dawn. That is also when many households program the heat to drop. A deep overnight setback during a cold snap removes heat at the moment pipes are most exposed. Holding the daytime setting through the night during a hard freeze uses more fuel, but it keeps a margin of warmth around the plumbing.

Trips away raise the same issue on a longer timeline. Turning the heat off or down sharply before a winter vacation can leave an empty house cooling for days. A commonly cited guideline is to keep the thermostat no lower than 55 degrees Fahrenheit while away. Treat that figure as a general floor rather than a guarantee. Older homes, drafty layouts and pipes in exterior walls may call for a higher setting.

A steady thermostat only helps if the heating system keeps running. Before a trip, check that the furnace or boiler is working. Confirm that any fuel supply, such as heating oil or propane, will last for the time away. Replace the thermostat batteries if the model uses them. A dead battery can stop the unit from calling for heat.

Asking a neighbor or friend to check on the house during an extended absence adds another layer of protection. A visitor can confirm the heat is still on and spot a problem before it spreads. Smart thermostats that send alerts or allow remote adjustment can serve a similar purpose when the home has a working internet connection.

Inside the house, keeping interior doors open lets warm air circulate into rooms that would otherwise stay cooler. Bedrooms, laundry rooms and bathrooms on outside walls are the rooms most likely to need that shared heat.

Opening the cabinet doors under sinks that sit against exterior walls lets warm room air reach the water pipes inside. The step requires no tools or materials.

The cabinet itself is the problem. A closed vanity or base cabinet forms a small, enclosed box. Its back panel often sits directly against an outside wall, where the wall cavity can get much colder than the room. Household heat has to pass through the cabinet doors to reach the pipes. Closed doors slow that exchange.

Several plumbing parts sit inside. A typical sink cabinet holds the hot and cold supply lines, their shutoff valves and the drain trap. Supply lines often enter through the back of the cabinet. On an exterior wall, that means water may run through one of the coldest parts of the house just before it reaches the faucet.

Kitchen sinks are frequent candidates. Many sit under a window on an outside wall. Bathroom vanities and laundry sinks on exterior walls carry the same exposure. Cabinets on interior walls are less vulnerable because the wall behind them stays closer to room temperature.

Leave the doors open whenever temperatures drop well below freezing, especially overnight, when outdoor temperatures usually reach their lowest point. Pull stored items away from the back of the cabinet so they do not block air from reaching the pipes. Packed rows of bottles, sponges and cleaning supplies can act as a barrier between the room and the plumbing.

That stored material is also the main safety concern. Under-sink cabinets commonly hold drain cleaner, bleach, dishwasher detergent and other household chemicals. In homes with young children or pets, move those products to a high shelf or a locked cabinet before propping the doors open. A child-safety latch offers no protection once the door is left standing open.

This step depends on the room being warm. An open cabinet in a heated kitchen exposes the pipes to that heat. An open cabinet in a cold, unheated room gives the pipes little added protection.

Remove every garden hose from its outdoor spigot before the first hard freeze. Then shut off the water to each spigot from inside the house and drain the line. Outdoor faucets sit on the outside face of the house wall, and the pipe feeding them is among the most exposed in the home.

An attached hose holds water. When that water freezes, the ice can back up from the hose into the faucet and into the pipe behind it. The faucet may look fine from outside while the damage sits inside the wall.

Start by unscrewing the hose and emptying it. Stretching it out on a slope or lifting one end lets the water run out. A drained hose can then be coiled and stored in a garage, shed or basement for the winter. Keeping it out of the cold also protects the hose itself from cracking.

Next, find the indoor shutoff valve for each outdoor faucet. It is usually on the same pipe, a short distance inside the wall. Look for it in a basement, crawl space or utility area. Close that valve. Then go outside and open the spigot so the water left in the line can drain out.

Some indoor valves have a small drain cap on the side. Opening it with a bucket underneath releases water trapped between the valve and the wall. Leave the outdoor faucet open through the winter. Any water that remains in the short section of pipe then has an open path out.

Frost-proof sillcocks offer extra protection, but not complete protection. These faucets have a long stem that places the actual valve inside the heated part of the house. When the handle is closed, water in the stem is meant to drain out through the spout. A hose left connected blocks that drainage. Water stays in the stem, freezes and can split the pipe.

A split in an outdoor faucet line often stays hidden until spring. The leak may only appear the first time someone turns the faucet on, sending water into the wall or basement. Watching the spigot and the indoor pipe behind it during that first use helps catch the problem early.

Electric pipe heating cable, often sold as heat tape, adds warmth directly to a pipe that would otherwise freeze. It is safe only when installed exactly as the manufacturer directs. The product must also be rated for the pipe material and for the location where it goes.

Heat cable fills a gap that other prevention steps leave open. Pipe insulation only slows heat loss. A cable connected to power produces its own heat. That makes it useful on lines in crawl spaces, unheated garages and other spots where the surrounding air stays below freezing for long stretches.

Two main designs are sold for home use. Self-regulating cable changes its heat output as the temperature around it changes. It gives off more warmth as the pipe gets colder. Constant-wattage cable produces the same amount of heat whenever it is on. Many constant-wattage versions rely on a built-in thermostat that switches the cable on as temperatures approach freezing.

The difference matters during installation. Constant-wattage cable generally must not cross over or overlap itself, because the doubled section can overheat. Self-regulating cable is often more forgiving on this point. Even so, the product's own instructions decide what is allowed, not the general category.

Pipe material is the next check. Some cables are approved for metal pipe only. Others are approved for plastic pipe, sometimes with a layer of aluminum tape required underneath to spread the heat evenly. Using a cable on a pipe it is not rated for can damage the pipe or create a fire risk.

Location ratings carry the same weight. A cable made for indoor use may not hold up outdoors or in damp areas. The manufacturer also sets whether insulation can be installed over the cable, and what type.

Choose a cable listed by a recognized testing laboratory, and plug it into an outlet with ground-fault circuit interrupter protection. Inspect it before each winter for cracks, discoloration or a brittle outer jacket. Replace a damaged cable rather than patching it.

Never improvise by wrapping an extension cord or other ordinary electrical cord around a pipe. Standard cord is not designed to heat anything. It lacks the temperature control and safety features built into pipe heating cable.

Locate your home's main water shutoff valve before temperatures drop, and confirm that it turns. If a frozen pipe splits, closing that valve quickly cuts off the supply and limits how much water reaches floors, walls and ceilings.

A burst pipe keeps releasing water for as long as the supply stays on. Every minute spent searching a dark basement for an unfamiliar valve is another minute of water spreading through the structure. Finding the valve on a calm afternoon removes that delay.

The main shutoff usually sits close to the point where the water service line enters the home. In houses with basements, that is often on a foundation wall facing the street. In homes built on a slab or over a crawl space, it may be in a utility closet, a garage or the crawl space itself. It can also sit near the water heater. Some homes in warmer climates have the valve outdoors. If the home has an indoor water meter, the main valve is commonly beside it.

Two types of valve are common. A gate valve typically has a round wheel handle that turns clockwise to close and may need several full rotations. A ball valve has a lever handle that closes with a quarter turn. When it is closed, the lever sits perpendicular to the pipe. Knowing which type is installed tells you what the closed position looks like.

Test the valve before you need it. Older wheel valves can seize after years without use. Forcing a stuck handle during an emergency can break it. If the valve will not move, or leaks around the stem after turning, have it repaired or replaced while there is no crisis.

Many homes also have a second shutoff at the street, often inside a meter box near the curb. That valve generally belongs to the water utility and may require a special key. Check the local utility's rules before operating it.

Once the main valve is closed, open the faucets in the house to drain the water left in the lines. Start with a faucet on the top floor and finish with one on the lowest level. That order lets air in from above and lets water run out below. Flushing the toilets empties their tanks as well.

The same steps help when a home will sit empty during a cold stretch. Closing the main and draining the lines leaves less water in pipes that could freeze while no one is there to notice.

Label the valve with a tag, and show everyone in the household where it is and which way it turns.

Thaw a frozen pipe by opening the faucet it feeds, then applying gentle heat with a hair dryer, a heating pad or warm towels. Start closest to the faucet and work back toward the blockage. Never use an open flame.

The first clue usually shows up at the tap. A faucet that delivers only a trickle, or nothing at all, during freezing weather often sits on a line with ice inside it. The frozen stretch tends to be somewhere exposed to cold air. Pipes along an outside wall or through an unheated area are common culprits.

Open that faucet before any heat goes on. As the ice softens, the melted water needs somewhere to go. An open tap gives it an exit. Once water starts moving through the pipe, the flow also helps melt the remaining ice.

Begin heating at the faucet end of the pipe. Move gradually toward the frozen section from there. Working in this direction lets water from the thawed portion drain out through the open tap rather than collecting behind the ice.

Three common household items handle the job. A hair dryer can be passed back and forth along the pipe. An electric heating pad can be wrapped around it. Towels soaked in hot water and wrapped around the pipe add heat without any electricity. Each delivers gradual warmth rather than intense, concentrated heat. Keep applying heat until full water pressure returns at the tap.

Open flame is off the list entirely. That includes propane torches, blowtorches, kerosene heaters and charcoal stoves. A flame near a pipe can ignite wood framing, insulation or other building materials around it. Intense heat can also damage the pipe itself or cause it to burst.

Electric tools bring their own hazard. Thawing ice produces water, and a weakened pipe can leave puddles on the floor. Keep the hair dryer, the heating pad and their cords away from any standing water.

Once one pipe thaws, check the other faucets in the home. The same cold that blocked one line can freeze others in similar locations.

Call a plumber if you cannot find the frozen section of pipe, cannot reach it or cannot restore flow with gentle heat. Call one right away if you see a crack or a leak. If a pipe bursts, shut off the main water valve first and keep it off until the pipe is repaired.

Finding the frozen section is often the hardest part. It may sit inside an exterior wall, above a ceiling or under a floor. Reaching it can mean cutting into drywall or crawling into a tight space under the house. Opening a wall or floor to get at a pipe is repair work, not a household thaw.

Check every faucet in the house before treating the problem as solved. Pipes near a frozen line may also be cold enough to freeze. A single line can also freeze in more than one spot. If several faucets produce nothing, the blockage may be on a pipe that supplies a larger part of the house. That kind of blockage is harder to trace.

Gentle heat has limits. If a pipe stays blocked after a sustained, careful effort, stop and call a plumber rather than turning to stronger heat.

A crack may not show while the pipe is still frozen. Ice can plug a split, and water escapes only once the ice melts. Watch the pipe closely as it thaws. Look for drips, spraying water, damp patches or stains spreading across a ceiling or wall.

The water meter can also reveal a hidden leak. Turn off every faucet and every appliance that uses water. If the meter keeps moving, water is escaping somewhere in the system.

If a pipe bursts, close the main water valve at once and then call a plumber. Do not turn the water back on until the pipe is repaired. Restoring pressure to a damaged line pushes more water into walls, floors and ceilings.

Keep water away from outlets, appliances and the electrical panel. If water has reached any of them, stay out of the wet area. Shut off power at the panel only if you can reach it without standing in water.

While you wait for the repair, move furniture and belongings out of the wet area and soak up standing water. Photos of the damage and the failed pipe create a record of what happened.

#5432. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon says the best advice he ever got came from his grandmother in his 20s: ‘Don’t be in a hurry’

David Solomon runs one of the most powerful banks on Wall Street, but the best career advice he ever received didn’t come from a mentor in a corner office. It came from his grandmother.

“Don’t be in a hurry,” the Goldman Sachs CEO told NBC News’ Christine Romans in a rapid-fire interview about his daily routine and the lessons that have shaped his career. He said she gave him that advice when he was in his twenties.

The clip came out of Romans’ wider conversation with Solomon for NBC’s Business in America series. That conversation aired Oct. 23, one day after Goldman launched its Small Business AI Institute, part of a new $500 million commitment to its 10,000 Small Businesses program, with Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI as partners. In the segment that ran on Nightly News, Solomon said he’s excited about what AI could mean for businesses and for people’s longevity.

In the lightning round, though, he talked less about markets and more about how he manages his days and his life.

Asked to name three things he does before 7 a.m., Solomon kept it simple: He wakes up, goes to the gym, and generally has a cup of coffee and a protein shake.

He’s in good company. An early workout is a fixture of many executives’ routines, from the Bupa CEO who trains six days a week with his Gen Z son to the many leaders featured in Fortune’s Day in the Life of a CEO series.

The research suggests the habit matters more than the hour. A 2022 systematic review published in the Public Health Agency of Canada’s journal Health Promotion and Chronic Disease Prevention in Canada examined 35 studies. Eleven found morning activity more beneficial; 12 found afternoon or evening activity more beneficial; and 12 found no clear difference. The authors concluded there is no consistent evidence that exercising at one time of day is better for your health than another, and they rated the evidence quality as very low.

Solomon’s best trick for keeping his day on track is unglamorous: sticking to his schedule.

“The one thing that we can’t…get back is time,” he said, adding that he tries to be very purposeful with how he spends it. That means making commitments and keeping them, because, as he noted, it’s easy to drift off schedule.

The science backs him up, with a twist. A 2021 meta-analysis in PLOS One by Brad Aeon, Aïda Faber, and Alexandra Panaccio found that time management is positively linked to job performance. It was even more strongly linked to well-being, especially life satisfaction. In other words, the payoff from guarding your calendar may show up as much in how you feel as in what you get done.

At first glance, “stick to the schedule” and “don’t be in a hurry” seem to pull in opposite directions. For Solomon, they work on different timelines: Be disciplined with the hours in a day, and be patient with the arc of a career.

He repeats this message often. In August, he told Goldman’s summer interns at a town hall that taking more time can open up more opportunities, urging them to “try not to be in a hurry and enjoy the ride.” He offered small-business owners the same counsel about AI at the institute’s launch last week, telling them that “the important thing is to get it right, not to get it quicker.”

Solomon’s patience has a limit, and it’s the things he cares about. Asked whether he has any obsessions, he said it depends on what has captured his interest.

“If I’m interested in something, I get very obsessive about it. I don’t like to do things halfway,” Solomon said. When something grabs him, he added, he tends to go deep.

Psychologists have found that kind of intensity cuts both ways. In a 2007 study in the Journal of Personality, Robert Vallerand and colleagues distinguished between “harmonious” passion, an activity you freely choose that fits with the rest of your life, and “obsessive” passion, which feels compulsive. Obsessive passion predicted deliberate practice and mastery-oriented goals, which supported performance. But it was also tied to fear-of-failure goals that undercut results. Harmonious passion delivered the upside with less of the downside.

The takeaway: Going deep can fuel success, as long as the obsession serves you, not the other way around.

Not every passion turns into a career, of course. Solomon also named one ambition he’s had to let go of: playing professional basketball. He conceded that one isn’t on the table.

#5430. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.
