#5429. From attic insulation to water heater settings: 10 ways to lower winter energy bills

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 ways to cut your heating bill, from thermostat setbacks to attic insulation and duct sealing, target the places homes lose warmth in winter

A heating bill is, in large part, a record of warmth leaving a house. Heated air slips out through gaps around doors and windows. It rises into an attic that lacks enough insulation. It passes through glass at night, leaks from ductwork hidden in crawl spaces and drifts up an open chimney. The rest can reflect equipment working harder than it has to, such as a furnace straining against a clogged filter.

A furnace does not produce heat for its own sake. It replaces the heat a building loses to the outdoors. Every route that loss takes is a place where a household can intervene, and several of those steps need no contractor.

The 10 approaches in this slideshow fall into three broad groups. The first covers controls, meaning how and when a heating system runs. A programmable or smart thermostat can lower the temperature during sleep or time away. A ceiling fan set to spin clockwise at low speed in winter moves warm air that collects near the ceiling back toward the floor.

The second group covers the building envelope, the boundary between indoors and outdoors. Weatherstripping and caulk close drafts. Attic insulation slows the heat that rises toward the roof. Cellular shades, insulated curtains and clear window film reduce what escapes through glass.

The third group covers equipment and daily habits. Regular filter changes keep air moving freely through a forced-air furnace. An annual professional tune-up checks combustion and carbon monoxide safety. Sealed and insulated ducts deliver more heated air to the rooms they serve. A space heater can warm one occupied room while the rest of the house stays cooler, provided it is used safely. Closing the fireplace damper stops warm air from escaping up the flue.

One item addresses a different line on the energy bill. Water heating is a separate household cost from space heating. The same principle of cutting wasted heat applies to the tank and its pipes.

Which ways to cut your heating bill make sense depends on the home. A drafty older house with single-pane windows has different weak points from a newer house with ducts in an unheated attic. Climate, fuel type and heating system all shape which steps matter.

This list is a selection of approaches, not a ranking. Each slide explains how one fix works and what limits or safety points apply.

A programmable or smart thermostat lowers heating costs by dropping the indoor temperature on a schedule while people sleep or are away. The furnace, boiler or heat pump then runs less, and nobody has to remember to turn the dial down.

The mechanism is basic physics. A house loses heat to the outdoors at a rate that depends on the gap between the indoor and outdoor temperatures. When that gap narrows, heat escapes through walls, windows and the roof more slowly. A cooler house loses less energy for as long as the setback lasts. The heating system then has less lost heat to replace.

Longer setbacks have a larger effect than short ones. The overnight hours and the workday are the two long stretches most households can use. A thermostat that covers both on a fixed schedule makes the lower setting automatic every day.

A common question is whether warming a cold house back up cancels out the savings. The energy needed to reheat the rooms roughly matches the energy saved while the temperature drifted down. The house also loses less heat during every hour it sits at the lower setting. That reduced loss is where the net saving comes from. The U.S. Department of Energy publishes guidance on thermostat setbacks that addresses this point.

The two types of device differ mainly in convenience. A programmable thermostat follows a schedule the owner enters, often with separate settings for weekdays and weekends. A smart thermostat connects to home Wi-Fi and can be adjusted from a phone app. Some smart models learn a household's patterns or use a phone's location to detect when everyone has left.

Timing the warm-up matters for comfort. Setting the heat to rise shortly before the alarm goes off or before people return home means the house is warm when it is occupied. It also keeps the setback in place for as long as possible.

Heat pump owners have one extra consideration. Some heat pump systems switch to backup electric resistance heat when recovering from a deep setback. Many thermostats built for heat pumps manage that recovery more gradually to limit use of the backup heat.

Placement also affects how well any thermostat works. A unit on an interior wall reads the room more accurately. One near a drafty door, a sunny window or a heat source can misjudge the temperature and run the system at the wrong times.

Sealing air leaks with weatherstripping, caulk and a door sweep keeps heated air inside the house. Weatherstripping belongs on parts that move, caulk fills gaps in joints that stay fixed, and a sweep closes the space under an exterior door.

Drafts rarely come from one obvious hole. They gather around exterior doors and the sashes of windows that open. They also form around attic hatches and at utility penetrations, the spots where pipes, wires and vents pass through walls, floors and ceilings. Each gap may look minor on its own. As a group, these gaps give warm indoor air many exits, and cold outdoor air moves in to replace it.

Finding the leaks comes first. On a windy day, hold a hand or a lit incense stick near a suspected gap. A cool stream of air, or smoke that bends sideways, marks a leak. Daylight visible around the edges of a closed door points to the same problem.

Weatherstripping suits doors and operable windows because it compresses when they close and springs back when they open. It comes in several forms, including adhesive-backed foam tape, V-shaped vinyl or metal strips and felt. The right choice seals the gap fully without making the door or window hard to shut. A clean, dry surface helps adhesive strips stay in place through the season.

Caulk handles joints that never move. These include the seam where window trim meets the wall and gaps around pipes that enter through exterior walls. Old, cracked caulk should come out before a new continuous bead goes in. Silicone and acrylic latex are common types. The label states whether a product works indoors, outdoors or under paint.

A door sweep covers the gap at the bottom of an exterior door, which frame weatherstripping does not reach. Sweeps are strips of rubber, vinyl or brush, usually fastened along the lower edge of the door's inside face.

The attic hatch needs the same treatment. Because it lifts open, it counts as a moving part. Weatherstripping around its rim stops warm air from slipping into the attic.

Homes with fuel-burning furnaces, boilers or water heaters need enough air for safe combustion. A heating professional can confirm that a large sealing project leaves those appliances adequate ventilation.

Topping up attic insulation slows one of the main routes heat takes out of a house. Warm air rises toward the top-floor ceiling. In an attic with thin or patchy insulation, that heat passes into the roof space and out to the winter air.

Insulation is rated by R-value, a measure of how well a material resists the flow of heat. A higher R-value means more resistance. The rating depends on both the material and its thickness. A deeper layer of the same product delivers a higher total R-value.

The right target is not the same everywhere. Recommended attic R-values vary by climate zone, and colder regions call for more resistance than mild ones. The U.S. Department of Energy publishes recommended levels by zone. Homeowners can match their location to that guidance instead of relying on a single figure meant for every house.

A look into the attic shows whether the existing layer is thin. If the tops of the wooden floor joists are visible, the insulation sits below joist height. That usually means there is room to add more. Gaps, compressed patches and sections pushed aside during past repair work also reduce how well the layer performs.

Two materials are common in attic upgrades. Fiberglass or mineral wool batts are pre-cut blankets that fit between joists. Loose-fill insulation, usually cellulose or fiberglass, is blown in with a machine and settles around wiring and awkward framing. New material can generally be laid over old, as long as the existing layer is dry and free of mold.

Airflow and moisture need attention during the job. Vents at the eaves, called soffit vents, let outside air into the attic, and insulation should not block them. Plastic or foam baffles hold a channel open between the roof deck and the insulation so that air can keep moving through.

Some conditions call for a professional first. Older recessed light fixtures that are not rated for insulation contact need clearance to avoid overheating. Knob-and-tube wiring, found in some older homes, should not be buried under new material. Gray-brown, pebble-like vermiculite insulation may contain asbestos. It should be left undisturbed until a trained professional assesses it.

Anyone working in the attic should step only on joists or on boards laid across them. The ceiling drywall between joists is not built to hold a person's weight.

Closing cellular shades or insulated curtains at night slows the heat escaping through window glass. Opening them on sunny days lets solar warmth into the room. For single-pane windows, clear plastic shrink film adds an insulating layer of air at low cost.

Glass conducts heat far more readily than an insulated wall. On a cold night, a window becomes one of the coldest surfaces in a room. Warm indoor air touches the pane, cools and sinks toward the floor. That cycle pulls heat out of the room. It can also leave people sitting near the window feeling a chill even when the thermostat reads normal.

Window coverings work by placing a barrier between the room and that cold surface. Cellular shades, also called honeycomb shades, are made from fabric folded into hexagonal cells. Each cell holds still air, and still air resists the flow of heat. Insulated curtains do a similar job with thick fabric or a lined backing.

Fit also affects how well a covering works. A covering that leaves wide gaps at the sides or top lets room air circulate behind it and reach the glass. Curtains that hang close to the wall and run to the sill or floor keep more of that air in place. Shades mounted inside a window frame work best when they sit snugly against it.

Timing turns these coverings into a daily routine. Close them at dusk, when outdoor temperatures fall and the sun no longer adds warmth. Leave them closed through the night.

Open them again on sunny days. Sunlight passing through glass warms floors, furniture and walls, which then release that heat into the room. This is passive solar heating, and it requires no fuel. In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing windows receive the most direct winter sun. In the Southern Hemisphere, north-facing windows play that role. East- and west-facing glass collects direct sun for only part of the day. Coverings on those windows can stay open for a shorter stretch.

Shrink film addresses a different weakness. Kits typically include clear plastic sheeting and double-sided tape. The tape goes on the interior window frame, and the film is pressed onto it. A hair dryer then tightens the plastic until it is smooth and clear. The result is a sealed layer of air between the film and the glass, which acts much like a second pane.

That makes film a low-cost option for single-pane windows, which lack the built-in gap of double-pane units. It suits renters and anyone not ready to replace windows. The film keeps a window from opening while it is in place. It belongs on windows that will stay shut for the season, and it is meant to be removed when the heating season ends.

A clean filter and a yearly professional inspection keep a forced-air furnace from working harder than it needs to. A clogged filter restricts airflow, and a tune-up checks combustion and safety, including carbon monoxide risks.

The filter sits in the path of the air the system pulls back from the house before reheating it. Depending on the setup, it slides into a slot on the furnace cabinet or sits behind a grille on a return air vent. As it traps dust, pet hair and other particles, the material gradually fills up. Air then has a harder time passing through.

A forced-air system depends on moving a steady volume of air across its heat source and out through the ducts. When less air gets through, the blower strains. The system then runs longer to deliver the same warmth to each room. That extra run time adds to winter energy bills.

A common habit is to check the filter once a month during the heating season. Pull it out and hold it up to a light. If the material looks gray and caked, or light barely passes through, it is due for a change. Replacement intervals vary by filter type, so follow the schedule the manufacturer prints on the packaging or frame.

The frame also lists the filter's dimensions, which makes buying the right replacement simpler. Most filters carry an arrow showing which way air should flow. That arrow should point toward the furnace, away from the return duct. A filter in the wrong size can leave gaps that let air slip around it.

The annual tune-up covers what a homeowner cannot easily check. A qualified technician inspects how the furnace burns its fuel. The technician also checks whether combustion gases are venting out of the house as designed.

Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless. A problem with combustion or venting can go unnoticed without testing. A carbon monoxide alarm near sleeping areas adds a second layer of protection between inspections. Booking the visit before the first cold snap leaves time for any repair before the furnace runs every day.

Leaky ductwork in a forced-air heating system loses warm air before it reaches the rooms it is meant to heat. Sealing duct joints with mastic or metal-backed foil tape, and insulating ducts that run through unheated spaces, keeps more of that air on its intended path.

Picture a house with a furnace in the basement or garage. Heated air travels through a network of metal or flexible ducts to registers in each room. Every loose joint, gap or disconnected section along the way lets some of that air escape. When the leak sits in an attic, crawl space or garage, the warm air ends up in a space nobody is trying to heat.

Uneven temperatures can hint at duct trouble. A bedroom at the end of a long duct run may stay chilly while rooms nearer the furnace feel comfortable. A common response is to nudge the thermostat up. That makes the whole system run longer to make up for air lost in transit.

Exposed ducts are the place to start. Look along accessible runs in the attic, basement, crawl space and garage. Check for joints that have separated, seams that are open and connections at the registers or the furnace that look loose.

Mastic is a thick paste that is brushed or spread over seams and hardens into a durable seal. Metal-backed foil tape is the other standard option for joints. Ordinary cloth duct tape, despite its name, is not the usual recommendation for sealing ducts. Its adhesive tends to dry out and let go after long exposure to heat.

Insulation is the second half of the job. A sealed duct running through a cold attic or crawl space still sheds heat through its walls. Wrapping those runs in duct insulation slows that loss. Ducts already inside heated living space gain less from insulation. Any heat they give off stays in the house.

Many duct runs are hidden inside walls, floors and ceilings, where a homeowner cannot easily reach them. A heating contractor can assess and seal those sections. Homes heated by boilers and radiators, or by other systems without ductwork, have no ducts to seal. This step applies only to forced-air setups.

Switching a ceiling fan to turn clockwise at low speed in winter pushes warm air that has gathered near the ceiling back down into the room. The fan does not heat anything. It moves heat the furnace already produced to where people actually sit.

Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises and collects in a layer under the ceiling. That layering is called stratification. It is most pronounced in rooms with high, vaulted or cathedral ceilings, and in open stairwells and lofts. In those spaces, the air a few feet above the floor can feel cooler than the air near the top of the room.

Many ceiling fans have a small reverse switch on the motor housing, just above the blades. Some models change direction through a wall control, a remote or a manufacturer's app instead. Turn the fan off and let the blades stop completely before flipping a manual switch.

Direction is judged by standing underneath and looking up. In the winter setting, the blades turn clockwise. At low speed, this draws room air upward toward the ceiling. The warm layer is then displaced outward and travels down along the walls into the living space.

Fan speed also matters. A fast spin creates a breeze, and moving air across skin makes people feel cooler. That wind-chill effect is the reason fans run counterclockwise at higher speeds in summer. In winter, the goal is gentle circulation without a noticeable draft.

The mixing also changes what a wall thermostat reads. A thermostat mounted well below the ceiling measures the air around it, not the warm pocket overhead. Moving that warmer air down narrows the gap between floor and ceiling temperatures.

A ceiling fan still draws electricity while it runs. It does not change the temperature of an empty room. Switching it off when nobody is there avoids using power for no benefit. When the weather turns warm again, flip the switch back to counterclockwise for the cooling breeze.

Setting a tank water heater to 120 degrees Fahrenheit trims a household energy cost that is separate from space heating. The U.S. Department of Energy has suggested that setting for many homes. Insulating hot water pipes and older tanks also cuts the heat they lose while idle.

Water heating runs all year and often appears on the same gas or electric bill as the furnace. It is still a separate load. Turning down the thermostat on the wall does nothing for it.

A conventional storage heater keeps a full tank of water hot around the clock. Heat moves from that water through the tank walls into the surrounding room. The burner or heating element then switches on again to replace it. This cycle is called standby heat loss. The hotter the water is kept, the faster it gives up heat to a cold basement, utility closet or garage.

Incoming water from the main is often colder in winter. That leaves the heater more work to do each time the tank refills. A lower setpoint reduces how far the water has to be raised.

On many gas models, the temperature dial sits on the control valve near the base of the tank. Electric models often place their thermostats behind access panels on the side, and some have two. Power to an electric unit should be shut off at the breaker before any panel comes off. The owner's manual lists the steps for each model. Some dials show labels rather than degrees. A kitchen thermometer held under a hot tap a few hours after an adjustment shows the real temperature.

Pipe insulation deals with a second route for lost heat. Hot water cools as it travels through bare pipe, especially through unheated crawl spaces and basements. Pre-slit foam sleeves sized to the pipe slip over it and close along the seam. Exposed runs near the heater are the easiest to reach. On gas heaters, insulation should stay clear of the flue.

A tank blanket is an insulating jacket that wraps around the outside of the tank. It suits older models with less built-in insulation. Many newer tanks are already well insulated, and the label or owner's manual states whether a blanket is appropriate. On gas units, a blanket must not cover the top of the tank, the burner compartment, the flue or the controls. On electric units, the access panels and thermostat covers need to stay reachable.

A space heater can warm the one room people are actually using while the whole-house thermostat stays at a lower setting. This approach, often called zone heating, trims winter energy bills only when the central system is turned down to match.

The logic comes down to where the heat goes. A central furnace or heat pump warms every room it serves, including guest rooms, hallways and spare bedrooms that may sit empty for most of the day. Zone heating concentrates warmth in an occupied space, such as a home office during work hours or a living room in the evening. Less energy goes into rooms no one is in.

The savings depend on that trade. A space heater uses energy of its own. Running one while the central system holds the house at its usual temperature adds to the total bill rather than reducing it. Zone heating pays off when the heater takes over some of the furnace's work, not when it runs alongside it.

Room size and layout shape how well a portable heater performs. A small unit suits a single room with the door closed. One heater placed on an open-plan floor tends to run constantly without making the larger space comfortable.

Fire safety is the main limitation. Space heaters need clear space around them, away from curtains, bedding, sofas, paper and anything else that can burn. They should be plugged directly into a wall outlet. Extension cords and power strips are not built for a heater's sustained electrical load and can overheat. Many current models include a tip-over switch and automatic overheat shutoff, and buyers can confirm those features on the product label or listing. A heater should be turned off when everyone leaves the room or goes to sleep.

A related idea comes with a caution. Some households try to get the same effect by closing the heating vents in rooms they don't use. In some forced-air systems, closed vents can upset the air pressure in the ductwork. Anyone considering it should ask a heating technician first. Closing vents is not a straightforward substitute for a lower thermostat setting paired with a heater in the occupied room.

A fireplace that is not in use can still pull heat out of a home. Closing the damper whenever no fire is burning stops warm indoor air from rising up the chimney and escaping outdoors.

A chimney is built to carry hot gases up and away from the house. That same design works against a household the rest of the time. Warm air is less dense than cold air. Heated room air drifts toward an open flue and exits through the top. An open damper over a cold hearth turns the chimney into a standing vent to the outside.

The damper is a movable metal plate or flap inside the chimney. Many fireplaces have a throat damper, which sits just above the firebox and is worked by a handle, lever or chain. Some homes have a top-sealing damper instead. It is mounted at the top of the chimney and opened with a cable that runs down into the firebox.

Timing matters in both directions. The damper has to stay open while a fire burns, including while embers still smolder. Closing it too early can send smoke and carbon monoxide into the room. Once the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold, the damper should be shut.

Using the fireplace carries its own heating cost. A burning wood fire needs air to keep going, and it draws that air from the room. Much of that air has already been warmed by the furnace or boiler. It goes up the chimney with the smoke. Colder outdoor air then leaks into the house to replace it.

Several add-ons reduce the loss. Glass fireplace doors close off the opening of the firebox and limit how much room air reaches the flue. An old throat damper that has warped or rusted may no longer seal well. A tight-fitting replacement closes that gap. A chimney balloon or plug is an inflatable or foam device placed inside the flue. It blocks airflow in a fireplace that sits unused for long stretches.

A chimney balloon or plug must come out before anyone lights a fire. Leaving one in place blocks the path smoke needs to leave the house.

Safety checks belong in the same routine. Annual chimney inspection is standard safety guidance for any home with a working fireplace. An inspection looks for blockages, damage and creosote, a flammable residue that wood smoke leaves on chimney walls. It is also a chance to confirm that the damper opens and closes fully before the heating season begins.

#5427. iPhone sales lifted Apple to record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record and Services reached an all-time high, while iPad revenue missed estimates

Apple $AAPL reported record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion on Monday, up 12% from a year earlier, thanks to soaring iPhone revenue and an all-time record in Services revenue.

Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue beat analyst expectations of $113.39 billion, according to Reuters. The quarter ended Sept. 26.

Apple stock barely moved in after-hours trading.

Diluted earnings per share were $2.10, up 14%, including a $0.05 benefit from tariff refunds. Gross margin was 47.9%, including a benefit of about 1 percentage point from the refunds. Analysts expected earnings of $1.99 per share and a gross margin of 47.5%, according to Reuters.

iPhone revenue was $57.58 billion, Mac revenue was $10.79 billion, and iPad revenue was $6.23 billion, the company said. Analysts had estimated $56.54 billion, $9.61 billion, and $6.70 billion, respectively, according to Reuters.

The iPhone figure covers eight days of iPhone 18 Pro sales and excludes the iPhone Duo, which reached stores after the quarter ended, according to CNBC.

"Apple delivered September quarter records for net income and EPS," CFO Kevan Parekh said in a statement. Apple generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter and returned $28 billion to shareholders. Revenue for fiscal 2026 reached $479 billion.

Apple's board declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share, payable Nov. 16 to shareholders of record as of Nov. 12.

Apple raised prices on some iPhone and MacBook models while memory-chip costs climbed, according to Reuters.

"We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," CEO John Ternus told Reuters. "These price increases provided some offset."

Ternus told Reuters that supply of the iPhone Duo trails demand. "Duo is constrained as of today," he said. He said a "very small percentage" of Duo devices were sent back over screen defects, and that Apple is swapping those out for new ones. He added that Apple is "not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance."

Apple had reported June-quarter revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% from a year earlier, in the last quarter under Tim Cook as CEO. Ternus took over on Sept. 1.

#5426. Sweetgreen managers could earn more than $200,000 a year under a new pay plan, as the salad chain bets higher pay will lift sales

A fast-casual chain favored by the office lunch set is sweetening compensation packages for managers at its restaurants.

Starting next year, Sweetgreen managers will be eligible to earn more than $200,000 a year if they meet certain milestones set by the company. The new offering, which will be paid through a mix of base salary and equity, is intended to empower managers who contribute to the business’s success, and “[share] those wins with those that are driving it,” co-founder and CEO Jonathan Neman said.

Under the new incentive plan, Sweetgreen managers (known as “head coaches”) will see their base pay increase by up to 45% if they work at restaurants with higher sales volume. The company declined to specify how high sales need to be to meet this threshold.

When restaurants outperform their sales goals, managers will get a revenue share bonus from the upside, with the percentage increasing based on their tenure in the business. Managers can also continue to receive equity in the company based on their performance.

Base salary increases will go into effect in Q1 of 2027, while head coaches will start to receive bonuses based on store performance on a quarterly basis from Jan. 1, 2027, according to Sweetgreen.

How Sweetgreen is making the case for higher pay. Higher labor and related costs cut into Sweetgreen’s earnings for the quarter ending in June, accounting for 29% of revenue, up from 28% the year prior. Same-store sales and restaurant profits also declined that quarter compared to 2025. (Sweetgreen will report Q3 earnings on Nov. 5.)

Amid such economic pressures, Neman recognized that investing in additional compensation for managers “is definitely a bet.”“But the data supports that if we’re able to attract, retain, and incentivize better head coaches, that they will drive higher sales and better margins,” he added. Neman noted that while Sweetgreen is investing some money upfront to raise managers’ base salaries, most of the investment is contingent on their stores meeting certain performance targets.

“Typically the company would take more of that upside. Now we’re sharing in that upside with our team, but…we think that’s a good trade,” he said.

Zoom out. Sweetgreen isn’t the first fast-casual chain to bet big on its managers. Chipotle announced in 2021 that workers in its highest general manager position could earn $100,000, on average, as it sought to hang onto workers in a tight labor market. The burrito business doesn’t appear to have taken a financial hit from this move, as its restaurant operating margins have stayed between 23% and 26% in recent years. More than 85% of general managers at Chipotle were promoted internally in 2025, according to its 2026 proxy statement.

Neman said Sweetgreen took inspiration from chains like In-N-Out Burger, which recently confirmed that store managers can earn more than $200,000 on average, and Raising Cane’s, which grants monthly bonuses to managers based on sales, and said in 2024 it paid managers up to $175,000 annually.

In addition to business performance, Sweetgreen will be looking at metrics like team member turnover, “head coach stability” (i.e. whether managers stay in their stores), quality and experience scores, and internal mobility to determine whether this incentive program is working, Neman said.

This report was originally published by HR Brew.

#5425. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5424. After topping 2024’s donor list, Elon Musk said he’d do ‘a lot less.’ Since then, he’s given more than George Soros has personally in his lifetime

In May 2025, Elon Musk said he was pulling back from political spending.

“I think in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” Musk said in an interview with Bloomberg at the Qatar Economic Forum. “I think I’ve done enough.”

He then left room to change course: “Well, if I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it,” he said. “I don’t currently see a reason.”

He had just finished the 2024 election cycle as the country’s biggest political donor, according to OpenSecrets. That year, he gave $291.5 million, all to Republicans. The next-largest donor, Timothy Mellon, gave $197 million.

In the 17 months since, Musk has given $427.5 million to federal political committees, according to a Fortune analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 14. That’s nearly $200 million more than George Soros, the man Musk has claimed “astroturfed” anti-Tesla protests. Soros, the Democratic megadonor, has given personally $243.2 million to federal committees in 47 years of FEC records.

Most of Musk’s money arrived after July 1 of this year. SLF PAC, the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, reported a $75 million check from Musk on Sept. 9 and an $83 million check on Sept. 23. Musk has spent more than $200 million to help elect Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, to the Senate, according to a New York Times analysis.

America PAC, the super PAC Musk funds, reported $165.6 million from him between July 1 and Oct. 14, in its October quarterly and pre-general reports. That includes $8 million in in-kind support from United States of America Inc., one of his companies, which America PAC attributed to Musk.

He also gave $20 million on Sept. 4 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republican candidates. And on Aug. 21, his trust gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton, who is running against Democrat James Talarico.

Other counts put him higher. The Times and OpenSecrets rank Musk as the top donor of the 2026 midterms, at $445.6 million for the full cycle (outside of the FEC, a Fortune analysis of IRS filings found he gave $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association on July 6). The Brennan Center for Justice, which counts his company alongside him, puts the total at $483 million.

Soros’s largest personal checks came before July 2026. He gave Democracy PAC II, one of his family’s two super PACs, $125 million in September 2021 and $50 million in November 2022. In the 2024 cycle, he gave $4.2 million personally to federal committees, FEC records show.

Soros has also given $67.8 million to political groups that report to the IRS, including $24.2 million to Justice & Public Safety PAC, according to IRS filings. FollowTheMoney, which compiles state campaign finance records, lists about $70 million more in state and local contributions. Together, that comes to about $381 million, still less than Musk has given since May 2025.

The comparison changes if groups Soros funds are counted. The Fund for Policy Reform, a nonprofit, has given $210.5 million to Democracy PAC since 2020, including $60 million in January 2024 and $50 million in January 2026, but the nonprofit doesn’t disclose its donors. The Times describes it as a channel for Soros family money and notes that Alex Soros, George’s son, is a director. Counting the fund, Soros’s federal total is $453.7 million, more than Musk has given since his remarks.

The Times counts George and Alex Soros together at $103.4 million this cycle and reports that the family’s two super PACs held about $173 million in cash as of mid-October.

Over his lifetime, Musk has given $723.8 million to federal committees, about three times Soros’s personal federal total, according to Fortune’s analysis of FEC filings. Fortune’s analysis counts contributions each man made to federal political committees as reported to the FEC, including in-kind gifts that recipients attributed to them, and excludes duplicate memo entries. Musk’s totals run through Oct. 14, 2026; Soros’s run through Sept. 9, 2026.

Musk’s totals exclude donations to groups that don’t disclose their donors, as well as any money given after Oct. 14.

#5423. How Trump’s trade policy is handing Asia to Beijing

Ted Osius is the former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

For a decade, Washington urged the world’s manufacturers to move their factories out of China and into friendly Southeast Asian states—only to attack the very countries and companies that answered the call.

Usually, U.S. economic statecraft is designed to help American companies succeed abroad. President Donald Trump’s punitive trade program is having the reverse effect. Broad-based import taxes have jolted manufacturers across ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations), including American ones.

Rather than checking China, trade policy is alienating regional partners, harming supply-chain diversification, and eroding America’s influence over the bloc’s trade decisions. The U.S. is engaged in what Evan Feigenbaum, a veteran diplomat and former Republican, terms a “reverse pivot.” Bogged down in foreign crises elsewhere, Washington now projects hesitation and retreat in Asia rather than dynamic leadership.

In the months after President Trump’s April 2025 announcement of “Liberation Day” tariffs, some of ASEAN’s non-tariff barriers fell. A few countries used the exogenous threat to bring about needed reforms.  Deals were done, including Boeing sales and–at least prospective–LNG contracts. It appeared that coercion worked, at least in the short term. In February the Supreme Court struck down much of the initial tariff regime and the administration pivoted to workarounds: 150-day emergency measures under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, and expansive Section 301 investigations into forced labor, intellectual property violations, and “excess capacity.”

America’s labor, intellectual property, and excess-capacity concerns are really about China, not Southeast Asia. The administration substituted an improvised China policy for a coherent Southeast Asia policy—a strategic blunder. By treating regional partners as collateral damage to show that China isn’t singled out, Washington is undercutting its most reliable partners and allies.

Nowhere is the absurdity of this approach more evident than in the supply chains themselves. For nearly a decade, multinational corporations have redirected capital and manufacturing from China into Vietnam, Malaysia, India, and the Philippines. The goal of these “China plus one” strategies was to insulate critical industries from geopolitical risk and move them into friendly states.

Washington’s tariff regime now undercuts this strategy. Southeast Asian export hubs suffer far more than the United States when Chinese firms attempt illicit transshipment, while subsidized Chinese overcapacity squeezes local producers. The broader reality, though, is not widespread evasion but deep and legitimate supply-chain integration. By imposing blanket punitive duties, Washington is tightening the vise on the very partners helping achieve that diversification.

As Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, has observed, Washington created the incentive structure for alternate supply routes and is now penalizing regional partners for using them.

These tariffs aren’t even achieving Trump’s stated goals. Higher costs and a shortage of skilled domestic labor mean production lines won’t magically shift to U.S. shores. Bilateral trade deficits with Southeast Asian economies remain largely unchanged; regional exporters, U.S. importers, and consumers are simply absorbing higher costs.

ASEAN nations have long been masters of dynamic hedging—exemplified by Vietnam’s “bamboo diplomacy”—balancing China against the United States. None of them want to be dominated by Beijing, making Washington their natural partner. Yet as U.S. policy grows increasingly erratic and punitive, it inadvertently pushes them to hedge elsewhere.

As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, the weaponization of economic tools forces middle powers to organize: “If we are not at the table, we are on the menu.”

Coercive tactics failed with Canada, and they will fail in Asia. Recently, politically appointed U.S. ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha told local and international business leaders that he received orders from the President to “bring home the money,” so they needed to double their U.S. investments.  The demand went over like a lead balloon. Capital flows are not surging into the United States; they are pivoting further into Asia.

This friction runs counter to decades of bipartisan precedent. Since the 1985 Plaza Accord, which catalyzed an era of industrial integration in Southeast Asia, American leaders have recognized that regional partners thrive under predictable, rules-based frameworks rather than blunt coercion. Today’s transactional posture risks creating a durable trust deficit that will penalize American enterprise for a generation.

Since America pulled out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership in favor of country-by-country negotiations, its absence at the table has been filled by others. ASEAN is now building institutional networks that bypass Washington altogether. Member states are working with accords like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

American companies have not forgotten the benefits of clear rules of the road in a multilateral context. They have worked closely with ASEAN negotiators toward the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). Spanning 11 nations, nearly 700 million consumers, and an estimated $2 trillion digital marketplace, DEFA would establish comprehensive standards for cross-border data governance, cybersecurity, digital identity, and artificial intelligence.

As Washington retreats behind tariffs and procedural disputes, Southeast Asia—with input from U.S. companies—is writing the regulatory architecture of the 21st-century digital economy.

Washington builds walls while ASEAN builds architecture.

Southeast Asia does not wish to decouple from the United States. Four ASEAN nations—Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore—rank among America’s top 20 bilateral trading partners. Private enterprise, investment flows, and educational links remain extraordinarily resilient.

But in statecraft, trust is the ultimate currency. U.S. influence in the Indo-Pacific was never sustained through sheer market size or coercive leverage alone; it thrived because Washington offered an institutional vision grounded in mutual benefit and reliable rules. If Washington continues to treat its Asian partners as transactional pawns in a zero-sum struggle with Beijing, it will discover they have other trading partners. America risks economic isolation and strategic diminishment in the century of the Pacific Rim.

#5422. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5421. There is a Preparedness Paradox Facing America’s Small Businesses

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

There is often a wide gap between how prepared small businesses feel and how ready they actually are. Here’s how to close it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When disaster strikes, assumption is the greatest vulnerability. While many business owners feel confident they can weather an emergency, genuine operational readiness requires more than optimism — and closing that gap starts with simple, actionable steps you can take today to shore up your resilience.

A reliable network is the foundation of any disaster response plan. If a storm takes out a fiber line or a cell tower, a single internet connection means a single point of failure and that failure cascades fast: payments stop processing, orders go unfilled, customers can’t reach you. Backup connectivity solves that. Whether it’s fixed wireless or a mobile hotspot, businesses can continue to operate when primary lines are down. Backup connectivity is one of the easiest, most-affordable protections small businesses can buy, and often one of the most overlooked.

Files sitting in the cloud can look perfectly fine and still turn out to be corrupted, unreadable or even locked behind credentials that expired months ago. The toughest part is that you won’t discover any of that until the moment you actually need them, which is the worst possible time to find out.

But having a backup is only half the job. Testing your backups tells you something just as important: how long a full restore actually takes. If the answer is three days, that’s three days your business isn’t operating, and you’d want to know that now rather than in the middle of a crisis.

Set up automated cloud-based backups for your business records, customer data and financial information, then schedule a test restore at least once a quarter. A data backup you’ve never tested is a backup you can’t count on.

In an increasingly digital world, investing in cybersecurity is a must, even for small businesses that operate mostly in the physical world. Do you use card readers, store customer information, or manage inventory through software? If so, your business is vulnerable. And disasters make it worse. When systems go down and attention is elsewhere, bad actors move in, betting on the confusion.

The good news is that small business cybersecurity solutions now include AI-powered security tools. These AI tools monitor for unusual activity and flag threats in real time without requiring dedicated staff to watch a dashboard, meaning that you can be alerted automatically to fix vulnerabilities before they’re exposed.

Even when you test backups, incorporate cybersecurity and invest in a reliable network, disasters can introduce unforeseen variables. In other words, even the most foolproof plan may not hold up in the face of a disaster. What separates businesses that recover quickly from those that don’t is often just knowing who to call. When the power is out and your phone is backlogged with messages and missed calls, that’s not the moment to figure out who tells your employees not to come in, who reaches out to your customers or who calls the vendor expecting a delivery.

Decide now who contacts employees, customers and vendors when disaster strikes. Document it, share it with your employees, and keep a copy accessible outside of your primary office or system. A clear communications protocol before a disaster is as important as any technical solution.

Ask yourself a hard question: if you had to close tomorrow, how long could you keep paying your people? About a third of small business owners surveyed said the answer is weeks, not months. Relief funding for small businesses exists, but it’s not guaranteed and it rarely arrives quickly.

Know your number now, and decide whether a line of credit or a dedicated emergency fund could bridge the gap between the day you close and the day you reopen.

Hurricanes present different challenges than wildfires do, and natural disasters vary by region. Yet many business owners never map out the hazards common to their geographic area until an emergency is already unfolding.

Knowing your risk profile is what makes every other step on this list actionable. It tells you what kind of insurance you need, whether your backup power needs to run for hours or days, and whether your continuity plan should assume you’ll be operating remotely for a week or a month. It also tells you what you can reasonably expect from your local infrastructure.

Visit Verizon’s Small Business Digital Ready platform to start your preparedness journey today. Explore new courses that can help identify your risks and build your business continuity and mitigation plans. Additionally, completing one of these courses will unlock the opportunity to apply for a competitive $5K grant through the US Chamber of Commerce Foundation’s Readiness for Resiliency program to help prepare your business before disaster strikes.

From there, the rest gets easier: explore backup connectivity options, schedule a test restore of your data, research AI-powered security tools that fit your budget, and write down who does what when something goes wrong.

Disaster preparedness isn’t just insurance. It’s an investment in the longevity of the business you’ve spent years building and in the community that counts on it being there.

When disaster strikes, assumption is the greatest vulnerability. While many business owners feel confident they can weather an emergency, genuine operational readiness requires more than optimism — and closing that gap starts with simple, actionable steps you can take today to shore up your resilience.

A reliable network is the foundation of any disaster response plan. If a storm takes out a fiber line or a cell tower, a single internet connection means a single point of failure and that failure cascades fast: payments stop processing, orders go unfilled, customers can’t reach you. Backup connectivity solves that. Whether it’s fixed wireless or a mobile hotspot, businesses can continue to operate when primary lines are down. Backup connectivity is one of the easiest, most-affordable protections small businesses can buy, and often one of the most overlooked.

The toughest part is that you won’t discover any of that until the moment you actually need them, which is the worst possible time to find out.

#5420. Palantir’s posts ‘highest-ever’ revenue growth rate of 96% to $2.3 billion as investors’ patience rests on a hair trigger

Palantir Technologies said Monday that third quarter revenue rose 96% year over year to $2.3 billion, surpassing last year’s 63% growth and $1.2 billion in revenue. Chief financial officer David Glazer called it the “highest-ever” reported year-over-year growth rate as well as the highest ever sequential revenue growth rate of 20%. Moreover, quarterly revenue crossed the $2 billion milestone marker for the first time.

It raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, roughly 91% growth, from as high as $8.2 billion a quarter ago. However, investors didn’t seem swayed immediately. In after-hours trading shares began to climb, rising about 1.5% immediately after the figures were published, before dropping 3.6%.

In the third quarter, Palantir reported adjusted and GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents. That compares to third quarter 2025, when adjusted EPS was 21 cents and GAAP EPS was 18 cents. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.18 billion and adjusted earnings of 41 cents per share.

In his quarterly letter to investors, CEO Alex Karp touted the firm’s results, writing “it would be an understatement” to say Palantir’s results in Q3 “were extraordinary.” He said the company’s growth rate of 96% was “absolutely striking.” Palantir had guided revenue to roughly $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion.

Palantir’s quarterly results came after last week’s bloodbath in certain tech stocks, and served as something of a temperature read on the AI trade. Karp made no bones about the change he sees on the horizon and how it could demolish certain sectors.

“Every industry in the world—from banks to insurers to hospitals and even once-storied law firms—will either be remade or set briskly aside,” wrote Karp. He continued his aggressive optimism about the company he helped found in 2003 with investor Peter Thiel and others as the quarterly call with analysts got underway.

Karp said Palantir’s quarterly earnings calls have grown beyond its financial results to serve as “the focal point of tech, society, and general trends.” He said Palantir’s earnings calls, streamed on YouTube, are “by far the most-watched earnings calls in the world.”

The software maker has become a bellwether for public market confidence in AI software converting into revenue growth. Its latest financials come days after Alphabet suffered its worst one-day drop on record in its 22-year history as a public company. Disappointing reception to Amazon and Intel last week deepened concerns that relentless spending on AI—which is approaching $2 trillion in two years, according to S&P Global research—is sprinting well ahead of returns for investors. Google parent Alphabet lost $505 billion in market value since it published third-quarter figures last week and Intel’s stock dropped about 29% last week. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 1% Monday and the benchmark is down 4% over the past five days.

At Palantir, investors keep a gimlet eye on U.S. commercial revenue as evidence that companies as well as governments are willing to pony up for AI software. That business grew 148% to $984 million, compared to $397 million a year ago.

And for the first time, U.S. commercial revenue skipped ahead of U.S. government revenue, clocking in at $984 million versus $953 million. U.S. government revenue grew to $953 million, up 96% from $486 million a year ago.

Meanwhile, total contract value rose 6% to $2.9 billion and U.S. commercial contract value grew 11% to $1.5 billion.

For the current quarter, Palantir forecast revenue of roughly $2.64 billion to $2.65 billion, or about 88% growth at the midpoint. Analysts expected about $2.46 billion. Fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance also rose to 91% year over year growth, and U.S. commercial revenue guidance rose to 143%.

The backdrop for Palantir is markedly different from its second quarter results in August even though Karp’s tone this quarter is just as ebullient as he was three months ago. This quarter, as last quarter, the $430 billion tech firm’s own quarterly release to investors said its results were “crushing consensus expectations.”

Karp maintained the same tone throughout the call and in response to a question for tech bull Dan Ives, said potential clients seek out Palantir because they’re concerned about their intellectual property and getting value from it. He compared it in various ways to types of romantic relationships. He said “warm leads” now turn quicker into “hot leads” the way a first date can progress further romantically.

“We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team kind of thing,” he continued. “I mean, not that I did that.”

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5418. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5417. Apple outpaces sales expectations as it continues to battle surging memory chip costs

Apple beat its quarterly financial expectations in Chief Executive John Ternus’s first earnings report since taking over Tim Cook’s post in September, though the company continues to be pressured by a surge in memory chip costs.

The iPhone maker posted revenue of $114.5 billion in its fiscal fourth-quarter, up 12% year-over-year and above Wall Street targets. Its profit was $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per share.

Ternus extolled the company’s expanding line up of products during a conference call with analysts, including the all-important iPhone business, which grew 17%, to $57.58 billion, in the three months ended September 26.

Apple said that it expected overall revenue to grow between 7% and 10% year-over-year in the current, holiday quarter, seasonally Apple’s strongest quarter of the year. The forecast suggests a range of $153.8 billion to $158.2 billion, compared to the $153.2 billion that analysts were expecting. But the outlook for profit margins seems to have left investors cold.

Shares of the $4.9 trillion company fell as much as 4% in after hours trading on Monday, before recovering some ground to trade down 2.7%.

Many investors have been watching the impact of rising memory chip prices on Apple and how it will weigh on profit margins. To help offset what Ternus described on Monday’s call as an “unprecedented” situation in the memory market, Apple has raised prices across its product line. Apple’s gross margin weighed in at 47.9% in the recently ended quarter, landing near the high end of its forecast range and above the 47.2% gross margin it posted in the year-ago period. But Apple’s CFO said the margins had been bolstered by tariff refunds, without which, the gross margin would have been roughly one percentage point lower.

For the current, holiday quarter, Apple said it expected gross margins to decline, ranging between 45% and 46% due to rising memory costs and some costs associated with ramping up its Siri AI service.

Ternus has marked his first couple of months at Apple with a slew of product releases that have helped the engineer savant show off Apple’s latest innovations and ease into the new job. That has included the September launch of the foldable iPhone Duo, followed by new home products, and last week’s unveiling of Apple’s first touch screen MacBook Pro.

Ternus said in a written statement that iPhone revenue reached a September quarter record and Services posted an all-time high, “capping off our best fiscal year ever.”

“We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” he said. “Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.”

Apple’s Services revenue, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, was $31.57 billion, up roughly 10% year-over-year. But sales in the company’s iPad business and its wearables business both declined.

Apple’s earnings followed financial reports from its Big Tech peers. Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon all revealed their latest earnings in the last two weeks. While the companies generally had positive results, shares in the Nasdaq Composite have sunk in recent days as investors have weighed Big Tech’s positive growth, especially in cloud-computing demand for AI services, against the hundreds of billions Microsoft, Amazon, and others are spending in AI infrastructure.

#5416. Burger King’s Kids’ Meal Sales Are Up 40%. Here’s Why Kids Aren’t the Only Ones Ordering Them.

Sure, upgraded nuggets and an anime tie-in helped, but the company’s president sees another trend emerging.

Burger King’s kids’ meals are all the rage — and not only with kids. Sales of the King Jr. meal jumped 40% year over year last quarter, reaching their highest level in a decade, according to Restaurant Business.

The chain credits upgraded chicken nuggets, with sales up 35%, and a themed tie-in with the anime series Dragon Ball Super. Circana data shows adult kids’ meal orders up 28% since 2019, and Technomic finds six in 10 kids’ meal orders happen with no kids present. Curtis can’t say for sure whether GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are fueling the Burger King kids’ meal surge.

The shift comes during a strong year for the chain, with U.S. same-store sales up 8.4% last quarter. Now Burger King is rethinking the King Jr. meal to serve both audiences. “We need to figure out what that looks like so we don’t alienate either side,” Curtis says.

#5415. These Millionaires Have the Cash to Buy a Home. Here’s Why They’re Renting Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For a growing number of wealthy households, renting is a choice to seriously consider.

More millionaires are renting, despite being able to afford homeownership. This group of wealthy renters is choosing a different path on purpose.

According to a recent report from apartment search website RentCafe, millionaire renters are growing at a faster rate than millionaire homeowners. The report qualified individuals from households that have a total annual household income of $1 million or more as millionaires.

From 2020 to 2024, the number of millionaire households renting their homes surged 229%, more than tripling in five years, compared with a 193% increase among homeowners in that same time period, according to RentCafe’s analysis of American Community Survey estimates.

Choosing to rent contradicts a long tradition of treating homeownership as a defining symbol of the American Dream, especially for affluent Americans.

“For a growing number of millionaires, renting is now a deliberate choice,” the report said. “That’s because many prioritize mobility without the commitment of owning a home, as well as the ability to relocate without going through the lengthy process of selling a multi-million-dollar house.”

The report also pointed out that many wealthy renters would rather keep their money accessible and pursue returns in a strong stock market rather than lock their funds into a home.

Most millionaires reach that status with two incomes. According to the report, couples with high earnings account for 75% of these households, while individuals make up the remaining quarter.

RentCafe found that millennials represent the largest share of millionaire renters at 49%. However, Gen Z is the fastest-growing group, with its count rising 46-fold from fewer than a dozen households renting in 2020 to more than 400 in 2024. The report revealed that despite that jump, Gen Z still comprises just 2% of millionaire renter households.

Gen Z “was barely entering the workforce in 2020,” Adina Dragos, RentCafe writer and research analyst, said in an interview with USA Today. She noted that “by 2024, the oldest Gen Zers were approaching 30.”

“Many who struck it big early — through the creator economy, crypto or startup equity — were choosing to rent precisely because their wealth isn’t tied to a traditional career ladder,” she said. “With no employer anchoring them to one place, they have little reason to put down roots.”

According to RentCafe, millionaire renters typically hold lucrative white-collar jobs as chief executives, technology professionals and senior financial managers. These roles offer flexibility about where they live and work.

The group also includes less obvious high earners, such as professors and operations managers. It’s “a sign that the millionaire renter isn’t always who you’d expect,” per the report.

New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles remain major hubs for millionaire renters, but their numbers are climbing rapidly in Texas and Florida.

Houston recorded the fastest growth of any major metro, with millionaire renter households rising from 18 in 2020 to 232 in 2024, a 1,189% increase.

“Granted, 232 households is still a tiny fraction of the Houston metro’s roughly 2.7 million households, but the growth rate far outpaces any other major metro,” RentCafe noted.

More millionaires are renting, despite being able to afford homeownership. This group of wealthy renters is choosing a different path on purpose.

According to a recent report from apartment search website RentCafe, millionaire renters are growing at a faster rate than millionaire homeowners. The report qualified individuals from households that have a total annual household income of $1 million or more as millionaires.

From 2020 to 2024, the number of millionaire households renting their homes surged 229%, more than tripling in five years, compared with a 193% increase among homeowners in that same time period, according to RentCafe’s analysis of American Community Survey estimates.

#5414. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.
